email_papers.title: Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms
email_papers.abstract: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. More details are available on our project page at https://guoweixu.com/mpt/.

Decentralized Agent Swarms

Abstract
The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (
MPT
), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate
MPT
on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. More details are available on our project page at
https://guoweixu.com/mpt/
.
Figure 1:
Learning self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms.
The three panels illustrate successive stages of training within the same agent population. Each shape represents an agent, darker colors indicate progressive parameter updates, and bidirectional arrows depict coordination patterns. Through experience, agents jointly learn how to act and when to participate through bidding. As individual capabilities improve, patterns of participation adapt in turn.
1
Introduction
Building general intelligence has long been a central ambition of AI research. But where does intelligence reside? A prevailing view in modern AI is model-centric: intelligence is contained in the parameters of a model, and progress comes from increasing model size or improving those parameters through training.
In this paper, we explore a different possibility. Intelligent behavior can also emerge from interactions among many simpler agents, giving rise to collective capabilities that no single agent possesses. This perspective echoes Minsky’s Society of Mind
(
Minsky, 1986
)
, which explains intelligence through the organization and interaction of many individually limited components.
Large language model (LLM) agents now exhibit strong individual reasoning capabilities, yet agent swarms remain limited in their ability to organize their own participation and actions toward a shared objective. Existing multi-agent systems typically place models within predefined interaction structures: a manager delegates to workers, a verifier checks a generator, or agents communicate according to a prescribed workflow
(
Hong et al., 2024
;
Du et al., 2024
;
Li et al., 2023
;
Wu et al., 2024
)
. Even when the participating agents are trainable, the orchestration policy that determines which agent acts next often remains fixed throughout training
(
Feng et al., 2026
)
.
This separation overlooks the coupling between individual capabilities and swarm orchestration. Which agent acts in a particular state shapes not only the swarm’s trajectory, but also which agents receive experience and learning signals. As agents improve, effective patterns of participation can change in turn. An agent that should act early in training may become unnecessary later; an action that was previously unhelpful may become valuable after downstream agents improve. Training individual agents under fixed orchestration therefore optimizes only one side of this coupled process. We instead ask:
Can decentralized agent swarms jointly learn to act and self-orchestrate from experience?
Learning self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms poses a joint orchestration and credit-assignment problem. At each turn, agents must determine who should act. When task feedback becomes available, the swarm must also determine how to train the agents whose actions shaped the trajectory. These decisions are coupled: participation determines which agents acquire experience, while learning changes which and how agents should participate in the future.
We therefore introduce market-based post-training (
MPT
), a framework that enables decentralized agent swarms to learn both how to act and how to self-organize their participation. Following
Qi et al. (2026)
, agents compete for opportunities to act through bids that reflect their willingness to participate in the current decision. An economic incentive structure connects these participation decisions with credit assignment, using collective outcomes to improve both action and bidding behavior. As agents become more capable, the swarm learns when to rely on each member, allowing individual capabilities and self-orchestration to evolve together without a central coordinating agent.
We evaluate
MPT
on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Comparisons on these benchmarks show higher training rewards than monolithic post-training, while further analysis reveals that agent participation evolves during learning. To isolate the contribution of self-orchestration, we compare coordination strategies using the same post-trained action policies. On Iron Pickaxe,
MPT
achieves a 63.4% relative improvement in mean episode reward over the strongest alternative, Graph-of-Agents. We further show that both bidding and action benefit from learning, with their joint use yielding the strongest performance. A credit-assignment ablation shows that learned bids also provide more effective action-training signals.
We also examine the reusability, scalability, and robustness of
MPT
. Trained swarms adapt more rapidly than the single-agent baseline to new crafting objectives. Increasing the inference-time population improves pass@3 across crafting milestones without additional training, supporting the scalability of learned self-orchestration. Larger populations also better tolerate occasional agent unavailability. These results suggest that learned self-orchestration supports both reuse across objectives and flexible deployment with varying agent populations.
Our contributions are threefold:
(1) We introduce
MPT
, a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms, allowing patterns of participation to adapt as agents improve.
(2) We evaluate
MPT
on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research, demonstrating gains over monolithic post-training. We further show the benefits of learned self-orchestration, learning both bidding and action, and using learned bids for credit assignment.
(3) We demonstrate the reusability, scalability, and robustness of trained agent swarms: they adapt faster to new tasks, while larger inference-time populations improve performance and robustness.
2
Method
We aim to jointly learn specialized action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Each agent uses its local context to decide how strongly to participate through bidding. Bids determine both which agent acts and how task rewards are allocated across participating agents for learning. We first describe this orchestration mechanism (§
2.1
), then explain how agents learn to act from the resulting credit (§
2.2
) and learn to bid through counterfactual comparisons (§
2.3
).

2.3
Learning to Self-Orchestrate
Figure 4:
Learning to self-orchestrate through counterfactual comparisons.
Starting from the same state, two alternative bids from the same agent induce different turn allocations. The alternative branch is continued from the restored state, and both branches are evaluated, producing returns that determine which bid is preferred. Preference learning then increases the relative likelihood of the bid associated with the better outcome, teaching the agent when to participate.
Learning to self-orchestrate requires feedback about participation: would the trajectory have improved if another agent had acted at the same turn? We obtain this feedback by comparing counterfactual rollouts from the same state, as illustrated in Figure
4
.
We define a turn as contested if the runner-up submits a nonzero bid. The
original branch is the collected trajectory, in which the selected agent
acts at the contested turn. To construct the alternative branch, we restore
the environment and agent states at the contested turn in a replica and
resample the selected agent’s bid up to three times until it falls below the runner-up’s bid, so that the runner-up acts instead. If no such bid is obtained, the contested turn is discarded from bidding training. The
alternative branch is then continued until the episode terminates. Each branch is scored by its sum of environment rewards from the contested turn onward. The bidding response associated with the higher-scoring branch becomes the preferred response

3
Experiments
3.1
Setup
We evaluate
MPT
on decision-making and reasoning tasks spanning embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Each setting uses three agents with complementary roles.
Benchmarks and Models.
(1)
Embodied crafting
: three Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct agents (Logger, Miner, and Smith) specialize in gathering wood, mining resources, and crafting. Starting from an empty inventory in Minecraft MineStudio
(
Cai et al., 2025
)
, they must progress through the crafting chain to obtain an iron pickaxe. Agents receive RGB observations and textual state information, including inventory and recent interaction history. The selected agent issues a language instruction to a frozen STEVE-1 controller
(
Lifshitz et al., 2023
)
, which executes it for 40 game frames.
(2)
Robot navigation
: three NaVILA-8B agents
(
Cheng et al., 2025
)
perform continuous vision-and-language navigation on VLN-CE R2R in Habitat
(
Krantz et al., 2020
;
Anderson et al., 2018
;
Savva et al., 2019
)
. Given a route instruction and an eight-frame window of egocentric observations, the agents coordinate through partitioned action spaces: Turner controls rotations, Mover controls forward movement, and Stopper decides when to stop. Episodes contain at most 64 decisions.
(3)
Deep research
: three
gemma-4-E2B-it
agents
(
Team et al., 2026
)
answer questions by browsing a searchable document corpus. Searcher, Opener, and Finder specialize in
browser.search
,
browser.open
, and
browser.find
; all agents share the interaction history and may submit a final answer. We use OpenResearcher
(
Li et al., 2026
)
for training. Episodes contain at most 64 decisions and receive a binary terminal reward based on answer correctness, assessed against the reference answer by a
qwen3.5-flash
judge.

All agents have independent model parameters and undergo a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) cold start before post-training. Each agent in
MPT
is fine-tuned on demonstrations corresponding to its role. We compare
MPT
against a monolithic REINFORCE baseline with a discount factor of
γ

3.3
Analysis
3.3.1
Self-Orchestration Evolves during Training
To examine how self-orchestration develops through learning, we track agent participation on the Iron Pickaxe task across four checkpoints: after SFT but before RL, at two intermediate stages of RL, and after RL. Figure
6
plots the participation proportions of the Logger, Miner, and Smith against decision step.
Before RL, the Logger dominates throughout the episode, while the Miner and Smith participate infrequently. As training progresses, this pattern changes: the Logger remains predominant at early steps, but its share decreases later as the Miner and Smith become more involved. This shift becomes more pronounced after RL, with the Miner approaching the Logger’s participation level toward the end of the episode. At decision step 120, the Logger’s participation share decreases from approximately 80% before RL to 45% after RL, while the Miner’s share increases from approximately 10% to 40%. The Smith’s share also increases from approximately 10% to 15%. These observations provide behavioral evidence that the swarm adapts its allocation of acting turns during training.
Figure 6:
Self-orchestration evolves during training.
Participation proportions of the Logger, Miner, and Smith on Iron Pickaxe. From left to right: after SFT and before RL, two intermediate RL checkpoints, and after RL. As training progresses, participation increasingly shifts toward the Miner and Smith at later decision steps.
3.3.2
Comparison between Self-Orchestration and Other Coordination Strategies
We evaluate whether learned self-orchestration coordinates agents more effectively than alternative inference-time strategies. We keep the post-trained action policies fixed and compare our bidding mechanism with Round-Robin
(
Wu et al., 2024
)
, AgentNet
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
, and Graph-of-Agents (GoA)
(
Yun et al., 2026
)
. All configurations are evaluated on the Iron Pickaxe crafting task over the same 32 seeds.
As shown in Table
2
(left),
MPT
substantially outperforms all three baselines. Specifically,
MPT
achieves a mean episode reward of
41.5
41.5
, compared with
25.4
25.4
for GoA, the strongest alternative coordination strategy, which corresponds to a 63.4% relative improvement. These gains demonstrate that learned self-orchestration coordinates agents more effectively.
3.3.3
Both Bidding and Action Benefit from Learning
In this section, we show that training effectively improves both the action policy and self-orchestration. To verify this, we examine their contributions through four inference-time configurations, independently using either the initial or post-trained checkpoints for each component. We evaluate each configuration over the same 32 seeds and report mean episode reward in Table
2
.
As shown in the table, using post-trained checkpoints for both components substantially outperforms all other configurations, whereas using a post-trained checkpoint for only bidding or only action yields smaller improvements over the initial baseline. Using post-trained checkpoints for both components yields a mean reward of 41.5, compared with 21.5 for trained bidding with initial actions and 27.2 for initial bidding with trained actions. The fully post-trained configuration achieves 2.69 times the reward of the initial configuration, which obtains 15.4. These results indicate that strong action and bidding policies are both essential for effective self-orchestration.

3.4
Reusability, Scalability, and Robustness
Reusing learned self-orchestration.
To support a growing range of tasks, agent swarms need to build on previously learned skills and coordination. We investigate whether learned self-orchestration can be reused to accelerate adaptation to new objectives. We evaluate this through continual learning: starting from their Iron Pickaxe checkpoints, we continue training
MPT
and monolithic RL separately on two additional crafting tasks, Torch and Stone Bricks. Figure
8
reports mean episode reward against the training FLOPs.
Figure 8:
Trained swarms adapt faster to new objectives.
Adaptation to (a) Torch and (b) Stone Bricks. Monolithic RL (Single) and
MPT
(Society) start from their respective Iron Pickaxe checkpoints and continue training separately. Curves show mean episode reward against training FLOPs.
The society adapts more rapidly and achieves higher rewards at comparable training FLOP budgets on both tasks. At approximately
10
18
10^{18}
adaptation FLOPs, the society achieves mean episode rewards of about 35 on Torch and 38 on Stone Bricks, compared with 17 and 19 for the monolithic baseline. These results support reusing the trained agent population for efficient adaptation to new objectives.
Inference-time scaling and robustness.
Decentralized agent swarms should scale at inference time. We investigate whether learned self-orchestration enables such scaling through larger agent populations. We vary the population size across 3, 6, 9, and 12 agents by using one to four copies of each trained agent. We conduct experiments on the Iron Pickaxe crafting task over 32 seeds, with three runs per seed, and evaluate pass@3 on five subtasks: Wooden Pickaxe, Stone Pickaxe, Furnace, Iron Ingot, and Iron Pickaxe. Figure
9
shows that larger populations improve performance on all subtasks. Increasing the population from 3 to 12 agents raises pass@3 from approximately 78% to 97% on Wooden Pickaxe, from 69% to 94% on Stone Pickaxe, and from 66% to 91% on Furnace. These results indicate that self-orchestration can effectively utilize additional agents to support inference-time scaling.
Figure 9:
Larger swarms improve inference-time performance.
Pass@3 across five crafting milestones as the agent population increases from 3 to 12.
Another advantage of decentralized agent swarms is that they do not rely on a central agent. This can limit the impact of occasional agent unavailability, which becomes increasingly likely as the population grows. To evaluate this, we introduce agent dropout at inference time and measure the reward under dropout. We conduct experiments on the Iron Pickaxe task over 32 seeds, averaging three runs per seed. Figure
10
shows that larger populations can preserve more capability even under severe dropout. At a dropout probability of
p

0.9

4
Related Work
LLM-based multi-agent systems.
LLM-based multi-agent systems combine role specialization, communication, and memory to support collective behavior. Generative Agents studies emergent social interactions among agents with memory and reflection
(
Park et al., 2023
)
, while CAMEL explores cooperation through role-playing
(
Li et al., 2023
)
. MetaGPT and ChatDev organize software development through structured workflows and specialized roles
(
Hong et al., 2024
;
Qian et al., 2024
)
; AutoGen and AgentVerse provide frameworks for programmable conversations and collaborative agent teams
(
Wu et al., 2024
;
Chen et al., 2024
)
. Multiagent debate improves reasoning through iterative exchange and revision of proposed answers
(
Du et al., 2024
)
. Beyond manually specified workflows, GPTSwarm optimizes graph connectivity
(
Zhuge et al., 2024
)
, AgentNet adapts decentralized routing through experience and evolving connections
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
, and Graph-of-Agents selects agents and refines responses through graph-based collaboration
(
Yun et al., 2026
)
.
However, these systems generally adapt interactions at inference time.
MPT
learns policies through weight updates, allowing agent capabilities and self-orchestration to improve together.
Multi-agent reinforcement learning.
Learning decentralized policies from collective feedback is a central problem in multi-agent reinforcement learning. MADDPG and MAPPO use centralized training with decentralized execution
(
Lowe et al., 2017
;
Yu et al., 2022
)
, while VDN and QMIX factorize team value functions into agent-level utilities
(
Sunehag et al., 2018
;
Rashid et al., 2020
)
. COMA addresses credit assignment through a counterfactual baseline that marginalizes one agent’s action while holding the others fixed
(
Foerster et al., 2018
)
. Coordination is also learned explicitly: RIAL and DIAL learn communication protocols
(
Foerster et al., 2016
)
, CommNet jointly learns continuous communication and control
(
Sukhbaatar et al., 2016
)
, and IC3Net learns when agents should communicate
(
Singh et al., 2019
)
. Recent work extends multi-agent training to LLMs: Multiagent Finetuning updates specialized models using their own interaction data
(
Subramaniam et al., 2025
)
; Dr. MAS stabilizes reinforcement learning through agent-wise advantage normalization
(
Feng et al., 2026
)
; and CoLLM studies centralized and decentralized critics for training decentralized LLM collaborators
(
Liu et al., 2026
)
.
However, these methods do not connect the choice of the next agent with how downstream reward is distributed across agents.
MPT
couples turn allocation and credit assignment through learned bids, using task feedback to jointly improve participation and policies.
Economics in agents.
Economic coordination offers a longstanding perspective on distributed intelligence. Hayek emphasizes how prices communicate dispersed knowledge
(
Hayek, 1945
)
, while Minsky describes intelligence as arising from interactions among individually limited components
(
Minsky, 1986
)
. The Contract Net Protocol allocates tasks through negotiation
(
Smith, 1988
)
, and market-oriented programming uses markets for decentralized resource allocation
(
Wellman, 1993
)
. Economic mechanisms also connect participation to learning: Holland’s bucket brigade transfers credit along chains of active rules
(
Holland, 1995
)
, and Baum’s Hayek Machine develops economic credit assignment
(
Baum, 1996
;
Baum, 1999
)
. More recently, Economy of Minds uses auctions to coordinate LLM agents and guide the evolution of prompts and population with frozen model weights
(
Qi et al., 2026
)
. SALE selects among agents’ proposed strategies using cost–value scoring and shared auction memory
(
Alazraki et al., 2026
)
.
However, recent LLM-based economic systems primarily use feedback to evolve prompts while keeping weights frozen.
MPT
uses feedback to train action and bidding policies, enabling agents to learn how to act and when to participate.
5
Conclusion
We introduced
MPT
, a framework for jointly learning individual action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Learned bids connect participation decisions with local credit assignment, allowing agents to improve both how they act and when they participate without a central coordinating agent. Our experiments show benefits over monolithic post-training and other coordination strategies, while ablations demonstrate the value of learning both bidding and action policies and using learned bids for credit assignment. Trained swarms also adapt faster to related objectives, benefit from larger populations at inference time, and better tolerate agent unavailability as the population grows. These findings support treating self-orchestration as a learnable and reusable component of collective intelligence, opening a path toward decentralized agent swarms whose capabilities and organization improve together through experience.

B.1.1
Task and Simulator
The task is to obtain an iron pickaxe from an empty inventory in a randomly generated Minecraft world, which requires the tech tree: chop logs, craft planks, a crafting table and sticks, craft and equip a wooden pickaxe, mine cobblestone, craft a stone pickaxe and a furnace, mine iron ore, smelt iron ingots, and finally craft the iron pickaxe. (

Episode, Observation and Decision
An episode contains 120 decisions. At each decision the policy receives a

128\times 128
RGB screenshot and a text description: the task, crafting rules, current decision step, cumulative events, world status, a rolling history of the last six steps, the live inventory, and the outcome of the previous instruction. B.1.5
SFT Cold Start
To teach the models the input and output formats and establish basic task capabilities, we perform an SFT cold start in both settings. Specifically, we use Claude Sonnet 5 to generate demonstrations of crafting-task execution and record all model responses. We collect 4,791 examples from actual Minecraft interactions, including 1,677 for
Logger
, 2,380 for
Miner
, and 734 for
Smith
. We fine-tune the monolithic agent on the full dataset and each society agent on its corresponding subset, matching the total training compute between the two settings during cold start. SFT for each model is performed on a single B200 GPU.
We fine-tune all model parameters in bf16 using AdamW with a cosine learning rate schedule. Detailed settings are listed in Table
3
.
B.1.6
Post-training
Our post-training dataset consists of 1,614 random seeds, each generating a different Minecraft world. We host the Minecraft environments and the STEVE-1 model on four RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, allowing 32 Minecraft worlds to run in parallel. Reinforcement learning is performed on four B200 GPUs. Detailed settings are listed in Table
3
.

B.2.5
SFT Cold Start
To teach the models the input and output formats and establish basic navigation capability, we perform an SFT cold start in both settings. Starting from the multimodal-alignment checkpoint of NaVILA, we render oracle trajectories on R2R-CE training episodes with Habitat’s shortest-path follower. We keep successful episodes containing 1,931 decisions (800 turns, 800 moves and 331 stops), and use Claude Sonnet 5 to annotate data.
We fine-tune the monolithic agent on all data and each society agent on its own data. SFT for each model is performed on a single B200 GPU.
We fine-tune all model parameters in bf16 using AdamW with a cosine learning rate schedule. Detailed settings are listed in Table
4
.
B.2.6
Post-training
Our post-training dataset consists of 10,744 R2R-CE training episodes different from SFT. We host the Habitat environments on 2 RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Reinforcement learning is performed on 4 B200 GPUs. Detailed settings are listed in Table
4
.

B.3
Deep Research
B.3.1
Task and Environment
The task is open-domain deep research: given a question, the agent must browse a local web corpus with three tools and return a short final answer. We use the OpenResearcher benchmark
(
Li et al., 2026
)
: the questions are the OpenResearcher-Dataset, and the corpus is the OpenResearcher-Corpus, served by a BM25 search service. Each question comes with one reference answer.
The browser exposes OpenResearcher’s own three tools, called from the model output as JSON:
browser.search
(a query, returning the top-10 hits as title, URL and summary),
browser.open
(a link id from the current page, a URL, or a page cursor, with
loc
/
num_lines
to scroll) and
browser.find
(an exact-text pattern inside the currently open page).

B.3.3
Episode, Observation and Decision
An episode contains at most 64 decisions. The observation is the full conversation so far: the system prompt (OpenResearcher’s browsing instructions, the date, and the three tool schemas), the question, and the alternating assistant turns and tool responses. The prompt budget is 16,384 tokens. The policy answers with reasoning followed by either one tool call or the final answer,
<think>...</think><tool_call>{...}</tool_call>
or
<think>...</think><final_answer>{...}</final_answer>
. Generation stops at
<tool_response>
, and the tool call is executed by the browser against the search service.
B.3.4
Agent Design
The population consists of three agents,
Searcher
,
Opener
and
Finder
, each a separate full fine-tune of gemma-4-E2B-it
(
Team et al., 2026
)
. They see the same conversation and partition the tool space:
Searcher
owns
browser.search
,
Opener
owns
browser.open
, and
Finder
owns
browser.find
; any agent may end the episode by giving the final answer.
The monolithic agent is the same base model fine-tuned on turns spanning all three tools.

B.3.5
SFT Cold Start
To teach the models the input and output formats and establish basic browsing capability, we perform an SFT cold start in both settings. The demonstrations are the OpenResearcher-Dataset’s own browsing trajectories, produced by gpt-oss with the same three tools over the same corpus. We use 568 assistant turns, including 222 for
Searcher
, 273 for
Opener
and 73 for
Finder
. The monolithic agent is fine-tuned on all action turns. Each society agent is fine-tuned on the action turns it owns. SFT for each model is performed on a single H200 GPU.
We fine-tune all models in bf16 using AdamW with a cosine learning rate schedule. Detailed settings are listed in Table
5
.

Appendix D
Potential Limitations
We acknowledge the following limitations:
(1)
MPT
relies on externally evaluated task rewards to train both action and bidding policies. Its effectiveness depends on the quality of these signals. We have not evaluated settings where outcomes are primarily subjective or where reliable feedback is difficult to obtain.
(2) Bidding updates require counterfactual rollouts from the same environment and agent states. Therefore, extending this approach to irreversible real-world interactions remains an open problem.
(3) Despite our efforts to broaden the experimental evaluation, computational constraints limit the scale of our study. We have not explored training swarms composed of multiple models with more than 10B parameters each, or jointly training substantially larger agent populations.

article.headline: 拍卖式自组织让智能体群体边行动边学习
article.lede: 哈佛团队提出市场式后训练MPT，让智能体靠出价竞争行动权，在具身合成、机器人导航与深度研究上均优于单体强化学习。
article.problem: 现有多智能体系统通常把模型放进预设的编排结构里：管理者派活给工人、验证者检查生成者，谁在何时行动往往在训练全程固定不变。这样就把个体能力的训练与群体组织方式的学习割裂开了，忽略了二者其实互相耦合——谁行动决定了谁获得经验，而能力变化又会改变谁该行动。作者因此追问：去中心化的智能体群体能否同时学会如何行动与如何自我编排。
article.method: 论文提出市场式后训练（MPT）：每一回合各智能体独立提交出价，最高者获得行动权，出价同时决定奖励沿行动链向后传递的比例，作为本地训练信用（类似 bucket brigade），动作策略用 REINFORCE 更新。出价策略则通过反事实比较学习——在同一状态下重采样被选中者的出价让次高者行动，从该状态续跑另一条分支，用 Bradley–Terry 偏好目标提高带来更高回报的出价相对似然。训练在四个动作步与一个出价步之间交替，同一套参数同时承担行动与竞标。
article.results: 在训练算力匹配的条件下，MPT 在留出集上三项任务均优于单体强化学习：具身合成平均回合奖励 41.5±5.9 对 20.3±4.1，机器人导航 1.23±0.18 对 0.52±0.14，深度研究准确率 21.0%±4.1% 对 9.0%±2.1%。固定同一批动作策略只比较编排方式时，MPT 在 Iron Pickaxe 上以 41.5 对 25.4 胜过最强的 Graph-of-Agents，相对提升 63.4%。训练中参与格局确实改变：决策步 120 处 Logger 的参与比例从 RL 前约 80% 降到 45%，Miner 从约 10% 升到 40%；把学习到的出价换成随机信用后奖励约为 31，轮询约为 15，均低于 MPT 的约 42。推理期把群体从 3 扩到 12 个智能体，Wooden Pickaxe 的 pass@3 从约 78% 升到 97%；丢包率 p=0.9 时，12 体群体仍保持约 33 的回合奖励，而 3 体只有 19。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“谁来做”从人工设定的编排结构变成可训练、可复用的组件，说明集体智能的组织方式本身也能像策略一样从经验中学出来，并可在推理时通过扩大群体规模换取性能与冗余。
article.limitations: 方法依赖外部可验证的任务奖励来同时训练动作与出价，对于结果主观或反馈不可靠的场景尚未评估；出价训练需要从同一环境与智能体状态做反事实重跑，能否延伸到不可逆的真实世界交互仍是开放问题。作者也承认受算力限制，未探索由多个各自超过 10B 参数的模型组成、或规模更大群体的联合训练。
article.figure_caption_zh: 具身合成中的出价式自组织：(a) Iron Pickaxe 一局中 Logger、Miner、Smith 随采集与合成需求变化轮流参与；(b) 每步各智能体提交出价、最高者行动，此处 Smith 以 0.8 的出价赢得回合并合成工作台，环境随后返回奖励与新状态。

(b) At each decision, agents submit bids, and the highest bidder acts. Here, the Smith wins with a bid of 0.8 and crafts a crafting table; the environment then returns a reward and the next state.

email_papers.title: Remembering Has a Price: Learning Memory Worth under Resource Constraints
email_papers.abstract: Lifelong agents continually accumulate and reuse experience to improve after deployment, yet in practice they often operate under tight generation, interaction, and memory budgets. Under such stringent joint constraints, we find that existing lifelong-memory methods can become ineffective, with several sophisticated approaches offering little advantage over simple retrieval or even no-memory agents. This reveals a more fundamental problem: resource scarcity makes each memory decision more consequential. When only a small amount of past experience can be retained or reused and opportunities for reasoning and recovery are limited, retrieving a relevant but ineffective memory can consume scarce context and hinder downstream execution. The key challenge is therefore not simply to retrieve relevant experience, but to determine which experiences are actually worth retaining and reusing. To address this challenge, we propose TokenWorth, a lightweight online memory framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution feedback and applies it consistently to memory retrieval and bounded memory management. Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and both local and API-based deployments, TokenWorth achieves the highest task success rate while using the fewest output tokens among the evaluated methods. These results suggest that effective lifelong adaptation under resource constraints depends not on remembering more, but on learning what is worth remembering. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AIGNLAI/TokenWorth.

Abstract
Lifelong agents continually accumulate and reuse experience to improve after
deployment, yet in practice they often operate under tight generation,
interaction, and memory budgets. Under such stringent joint constraints, we
find that existing lifelong-memory methods can become ineffective, with several
sophisticated approaches offering little advantage over simple retrieval or
even no-memory agents. This reveals a more fundamental problem: resource
scarcity makes each memory decision more consequential. When only a small
amount of past experience can be retained or reused and opportunities for
reasoning and recovery are limited, retrieving a relevant but ineffective
memory can consume scarce context and hinder downstream execution. The key
challenge is therefore not simply to retrieve relevant experience, but to
determine which experiences are actually worth retaining and reusing. To
address this challenge, we propose
TokenWorth
, a lightweight online
memory framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution
feedback and applies it consistently to memory retrieval and bounded memory
management. Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and both local and
API-based deployments, TokenWorth achieves the highest task success rate while
using the fewest output tokens among the evaluated methods. These results
suggest that effective lifelong adaptation under resource constraints depends
not on remembering more, but on learning what is worth remembering. Our code is publicly available at
https://github.com/AIGNLAI/TokenWorth
.
1
Introduction
Lifelong agents continually accumulate, retain, and reuse experience from an
evolving task stream, enabling continued adaptation after deployment
[
35
]
. This capability is particularly valuable for
long-running interactive agents that must adapt to changing users,
environments, and tasks
[
4
,
6
,
16
]
.
In practice, however, lifelong adaptation rarely operates with unlimited
resources. Generation is constrained by latency, computation, or inference
cost; interaction opportunities are finite; and only a bounded amount of
historical experience can be stored or supplied to the agent at each decision
step
[
8
,
11
,
29
]
. This raises a
fundamental question:
do existing lifelong-memory mechanisms remain
effective when generation, interaction, and memory resources are jointly
constrained?
Figure 1
:
Left: Representative local results with Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct under the
evaluated stringent joint resource constraints; TokenWorth remains effective
where several memory baselines do not.
Right: Resource-constrained lifelong agents operate under bounded generation,
interaction, and memory budgets.
Our evaluation reveals that they often do not. As shown in
Figure
1
(a), under stringent joint resource constraints, several
sophisticated lifelong-memory approaches provide limited improvement over
simple retrieval or even no-memory agents, and can substantially underperform
in some environments. These results highlight the need to evaluate lifelong
agents for their effectiveness under a specified joint resource budget, where
generation, interaction, and memory resources are severely limited. Importantly,
this failure cannot be attributed simply to insufficient
memory capacity: under the same resource budget, different memory policies can
lead to markedly different downstream task performance.
To study this problem systematically, we formalize
resource-constrained lifelong agents
: lifelong agents that must
continually improve from experience while operating under bounded generation,
interaction, and memory budgets. As illustrated in Figure
1
(b),
we jointly constrain the resources available for both task execution and
experience reuse. Specifically, the agent operates with a bounded output budget
and a limited number of interaction rounds, while its external memory is
constrained in capacity, the number of retrieved experiences, and the amount of
memory that can be injected at each step. These inference-time constraints leave backbone capacity unchanged, allowing us to
study lifelong adaptation under a controlled, stringent resource budget.
Why do existing memory mechanisms become fragile under such constraints? When
only a small amount of past experience can be retained or supplied to the
agent, and opportunities for reasoning and recovery are limited, each memory
decision becomes more consequential. In particular, semantic relevance alone
may be insufficient for allocating scarce memory resources: an experience can
appear relevant to the current query yet provide little downstream utility.
Conversely, a useful experience that is not retained or selected cannot be
recovered by simply injecting more context or extending the interaction.
Resource scarcity therefore turns memory allocation into a more stringent
value-estimation problem. The central challenge is no longer merely to retrieve
the most relevant past experience, but to determine which experiences are
actually
worth
retaining and reusing when memory and execution resources
are limited.
To address this challenge, we propose
TokenWorth
, a lightweight online
memory framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution
feedback. TokenWorth combines an interpretable online base scorer with a
residual Recursive Feature Machine (RFM), allowing stable global patterns of
memory usefulness to be complemented by nonlinear, query-specific corrections.
The learned worth is used to guide both memory retrieval and bounded memory-bank
management, allocating limited memory resources toward experiences that are
most useful for future tasks.
We conduct our main evaluation on three LifelongAgentBench environments
covering database interaction, operating-system tasks, and knowledge-graph
reasoning, under both local and API-based deployments. Across all six
environment–deployment combinations, TokenWorth achieves the highest task
success rate among the evaluated methods while also using the fewest output
tokens. These results show that its gains do not rely on longer generations;
instead, selecting higher-value experience allows the frozen backbone to use a
limited generation budget more effectively.
Our contributions are threefold:
•
We formulate
resource-constrained lifelong agents
and study
effectiveness under stringent joint constraints on generation, interaction,
and memory.
•
We propose
TokenWorth
, which learns query-dependent memory
worth from online execution feedback and uses it consistently for memory
retrieval and bounded memory management.
•
We evaluate TokenWorth across three LifelongAgentBench environments
under both local and API-based deployments, demonstrating improved task
success and generation efficiency under stringent resource constraints.
2
Related Work
Lifelong Language Agents.
Lifelong language agents aim to continually improve from accumulated interaction experience, enabling continued adaptation after deployment
[
6
,
35
]
. Early agent systems demonstrated that past trajectories, reflections, or reusable skills can improve future decision making, including Reflexion
[
19
]
, ExpeL
[
33
]
, Voyager
[
24
]
, and SocioDojo
[
4
]
. More recent work has developed explicit memory and skill mechanisms for continual adaptation, such as MemoryBank
[
37
]
, Mem0
[
5
]
, MemRL
[
32
]
, MemSkill
[
30
]
, and AutoSkill
[
27
]
. Meanwhile, LifelongAgentBench
[
34
]
, AgentCL
[
21
]
, SkillLearnBench
[
36
]
, and XSkill
[
10
]
provide increasingly systematic evaluation of continual adaptation in language agents. Most of these studies focus on how agents can accumulate and exploit experience to improve capability; in contrast, we study whether such memory mechanisms remain effective under stringent joint constraints on generation, interaction, and memory.
Resource-Constrained Language Agents.
Resource efficiency has been extensively studied for LLM inference and serving, including memory-efficient execution
[
11
]
and collaborative inference under computation and communication constraints
[
29
]
. More recent work has begun to examine resource constraints at the agent level.
Hajimiri et al. [9]
study whether online memory and skill modules remain beneficial under fixed inference-token budgets, while
Wu et al. [25]
investigate continual learning with a hard-bounded on-device memory. BudgetMem
[
31
]
further considers query-aware routing across runtime memory budgets, and
Chen and Cheng [3]
model agentic memory value using multiple factors for memory retention and retrieval.
These studies highlight the importance of accounting for resource cost in agent memory, but largely focus on individual resource constraints, runtime budgeting, or memory valuation in isolation. Our work instead studies lifelong adaptation under a fixed joint budget on generation, interaction, and memory resources. We identify memory-worth estimation as a central challenge and introduce
TokenWorth
, which learns query-dependent worth from streaming execution
feedback to guide retrieval and bounded memory management.

4.1
Overview
Figure

TokenWorth consists of three components. First, an interpretable linear scorer
captures stable global patterns of memory usefulness, while a residual
Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) models nonlinear and query-specific corrections

bounded memory bank.

4.2
Learning Query-Dependent Memory Worth
TokenWorth aims to determine which past experiences are worth allocating the
agent’s limited memory resources to. Unlike a fixed memory utility, the
usefulness of an experience depends on the current query and must be inferred
from sparse and indirect execution feedback. Each task is executed only once,
feedback is observed only for the memory actually used, and an execution
failure may arise from factors beyond the selected memory itself.
To balance stability and adaptivity under such feedback, TokenWorth decomposes
memory worth into two complementary components. A lightweight linear base
scorer captures stable and interpretable patterns that generalize across the
task stream, while an RFM learns nonlinear residual structure not captured by
the base scorer. The linear component is updated conservatively around an
informative prior, whereas the RFM adapts more flexibly to local
query–memory interactions.

6
Conclusion
We study lifelong language agents under joint constraints on generation,
interaction, and memory. We propose
TokenWorth
, a lightweight online
framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from execution feedback and
uses it for retrieval and bounded memory management. Across three
LifelongAgentBench environments and local and API-based backbones, TokenWorth
achieves the highest task success rates among evaluated methods while using the
fewest output tokens. Additional experiments show competitive performance on
coding and embodied-agent tasks. Feedback is observed only for selected
memories, so their causal contributions remain unidentified. Developing
budget-efficient credit assignment is an important direction for future work.

Appendix A
Additional Experimental Details
A.1
Benchmarks
Our main experiments use three environments from
LifelongAgentBench
[
34
]
: database interaction
(DB), operating-system interaction (OS), and knowledge-graph interaction (KG).
Tasks are processed sequentially, and only experience from preceding tasks may
be reused. DB requires structured database operations and answers grounded in
retrieved observations. OS requires multi-step system management through Bash
commands. KG follows an AgentBench-style protocol in which the agent interacts
with a knowledge graph through structured tool calls, while SPARQL queries
are executed by the backend. The environments thus cover heterogeneous
forms of interactive decision making under a shared online
lifelong-learning protocol.
We additionally evaluate online lifelong variants of
BigCodeBench
[
38
]
and
ALFWorld
[
20
]
; their results are reported in
Appendix
C
.
Beyond language agents, class-incremental learning has examined
the impact of task ordering on continual adaptation
[
12
]
and the variability of performance across
evaluation sequences
[
14
]
.
These studies highlight the importance of evaluation protocols
in continual learning, while our experiments focus on online
memory adaptation under fixed resource budgets.

Within each environment and deployment setting, methods share the same task

and skill extraction; their generated output tokens are included in both the

article.headline: 记忆有代价：资源受限下学习记忆价值
article.lede: 南大团队提出 TokenWorth，用稀疏执行反馈在线学习查询相关的记忆价值，在六种设置下成功率最高、输出 token
article.problem: 终身学习智能体在部署后不断积累经验，但现实中往往同时受到生成、交互与记忆预算的联合限制。作者发现，在这种严格约束下多种复杂记忆方法几乎不比简单检索甚至无记忆智能体更好，有时还明显更差。原因在于资源稀缺让每次记忆决策代价更高：语义相关但无用的记忆会占用宝贵上下文，而未被保留的有用经验无法靠多轮交互补救。
article.method: TokenWorth 把记忆价值拆成两部分：一个带先验正则的可解释线性基础打分器捕捉稳定的全局规律，一个基于 RFM 的残差学习器建模查询相关的非线性偏差。残差部分采用两时间尺度更新，KRR 系数快速拟合，特征度量则通过 AGOP 缓慢调整。学到的价值既用于当前查询的记忆检索，也用于有界记忆库的准入与淘汰，整个控制器不更新主干模型、不做任务回放，也不产生额外的大模型调用。
article.results: 在 LifelongAgentBench 的 DB、OS、KG 三个环境与本地 Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct、API DeepSeek-V4-Flash 两种部署共六种组合中，TokenWorth 成功率均为最高：本地 DB 达 65.0%，比最强基线 RAG 的 33.0% 高 32.0 个百分点，OS 为 59.4%（高 4.8 点），KG 为 36.7%（高 6.0 点）；API 侧 DB 为 62.2%（高 30.0 点），OS 为 73.2%（高 3.0 点），KG 为 36.7%（高 4.7 点）。输出 token 相对无记忆基线在本地的降幅为 9.3%、51.5%、18.7%，在 API 侧为 31.6%、58.3%、21.3%，六种设置均为最低。DB 本地消融显示，仅用基础打分器为 64.2%，加上固定度量的 RFM 反而降到 63.0%，启用 AGOP 特征自适应后回升到 65.0%。
article.why_it_matters: 结果提示，资源受限下的终身适应关键不在于记得更多，而在于学出哪些经验值得占用稀缺的记忆与生成预算，这为智能体记忆机制的设计提供了一个以价值估计为核心的视角。
article.limitations: 实验只覆盖一组固定的严格预算，作者明确表示不主张方法在不同预算水平下的鲁棒性；监督信号只来自被选中的那条记忆，无法识别其因果贡献。此外，在 BigCodeBench 和 ALFWorld 上的优势很小，API 版 BigCodeBench 的 50.6% 还低于 RAG 的 50.9%，超参数敏感度测试中部分设置会带来 2.4 至 3.0 个百分点的下降。

email_papers.title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs
email_papers.abstract: Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents. Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs. We introduce HarnessPro, a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Across these benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at https://github.com/pzs19/HarnessPro

Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents.
Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs.

HarnessPro
, a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost.

Rather than returning a single harness,

Introduction
An agent harness is the software infrastructure that manages interactions between a large language model (LLM) and its environment
(
Grace et al., 2026
)
.
Recent work on recursive self-improvement (RSI)
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
uses past execution trajectories to diagnose problems and guide harness updates that improve performance on future tasks
(
Suzgun et al., 2026
;
Lin et al., 2026
;
Pan et al., 2026a
)
.
However, these methods often pursue performance gains through more extensive exploration and stronger verification
(
Lin et al., 2026
;
Pan et al., 2026a
)
.
These efforts improve performance, but often at the cost of higher token consumption and increased latency.
This trade-off is less appealing in practical deployment, where the execution cost and latency also matter.
We therefore ask:
Can recursive harness self-improvement deliver better performance at lower execution cost?
Toward this goal, we introduce

HarnessPro
, a label-free method for recursive harness self-improvement that uses both performance and cost metrics to guide harness updates and candidate selection.
It orchestrates several specialized agents to turn execution feedback into successive harness updates.
A trajectory analyzer examines repeated rollouts to identify failures and avoidable overhead.

HarnessPro
differs from prior work.

article.headline: 给智能体框架做帕累托自进化：性能升、成本降
article.lede: HarnessPro 用多智能体诊断执行轨迹，在无标签设定下同时优化性能与成本，在 SWE-Bench Pro 上成本更
article.problem: 现有基于递归自我改进（RSI）的 harness 优化方法，主要靠扩大探索范围和加强验证来取得性能提升，代价是 token 消耗与延迟上升。但在实际部署中，执行成本和延迟同样重要，这种「性能换成本」的取舍并不划算。作者因此提出：递归的 harness 自我改进能否在降低执行成本的同时提升性能？
article.method: HarnessPro 用多个专职 agent 把执行反馈转化为一轮轮 harness 更新：轨迹分析器检查重复 rollout，找出失败点和可避免的开销；planner 按不同的性能与成本优先级提出更新方案；再由实现 agent 落地为候选 harness。候选评估不依赖标准答案或官方测试，而由 LLM 生成的测试完成，属于无标签设定。方法最终不返回单一 harness，而是给出位于性能-成本帕累托前沿上的一组代表，供使用者按偏好挑选。
article.results: 在 SWE-Bench Pro 上，基线 RHO 的通过率从原 harness 提升到 80.0%，但单任务平均成本从 $1.88 涨到 $2.68（+42.6%）；HarnessPro-Heavy 在该基准上取得 80.7% 通过率、成本 $1.97，即性能略高而成本明显更低。在另一个基准（片段中未给出名称）上，RHO 为 76.3% 通过率、$1.09，HarnessPro-Heavy 为 80.8%、$0.72。偏向低成本的 HarnessPro-Lite 在两个基准上分别为 72.9% / $0.43 与 72.3% / $0.80，以更低通过率换取大幅成本下降。消融显示 planner 与 test synthesizer 都不可或缺：去掉 test synthesizer 后，Heavy 在两个基准上分别降到 74.6% 和 72.0%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「成本」变成 harness 自进化的一等目标，而非事后再压缩，让 agent 框架的自我改进更贴近真实部署约束。返回帕累托候选集而非单一方案的做法，也让性能与预算的取舍变得显式可调。
article.limitations: 无标签设定下以 LLM 生成测试替代官方测试，去掉 test synthesizer 后通过率明显下滑（80.8→74.6、80.7→72.0），说明结论高度依赖合成测试的质量；用于选择的核心集仅固定 10 个任务，有对选样过拟合的风险。此外成本以美元计、依赖具体 API 定价，片段中另两个基准的名称与规模、多次运行的方差均未给出。
article.figure_caption_zh: HarnessPro 总览：每个 epoch 分析 rollout 轨迹、生成候选 harness，并依据性能与成本挑选代表。

figure.caption: Overview of {}. In each epoch, it analyzes rollout trajectories, generates candidate harnesses, and selects representatives based on performance and cost.

email_papers.title: Empowering Edge Agents: A Systematic Analysis of Edge-Cloud Collaboration in LLM Agent Execution
email_papers.abstract: Edge-cloud collaboration combines the lower inference overhead and greater data locality of edge-side execution with the stronger capabilities of cloud-hosted models. However, as LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon scenarios, cloud participation becomes interleaved throughout execution rather than a one-shot decision for each query. Such interleaved participation introduces trajectory-level effects that remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we introduce EC2-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution. It provides executable digital-workspace agent tasks and a unified evaluation framework covering task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Using this benchmark, we empirically study diverse forms of edge-cloud collaboration. Our study reveals three findings. First, collaboration achieves a favorable balance among task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure compared with edge-only and cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across strategies shrink, while privacy exposure remains strongly strategy-dependent. Third, stronger edge capability shifts preferred collaboration from externally controlled cloud participation and direct cloud execution toward more edge-controlled collaboration. Further analyses identify cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction following as important edge-side abilities for effective collaboration. These findings provide a systematic understanding of edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution and insights for designing future edge agents that effectively collaborate with cloud models. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/EC2-Bench.

Abstract
Edge–cloud collaboration offers a promising way to combine the lower inference overhead and greater data locality of edge-side execution with the substantially stronger capabilities of cloud-hosted frontier models. However, as LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon scenarios, cloud participation becomes interleaved throughout execution rather than a one-shot decision for each query. Such interleaved participation introduces trajectory-level effects that remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we introduce EC
2
-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating edge–cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution. EC
2
-Bench provides executable digital-workspace agent tasks and a unified evaluation framework covering task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Using this benchmark, we empirically study diverse forms of edge–cloud collaboration. Our study reveals several key findings. First, edge–cloud collaboration provides an effective execution paradigm for long-horizon agents by achieving a favorable balance among task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure compared with edge-only and cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across collaboration strategies become smaller, while privacy exposure remains strongly dependent on the chosen strategy. Third, stronger edge capability changes the preferred collaboration mode, shifting from externally controlled cloud participation and direct cloud execution toward more edge-controlled collaboration. Further analyses identify cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction following as important edge-side abilities underlying such effective collaboration. These findings establish a systematic understanding of edge–cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution and provide insights for designing future edge models that can effectively collaborate with cloud models. All codes and resources are available at
https://github.com/OpenBMB/EC2-Bench
.
1
Introduction
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs)
(
Achiam et al., 2023
)
, together with the emergence of agent harnesses such as Claude Code
(
Anthropic, 2025
)
and OpenClaw
(
OpenClaw, 2025
)
, have shifted LLM applications from isolated prompt–response interactions toward long-horizon, goal-directed agent execution
(
Wang et al., 2024a
)
. These agents tackle complex end-to-end workflows, including software development, data analysis, information seeking, and workplace automation, through iterative interaction with external environments and tool use
(
Yao et al., 2022
;
Yang et al., 2024
;
Hu et al., 2024b
;
Shen et al., 2023
;
Zhou et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2024b
)
.
Bringing such agents to edge devices, however, remains challenging because edge platforms are inherently constrained by limited computational resources and memory
(
Qu et al., 2025
)
. Consequently, practical on-device deployment often relies on relatively small LLMs (e.g., models with
≤
\leq
10B parameters), which can struggle with demanding reasoning, planning, and tool-use tasks
(
Choi et al., 2026
)
, making reliable long-horizon execution challenging
(
Liu et al., 2024
)
. To address this limitation, recent work has explored edge–cloud LLM collaboration, where lightweight edge models are complemented by cloud-hosted frontier LLMs when additional capability is required
(
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
. This paradigm combines efficient edge-side execution with stronger cloud capabilities, but requires effective coordination of edge and cloud participation to realize these complementary benefits
(
Ding et al., 2024
;
Sun et al., 2024
;
Agrawal and Mayer,
)
.
Prior edge–cloud LLM systems largely treated collaboration as a one-shot coordination process for each query, typically through routing or escalation decisions
(
Pozi and Sato, 2025
;
Han et al., 2026
)
. In long-horizon agent execution, however, collaboration can become more interleaved, with edge and cloud models participating at different points along the trajectory as capability requirements change
(
Yi et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
. Such interleaving introduces trajectory-level dependencies: cloud participation decisions can influence subsequent execution steps, accumulate resource costs over the trajectory, and determine how much potentially sensitive information leaves the local environment. Yet existing analysis still largely focuses on isolated routing or escalation decisions at the query level, leaving these trajectory-level effects underexplored
(
Hu et al., 2024a
;
Lu et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2026a
;
Li et al., 2025
)
. To close this gap, in this paper, we conduct a systematic empirical study of edge–cloud collaboration in long-horizon agentic execution. Specifically, we organize our study around three research questions. We first ask:
does edge–cloud collaboration remain effective for realistic long-horizon agent execution?
(
RQ1
) We evaluate this question jointly in terms of task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. As edge models become more capable, more execution can be handled locally while cloud assistance is reserved for capability-demanding operations. We therefore ask:
how does increasing edge capability impact edge–cloud collaborative execution?
(
RQ2
); As increasing edge capability changes how computation is distributed between edge and cloud, collaboration strategies that are effective under one capability regime may not remain equally suitable under another. This motivates our final question:
how should edge–cloud collaboration evolve as edge capability advances?
(
RQ3
).
To provide a common empirical basis for this study, we introduce
EC
2
-Bench
(
E
dge–
C
loud
C
ollaborative Agent Benchmark), an evaluation framework that combines a diverse suite of real-world digital-workspace agent tasks with a unified execution and evaluation environment for edge–cloud collaboration.
EC
2
-Bench
characterizes each configuration along three dimensions: task performance
(
Yuan et al., 2026b
)
, resource usage
(
Fang et al., 2025
)
, and privacy exposure. We explicitly consider privacy because cloud participation may reveal sensitive workspace information encountered during agent execution, making privacy exposure an important dimension of evaluating such collaboration
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
. Using
EC
2
-Bench
, we systematically investigate edge–cloud collaboration across diverse agent tasks, collaboration strategies, and edge-capability regimes.
Our study yields three main findings. First, edge–cloud collaboration remains effective for long-horizon agents: partial cloud participation improves task performance over edge-only execution while requiring substantially less cloud resource usage and privacy exposure than cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across collaboration strategies become much smaller; however, their differences in privacy exposure remain substantial. Thus, privacy remains an important differentiator even when task performance converges. Third, the collaboration strategy that works best changes with edge capability. Weaker edge models benefit more from external routing and direct cloud execution, whereas stronger edge models benefit more from edge-controlled invocation and cloud advisory. Further analyses suggest that effective cloud-invocation decisions and instruction following are key edge-side abilities for stronger-edge collaboration modes. These findings highlight the value of optimizing future edge models for both standalone capability and effective cloud collaboration, enabling more capable edge agents.
2
Related Work
A growing body of work has investigated how edge and cloud LLMs can be coordinated to leverage their complementary capabilities and deployment characteristics, balancing overall task performance with local efficiency
(
Zhu and Yang, 2025
;
Dong et al., 2025
)
. A substantial line of work focuses on one-shot coordination for individual queries, either by routing each query to an edge or cloud model or by cascading from the local model to the cloud when additional capability is needed
(
Chen et al., 2023
;
Ong et al., 2024
;
Miao and Fang,
)
. These approaches therefore center on improving the accuracy of routing and escalation decisions
(
Ding et al., 2024
)
. More recent work has extended edge–cloud collaboration to agent execution, where edge and cloud participation can be coordinated at different steps throughout a multi-step trajectory rather than determined once for the entire query, enabling finer-grained use of their complementary capabilities. Within this setting, recent approaches have explored different designs for coordinating edge–cloud collaboration, mainly along two dimensions. Some dynamically determine when the cloud model should participate, either through dedicated rule-based controllers or routers, or by allowing the edge agent itself to decide when to invoke the cloud
(
Shao et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
;
Zeng et al., 2026b
)
. Beyond deciding when the cloud should participate, other approaches have explored complementary functional roles for edge and cloud models during execution, such as execution, planning, or providing guidance
(
Yi et al., 2025
;
Yuan et al., 2026a
)
.
Existing work has begun to develop dedicated evaluation resources for edge–cloud LLM systems. LLMSwitchBench
(
Liu et al., 2025
)
evaluates edge–cloud routing for smart-home queries, while M4A1
(
Yuan et al., 2026b
)
extends device–cloud evaluation to multimodal, multitask, and multi-turn conversations, focusing on where individual inference requests should be executed. More general LLM routing benchmarks instead abstract away from the edge–cloud setting and evaluate routing systems over heterogeneous model pools, primarily focusing on routing quality and overall cost–performance trade-offs
(
Huang et al., 2025
;
Lu et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2026b
)
. Despite this progress, existing evaluations pay more attention on routing decisions for individual queries, tasks, or turns, typically over standalone inference workloads such as knowledge, reasoning, coding, and instruction-following tasks. Our study instead treats edge–cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution as the primary object of empirical analysis, aiming to systematically characterize its effectiveness and system-level behavior across different edge capability levels and collaboration designs.

4.1
Task Suite Construction
We construct
EC
2
-Bench
by collecting executable agent tasks from existing benchmarks, curating them for the study of edge–cloud collaboration, and augmenting the resulting task suite with sensitivity annotations for privacy-exposure evaluation.
Data Collection.
We construct the task suite of
EC
2
-Bench
based on six established executable agent benchmarks: Claw-Eval
(
Ye et al., 2026
)
, WildClawBench
(
Ding et al., 2026

(
Qwen Team, 2026a

(

, PinchBench
(

(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
. We select these benchmarks because their tasks evaluate end-to-end agent execution through stateful, multi-step interactions with tools, applications, and workspace artifacts, with explicit task objectives and verifiable execution outcomes. Collectively, they cover a broad range of applications, interaction patterns, execution environments, and task difficulties, providing a diverse candidate pool for constructing
EC
2
-Bench
.
Task Curation.
Starting from the collected candidate pool, we further adapt and curate the tasks to construct the final task suite. Specifically, we first adapt tasks from different source benchmarks to a common execution environment and evaluation interface, enabling all tasks to be executed under the same agent runtime and evaluated under consistent conditions while preserving their original objectives, workspace states, required interactions, and success criteria. We then apply a collaboration-oriented difficulty filtering procedure to retain tasks that are informative for studying edge–cloud collaboration. We evaluate each adapted task under edge-only and cloud-only execution to characterize task difficulty at the two execution endpoints. Tasks that are consistently solved by both endpoints are removed because they provide limited opportunity to differentiate agent execution paradigms, while tasks where neither endpoint achieves meaningful completion are excluded because they provide limited basis for evaluating collaborative execution. Following these steps, we further supplement the task suite with tasks from underrepresented scenarios to maintain broad workload coverage. The resulting task suite consists of 128 executable tasks.
To measure the potential exposure of sensitive information from local workspaces to the cloud during collaboration, we further incorporate sensitivity annotations into
EC
2
-Bench
. Specifically, we first annotate sensitive information already contained in the original workspace artifacts. We then use an LLM-based approach to identify appropriate locations, generate realistic synthetic sensitive information, and insert it into relevant workspace artifacts, while preserving the original task objective, required interactions, and evaluation criteria. This process results in fine-grained sensitivity annotations for 100 tasks, where each sensitivity unit corresponds to an atomic piece of sensitive information grounded in a workspace artifact.
Detailed procedures for task adaptation, collaboration-oriented filtering, coverage supplementation, and sensitivity annotation are provided in Appendix
A.3
, Appendix
A.4
and Appendix
A.5
.

We now use

to systematically study edge–cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution. Our analysis follows the three research questions introduced in Section

, examining whether edge–cloud collaboration is effective, how improving edge capability affects collaborative execution, and how collaboration mechanisms evolve as edge models become stronger.

Effectiveness of Edge–Cloud Collaboration in Agent Execution (RQ1)

We first examine whether edge–cloud collaboration provides a useful execution regime between edge-only and cloud-only agents when task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure are considered jointly. As shown in Table
2
, the two execution extremes exhibit clear trade-offs. Cloud-only execution achieves the strongest task performance but incurs substantial cloud resource usage and privacy exposure, whereas edge-only execution avoids cloud usage and exposure at the cost of lower task performance. Collaborative execution occupies the space between these extremes, improving task performance over edge-only execution while substantially reducing cloud dependence relative to cloud-only execution. For example, with Qwen3.5-2B as the edge model, step-level routing improves task completion from 12.75 to 39.97 while using only 22.7% of the cloud-only cost. These results indicate that partial cloud participation can recover substantial capability without incurring the full cost of cloud-only execution.

6.2
Impact of Improving Edge Capability on Collaborative Execution (RQ2)
As edge models continue to advance rapidly
(
Xiao et al., 2025
)
, we study how improving edge capability changes edge–cloud collaborative execution. To probe how collaboration may evolve beyond current lightweight edge models, we additionally include Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.7-Plus as prospective proxies for stronger future edge models. As shown in Table
2
, stronger edge models consistently improve collaborative execution and bring its performance closer to cloud-only execution. The best available collaborative configuration increases from 39.97% completion with Qwen3.5-2B to 76.84% with Qwen3.7-Plus, approaching the 82.70% completion of cloud-only execution.
We further examine how increasing edge capability changes the variation among collaboration strategies. Specifically, for each edge model, we measure the gap between the highest and lowest completion scores and privacy exposure values. As shown in Figures
3(a)
and
3(b)
, task performance becomes substantially less sensitive to the collaboration strategy as edge capability increases. The completion gap among the evaluated strategies narrows from 25.22% with Qwen3.5-2B to 3.67% with Qwen3.7-Plus. In contrast, privacy exposure does not exhibit the same convergence, with substantial differences persisting across collaboration strategies. Notably, with Qwen3.7-Plus, the strategies differ by only 3.67% in completion but by 66.23% in privacy exposure. These results show that stronger edge capability substantially compresses performance differences across collaboration strategies, while privacy exposure remains highly differentiated.
6.3
How Does Edge–Cloud Collaboration Evolve with Edge Capability? (RQ3)
Beyond improving collaborative performance, increasing edge capability may also change effective collaboration mechanisms. We examine this shift along two dimensions: who determines cloud participation and what role the cloud plays once invoked. As shown in Table
2
, both dimensions exhibit clear shifts with improving edge capability. In terms of participation control, externally routed strategies generally outperform edge-controlled strategies with weaker edge models. For example, with Qwen3.5-2B, Per-step Routing achieves 39.97% completion, compared with 15.86% for Edge-Ctrl. Delegation. As edge capability improves, however, this pattern reverses. A similar reversal appears in the role of the cloud: weaker edge models benefit more from direct cloud execution, whereas stronger edge models favor advisory support.

Cloud-Assistance Decision Making.
The shift toward agent-controlled invocation motivates us to examine whether stronger edge models can make more effective cloud-assistance decisions. Since there is no explicit annotation indicating when cloud assistance is necessary, we compare Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation against a matched random-invocation baseline. Specifically, we preserve the same cloud-call rate as the agent-controlled strategy while randomly selecting invocation steps. As shown in Figure
4(a)
, edge-controlled delegation consistently outperforms random invocation. The gain is only 1.2% for Qwen3.5-2B, but reaches 3.0–4.4% for the more capable edge models. This pattern suggests that stronger edge models may make more effective cloud-invocation decisions.
Cloud Guidance Utilization.
We next examine whether instruction-following ability is associated with improved advisory collaboration. Starting from Qwen3.5-2B, we apply targeted instruction-following training and evaluate intermediate checkpoints under a fixed cloud-advisory setting. As shown in Figure
4(b)
and Appendix
A.10
, task completion under cloud advisory consistently improves as instruction-following ability develops during training, increasing from 24.8% before training to 28.8% after 600 steps. These results suggest that instruction-following ability is associated with improved utilization of cloud-provided guidance.
7
Conclusion
In this work, we study edge–cloud collaboration for long-horizon LLM agent execution, where cloud participation is interleaved throughout the execution trajectory. To enable systematic investigation of this problem, we introduce
EC
2
-Bench
, an evaluation framework that combines executable digital-workspace agent tasks with unified measurements of task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Our findings show that edge–cloud collaboration can achieve a favorable balance between capability, cost, and privacy compared with purely edge-side or cloud-side execution. As edge models become stronger, collaborative execution increasingly approaches cloud-only performance, while privacy exposure remains highly dependent on how cloud participation is organized. We further find that stronger edge models benefit from agent-controlled cloud invocation and advisory interaction. Additional analyses suggest that effective cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction-following are important abilities for edge–cloud collaboration, motivating future work to develop more capable edge agents by strengthening their ability to collaborate with cloud models.
AI Use Statement
Generative AI tools were used to assist with language polishing and improving the clarity of the manuscript. All research ideas, experimental design, implementation, analysis, and conclusions were developed and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the content of the paper.
Ethics Statement
This work studies edge–cloud collaboration for LLM-powered agents and evaluates different collaboration strategies in terms of task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure.
EC
2
-Bench
is designed for research evaluation and responsible system development. We do not use real private user data to construct privacy-sensitive benchmark content. When additional sensitive information is required for evaluation, it is synthetically generated and does not correspond to real individuals, organizations, credentials, or financial records. Human annotation is used only to validate benchmark annotations and synthetic content; no annotator personal information is collected or analyzed. The privacy annotations in
EC
2
-Bench
are intended to support systematic evaluation of sensitive information exposed during edge–cloud collaboration and to facilitate the development of more privacy-aware agent systems.
Reproducibility Statement
We provide detailed descriptions of the benchmark construction, collaboration strategies, experimental setup, and evaluation procedures in the main paper and appendix. In particular, we document the task adaptation and filtering process, sensitivity annotation procedure and validation, implementations of the four edge–cloud collaboration strategies, model and inference configurations, and the metrics used to evaluate task performance, cloud resource usage, edge computation, and privacy exposure. We further report the experimental settings and implementation details for the analyses conducted in each research question. These details are provided to facilitate reproduction of the benchmark and the reported experimental results.
