A.2
Detailed Comparison with Prior Benchmarks
We provide additional details on how
EC
2
-Bench
differs from representative benchmarks for LLM routing and edge–cloud collaboration. Overall, prior benchmarks primarily study model allocation over queries or conversational turns and evaluate task quality together with inference-related costs, whereas
EC
2
-Bench
extends the evaluation to long-horizon agent execution, broader collaboration mechanisms, and trajectory-level privacy exposure. We next compare these benchmarks along three aspects: evaluation scenario, collaboration mode, and evaluation dimension.
Evaluation Scenario.
Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate routing over conventional LLM queries or conversational interactions, while
EC
2
-Bench
focuses on long-horizon agent execution in interactive environments. RouterBench
(
Hu et al., 2024a
)
evaluates routing across a collection of general LLM tasks. LLMRouterBench
(
Li et al., 2026b
)
further broadens the task coverage to include software-engineering and tool-use benchmarks in addition to conventional reasoning, knowledge, and code-generation tasks. LLMSwitchBench
(
Liu et al., 2025
)
focuses on independent smart-home queries spanning binary, multiple-choice, and open-ended formats. M4A1
(
Yuan et al., 2026b
)
considers multi-modal and multi-task interactions within multi-turn conversations. In comparison,
EC
2
-Bench
evaluates collaboration over multi-step agent trajectories, where models repeatedly interact with tools, applications, and persistent workspace states.
Collaboration Modes.
Prior benchmarks predominantly study routing-based collaboration, whereas
EC
2
-Bench
additionally considers collaboration in which the edge agent itself controls cloud participation. RouterBench, LLMRouterBench, and LLMSwitchBench formulate model allocation primarily as query routing, where each input query is assigned to a selected model. M4A1 allows device–cloud placement to be reconsidered for different tasks throughout a multi-turn conversation.
EC
2
-Bench
includes both Query Routing and Per-Step Routing, and further considers two edge-controlled modes. Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation allows the edge agent to decide when to delegate the next execution step to the cloud, while Edge-Controlled Cloud Advisory lets the edge agent request cloud guidance while retaining responsibility for subsequent action generation.
Evaluation Dimensions.
Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate task quality and inference-related efficiency, while
EC
2
-Bench
additionally quantifies privacy exposure over the complete execution trajectory. RouterBench focuses on task performance and economic cost, while LLMRouterBench evaluates performance-oriented and performance–cost routing and additionally provides latency-aware analysis. M4A1 jointly considers response quality, latency, and usage cost in device–cloud offloading. LLMSwitchBench incorporates privacy-sensitive queries and privacy-aware routing mechanisms, including local execution and masking before cloud inference, while its main routing evaluation reports task-quality metrics and inference cost. In
EC
2
-Bench
, privacy exposure is directly quantified by tracking which annotated sensitive information from the local workspace becomes visible to the cloud during execution. Resource usage is likewise measured over the complete trajectory, including cloud-side token consumption and monetary cost as well as edge-side computation.
A.3
Task Suite Construction and Statistics
This section provides additional details on the construction and composition of the
EC
2
-Bench
task suite, including collaboration-oriented difficulty filtering, coverage supplementation, and task statistics.
We first collect candidate tasks from multiple Claw-style executable-workspace agent benchmarks and adapt them to the
EC
2
-Bench
execution environment following the protocol in Appendix
A.4
. We then perform collaboration-oriented difficulty filtering to retain tasks that provide meaningful room for edge–cloud collaboration. All filtering runs are conducted on the adapted task instances in the standardized
EC
2
-Bench
environment, using the same workspace states, tool interfaces, and task-specific evaluation checks defined after adaptation. Specifically, each task is evaluated under three endpoint configurations, using Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-9B as representative edge models and GLM-5.3 as the cloud model. We use the resulting task completion scores as the filtering signal to characterize whether a task is already handled by edge-only execution, can be completed by cloud-only execution, or remains challenging for both endpoints.

A.4
Task Adaptation Protocol
This section describes how tasks collected from heterogeneous executable-workspace benchmarks are adapted into standardized executable instances for
EC
2
-Bench
. The adaptation protocol consists of three components: standardizing task execution, standardizing task evaluation, and validating that the resulting instances preserve comparable task difficulty. We then illustrate the resulting task format and execution workflow with a representative
EC
2
-Bench
instance.
Standardization and Fidelity Check.
Inspired by the task format used in
Ding et al. (2026)
, we first standardize task execution by organizing each task into a unified configuration and workspace structure. Each task is converted into a unified configuration format specifying its prompt, workspace paths, tools, environment settings, and other execution requirements. Task-relevant files and resources are organized into a common workspace structure, while tool and skill settings are aligned across tasks so that instances from different sources can follow the same agent loop and logging mechanism. We next standardize task evaluation while preserving the original success criteria of each task. The original verification logic is converted into a set of task-specific evaluation checks compatible with
EC
2
-Bench
, including rule-based validation, file or application-state auditing, command-output inspection, and rubric-based LLM-as-a-judge verification when semantic judgment is required. The resulting check scores are aggregated into the task completion score defined in Section
4.2
.
To validate adaptation fidelity, we examine whether the adapted instances preserve comparable execution and evaluation outcomes. For each task, we execute both the original and adapted versions with Qwen3.5-9B and compare their average completion scores over three independent runs. Tasks whose absolute difference in average completion score exceeds 0.3 are discarded. This validation helps identify substantial behavioral or scoring shifts introduced during adaptation.

Representative Task Workflow.
To illustrate the resulting standardized task format, Table
5
presents a representative
EC
2
-Bench
instance for customer follow-up, including its task instruction, expected behavior, evaluation checks, executable workspace, and available skills. The example requires the agent to identify customers overdue for contact, inspect their previous email communications, and prepare tier-specific follow-up drafts using CRM and Gmail services.
Using this task as an example, the harness first parses the standardized task configuration to obtain the task instruction, workspace, required skills, environment settings, initialization commands, and evaluation checks. It then creates an isolated execution environment for the task, loads the task workspace and task-specific skills, and executes the warmup procedure to instantiate the required application state. In this example, the customer and inbox data are used to initialize local CRM and Gmail services, which expose the application interfaces subsequently used by the agent. The evaluation ground truth is kept separate from the execution environment and is not made available to the agent during this stage. The harness then configures the evaluated model, starts the OpenClaw runtime, and passes the task instruction to the agent. During execution, the agent iteratively interacts with the CRM and Gmail services through the provided skills, observes the resulting application states, and decides subsequent actions until the task terminates or reaches the time limit. The complete interaction history is recorded as the execution trajectory and retained for subsequent analysis. After execution terminates, the ground-truth evaluation data are injected into the evaluation environment, and the task-specific checks assess customer identification, email-style differentiation, and draft quality to compute the task completion score. For privacy evaluation, the annotated sensitivity units are matched against the cloud-visible contexts recorded during collaborative execution to determine privacy exposure. The harness additionally collects the execution transcript and model-usage statistics for resource evaluation.

This subsection describes how sensitivity-unit annotations are constructed in
EC
2
-Bench
. Since privacy-relevant information in digital workspaces can be distributed across heterogeneous files, application states, and other task artifacts, we adopt an LLM-based annotation process to identify and annotate sensitive information from two sources: information already present in the task environment and realistically synthesized sensitive content introduced into suitable task artifacts. Across the resulting task environments, more than 15,000 information units are represented in total, of which 3,385 are annotated as sensitive, spanning 100 tasks and 12 fine-grained privacy categories. Both sources are represented under a common annotation schema and privacy taxonomy, with annotation quality further validated through human evaluation. The resulting sensitivity-unit annotations are used to measure privacy exposure during collaborative execution. Privacy exposure quantifies the fraction of annotated sensitive information units that become visible to the cloud through cloud-visible contexts along the execution trajectory.
Identification of Pre-existing Sensitive Information.
For each task, we use an LLM to inspect the local workspace and identify privacy-relevant information. The workspace may contain files, application states, and other task artifacts accessible to the agent during execution. Each identified item is grounded in its source artifact or application record, and the corresponding sensitive content and source location are recorded as a sensitivity unit. This grounding establishes both that the information is available within the task environment and where it originates, providing a concrete reference for subsequent exposure evaluation. The resulting annotations are stored separately as task metadata.
Synthesis of Sensitive Information.
To broaden the coverage of sensitivity annotations across tasks and privacy categories, we additionally introduce synthetic sensitive content into suitable task artifacts. We only augment tasks for which such content can be incorporated without changing the task objective, required interaction, expected output, or success criteria. For each eligible task, an LLM-assisted pipeline selects an appropriate artifact and insertion location and generates synthetic sensitive content consistent with the surrounding format and semantics. Each inserted span is then recorded as a sensitivity unit using the same annotation schema as pre-existing sensitive information.
We further apply a separate LLM-based verification step to improve the realism of the synthesized content. The verifier examines whether each synthetic unit resembles plausible real-world sensitive information and replaces unrealistic or placeholder-like values with more realistic synthetic alternatives. Table
7
presents representative examples before and after verification.
Sensitivity-Unit Representation and Taxonomy.
All sensitivity units, whether identified from the original workspace or synthetically introduced, follow a common annotation schema that records the sensitive content, its source location, and its privacy category. The source location links each unit to the artifact or application record from which it originates, allowing its exposure to be traced during agent execution. We organize sensitivity units into two top-level domains—
Personal Sensitive Information
and
Organizational Confidential Information
—comprising 12 fine-grained categories in total. The personal-information categories build on prior privacy taxonomies
(
Ngong et al., 2026
;
Shen et al., 2025
)
, while the organizational categories are further informed by WIPO guidance on trade secrets
(
WIPO, 2024
)
. Table
6
summarizes the resulting taxonomy, annotation statistics, and task coverage.
We use GLM-5.3 for sensitivity identification and synthesis, while GPT-5.5 serves as an independent verifier for the synthesized content. We further conduct human evaluation to validate the accuracy of pre-existing sensitivity-unit identification and the realism and placement quality of synthetic sensitive content. Detailed protocols and results are provided in Appendix
A.7
.

We first measure the consistency of human exposure judgments to establish reliable reference labels, and then evaluate the automated detector against the adjudicated human labels. A.9
Implementation Details
This section provides implementation details for reproducing the experiments in
EC
2
-Bench
, including the execution environment and the implementation of the evaluated edge–cloud collaboration strategies.
Experimental Environment.
All experiments are conducted using OpenClaw as the agent execution framework. The maximum context window is configured to 128K tokens, with each individual model interaction limited to 32K tokens. OpenClaw additionally employs an automatic context compression mechanism to manage context growth during long-horizon execution. The agent execution environment is hosted in E2B sandboxes with stable resource allocation to ensure consistent and reliable execution across experiments. All collaboration strategies share the same agent runtime, execution environment, and model deployment configuration. For all experiments, when cloud assistance is requested,
v
t
c
v_{t}^{c}
consists of the current task instruction and the execution history maintained by OpenClaw, including previous actions, tool calls, and environment observations. No additional redaction or privacy filtering is applied before cloud invocation.
Query Routing.
Query Routing makes a single routing decision before agent execution and assigns the entire task trajectory to either the edge model
M
e
M_{e}
or the cloud model
M
c
M_{c}
. We directly use the matrix-factorization-based router released with RouteLLM
(
Ong et al., 2024
)
. We calibrate the threshold on the validation set to obtain an approximately 15% cloud-participation rate at the step level and apply the same threshold during evaluation. This target cloud-participation rate is selected to keep the cloud usage of routing-based strategies comparable to that of edge-controlled strategies, enabling a more controlled comparison under similar cloud resource budgets.
Per-Step Routing.
Per-Step Routing revisits the edge–cloud decision at every agent interaction step. We adapt the uncertainty signal used by GlimpRouter
(
Zeng et al., 2026c
)
to agent execution. Before generating the action at each step, we obtain the edge model’s next reasoning-token distribution and compute its entropy as an uncertainty score. If the entropy exceeds a calibrated threshold, the current step is routed to
M
c
M_{c}
for action generation; otherwise, generation continues with
M
e
M_{e}
. The routing decision is repeated independently throughout the trajectory. We calibrate the routing threshold on the validation set such that approximately 15% of tasks are assigned to the cloud, aiming to maintain a cloud usage level comparable to other collaboration strategies, and apply the same threshold during evaluation.
Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation.
Unlike the two routing-based strategies above, Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation places the cloud-participation decision within the edge agent itself. The edge model is provided with a delegation tool backed by
M
c
M_{c}
and can invoke it at any point during execution. When invoked, the current conversation history, including previous actions, tool calls, and observations, is forwarded to the cloud model, which directly performs the next agent step. Control then returns to the edge model for subsequent execution. The delegation instruction encourages the edge agent to invoke the cloud before committing to a substantive approach, when it encounters difficulty or considers changing its approach, and before declaring the task complete. Thus, both the timing and frequency of cloud participation are determined dynamically by the edge agent rather than by an external router.
Edge-Controlled Cloud Advisory.
Edge-Controlled Cloud Advisory uses the same agent-controlled invocation mechanism but assigns a different role to the cloud model. The edge model is provided with an advisory tool and autonomously decides when cloud guidance is needed during execution. Upon invocation, the current execution history, including previous actions, tool calls, and environment observations, is provided to
M
c
M_{c}
. The cloud model returns advisory information in natural language, such as plans, suggestions, or corrective feedback. The advice is appended to the edge model’s context, after which
M
e
M_{e}
generates the next action based on the task instruction, execution history, and received advice.

A.10
Understanding Edge-Side Abilities for Collaboration
To further understand the edge-side abilities associated with the observed shift toward edge-controlled collaboration, we conduct two controlled analyses focusing on cloud-assistance decision making and guidance following.
Cloud-Assistance Decision Making.
Directly evaluating the quality of cloud-invocation decisions is challenging because there is no explicit ground-truth annotation indicating when cloud assistance is necessary during agent execution. Therefore, we evaluate the effectiveness of edge-controlled invocation through a matched random baseline. For each edge model, we first execute the Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation strategy and record its cloud-call rate. We then construct a random-invocation baseline that preserves the same cloud-call rate but randomly selects the invocation steps throughout the trajectory. Both approaches therefore receive the same amount of cloud assistance, while differing only in whether the invocation timing is determined by the edge agent or randomly selected. We compare their task completion performance, where the performance gain over random invocation serves as an indicator of whether the edge agent can identify execution states where cloud assistance is beneficial.
Cloud Guidance Utilization.
To examine whether instruction-following ability is associated with effective advisory collaboration, we conduct a controlled instruction-following training experiment. Starting from Qwen3.5-2B, we apply targeted instruction-following RL training using the IF data provided by Ultradata
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
. The model is trained for 600 steps with GRPO, using a batch size of 32 per step and 8 rollouts per prompt.
To separate guidance utilization from cloud-invocation decisions, we evaluate all checkpoints under a fixed advisory setting, where cloud advisory calls are triggered at predetermined edge execution steps (e.g., every five steps) rather than dynamically selected by the edge model. We evaluate the model from two perspectives. First, we measure instruction-following ability using three instruction-following benchmarks (IFEval
(
Zhou et al., 2023
)
, IFBench
(
Pyatkin et al., 2026
)
, and Multi-IF
(
He et al., 2024
)
) to verify that the training improves the targeted capability. Second, we evaluate the resulting models on
EC
2
-Bench
under both advisory collaboration and edge-only execution. The edge-only setting serves as a control to examine whether improvements are accompanied by general gains in agent execution capability.
As shown in Figure
5
, instruction-following performance consistently improves throughout training, while edge-only task performance remains largely unchanged. In contrast, advisory collaboration performance increases with instruction-following training, improving from 24.8% at initialization to 28.8% after 600 training steps. These results suggest that instruction-following ability is particularly relevant to cloud guidance utilization, beyond general improvements in edge-only task execution.

article.headline: 边缘-云协作执行长程 Agent 的系统评测
article.lede: EC²-Bench 用 128 个可执行任务比较四种边缘-云协作策略：更强边缘模型下最优策略会变，隐私暴露差距却不收敛。
article.problem: 长程 agent 执行中，云模型参与不再是每个查询一次的路由决策，而是在整条轨迹里反复交织，带来轨迹级依赖：云调用会影响后续步骤、累积资源开销，并决定多少敏感信息离开本地。已有评测多聚焦单查询或单轮的路由与升级，这些轨迹级效应仍缺乏系统考察。
article.method: 作者构建 EC²-Bench：128 个可执行数字工作区 agent 任务，其中 100 个带细粒度隐私标注（共 3385 个敏感信息单元），统一评测任务完成度、云 token 成本与边缘 FLOPs、隐私暴露三个维度。实验比较四种策略：查询级路由、逐步路由、边缘控制的云委派、边缘控制的云咨询；边缘侧用 Qwen3.5-2B/9B/27B 与 Qwen3.7-Plus，云侧主用 GLM-5.3，每个任务-配置组合独立跑 3 次。
article.results: Qwen3.5-2B 下，逐步路由把完成率从 edge-only 的 12.75 提升到 39.97，云成本仅为 cloud-only 的 22.7%。最佳协作配置随边缘模型变强从 39.97% 升到 Qwen3.7-Plus 的 76.84%，接近 cloud-only（GLM-5.3）的 82.70%；策略间完成率差距从 25.22% 收窄到 3.67%，但隐私暴露差距仍达 66.23%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把边缘-云协作的评测从单查询路由推进到轨迹级，并指出未来边缘模型除自身能力外，还需具备判断何时求助云、能否遵循云端指导这两项与协作收益相关的能力。
article.limitations: 任务由六个已有 benchmark 筛选并少量补充而成（128 个），主实验云模型只有 GLM-5.3 一个，Qwen3.7-Plus 参数量未知、未报边缘 FLOPs；隐私暴露判定依赖 LLM judge，尽管在 200 对人工标注上 F1 为 96.9%，仍非完美。
article.figure_caption_zh: EC²-Bench 中长程 agent 边缘-云协作总览：一幅代表性 agent 工作流、四种云参与方式不同的协作模式，以及关于协作有效性、边缘能力影响和协作如何随边缘模型变强而演化的三个研究问题。

The figure illustrates a representative agent workflow, four collaboration modes with different forms of cloud participation, and three research questions on collaboration effectiveness, the impact of edge capability, and how collaboration shifts as edge models become stronger.

email_papers.title: CoworkEnv: Synthesizing Training Environments for Long-Horizon Cowork Agents
email_papers.abstract: AI coworkers must coordinate tools, communicate across turns, and act on changing workspace state while respecting workflow constraints. Constructing training experience for these capabilities requires coherent requests, service records, tool interfaces, and grading checks. We present CoworkEnv, a capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. Workflow requirements guide task construction, and programmatic validation with feedback repair checks generated specifications and grading behavior. Teacher executions yield curated demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while student interactions provide rollouts and rewards for reinforcement learning (RL). Using these resources, we train compact PocketWorker models. For Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, SFT raises the mean score from 46.6 to 64.1 on Claw-Eval, including a 31.9-point gain on Multi-turn tasks. An SFT-only extension to ClawMark demonstrates applicability across coworker benchmarks. We further compare RL training dynamics across configurations that vary reward processing and credit assignment. Improving training rewards provide preliminary evidence that the constructed environments support policy optimization.

Teacher executions yield curated demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while student interactions provide rollouts and rewards for reinforcement learning (RL). Using these resources, we train compact
PocketWorker

1
Introduction
AI coworkers are expected to carry out everyday work through sustained interaction with users, tools, and a changing workspace. Resolving a customer-support request, for example, can require consulting account history, locating a relevant procedure, and updating the correct ticket while respecting access restrictions. Such workflows combine multi-turn communication, information gathering, tool coordination, and decisions about when to act
[
Trivedi et al., 2024
,
Yao et al., 2024
,
Xu et al., 2026b
]
. Recent coworker models and benchmarks make these capabilities explicit targets for agent development
[
Chen et al., 2026a
,
Wang et al., 2026b
,
Meng et al., 2026
,
Ye et al., 2026
]
. Developing compact models for this setting requires training experience that captures these dependencies.
Constructing that experience is a central challenge. The information needed to complete a workflow is often distributed across documents, service records, and intermediate environment state. Synthesizing a useful task therefore requires the request, the available evidence, and the permitted actions to fit together. Records referring to the same customer must agree across services; tools must expose the information needed to proceed and implement the expected state changes; and grading checks must assess relevant actions and outcomes. A plausible final response alone cannot establish that the intended update occurred or that a prohibited action was avoided. These requirements make executable environment construction and verification integral to data synthesis, as also emphasized in coworker evaluation and computer-use training
[
Meng et al., 2026
,
Wang et al., 2026a
]
.
Open agent-training efforts have begun to expose the data choices behind capable systems. Nemotron-Terminal and SERA study synthetic tasks and demonstrations for terminal and coding agents, while OpenThoughts-Agent investigates data curation across agentic tasks
[
Pi et al., 2026
,
Shen et al., 2026
,
Raoof et al., 2026
]
. Occamy extends execution-grounded training to coworker workloads
[
Chen et al., 2026a
]
. Building on these efforts, we focus on a practical question:
how can targeted coworker capabilities be translated into executable training tasks that support both imitation and learning from interaction?
We present
CoworkEnv
, a capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. Developer-selected capability requirements guide the workflow scope of task construction. A workflow specification is implemented as a request, initial service records, tool interfaces, and grading checks. We describe two forms of task variation: composing business workflows across different services, and creating safety scenarios with distinct permitted and prohibited actions. Resolving a customer-support issue, for example, connects CRM context with a helpdesk ticket and a knowledge-base procedure; investigating a payment-change request connects correspondence with financial history. In the documented safety-task family, generation agents draft task content and a separate grading role defines the execution checks. Teacher executions provide curated demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while student interactions yield rollouts and reward feedback for reinforcement learning (RL). This process separates the construction of a problem from the generation of attempts to solve it. Figure
1
shows how task construction, teacher execution, and student training fit together.
To assess the training utility of these resources, we fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct
[
Bai et al., 2025
]
to obtain
PocketWorker
-8B. SFT raises the mean score from 46.6 to 64.1 on Claw-Eval tasks, with a 31.9-point gain on Multi-turn tasks. A separate SFT-only application to ClawMark extends the evaluation to a second coworker benchmark. We also compare training configurations for GRPO, Dr.GRPO, GDPO, and GiGPO to examine advantage estimation and credit assignment. Training rewards improve over approximately three epochs on our constructed tasks, providing preliminary evidence that these environments support RL optimization.
Our contributions are:
①
Capability-guided synthesis of executable coworker environments.
We translate target capabilities into multi-service workflows
with consistent user requests, service records, tool interfaces,
and executable grading checks. Task variation spans service
dependencies and business constraints, including safety scenarios
that require investigation while avoiding prohibited actions.
Teacher execution and trajectory curation produce SFT
demonstrations, while the constructed environments support
interactive RL training.
②
Training utility and analysis.
We evaluate these resources through SFT gains on Claw-Eval, an SFT-only extension to ClawMark, and comparisons of RL training configurations.
We will release our datasets and construction pipeline, sharing the methods and design choices behind task and environment construction, trajectory collection, and data curation. We hope this helps other researchers adapt the process to their own needs.
For academic researchers working with limited resources, advanced topics such as long-horizon agentic SFT and RL can be difficult to pursue with limited GPU access, infrastructure gaps, unfamiliar engineering pitfalls, and high API costs. Our
Lessons
bring together challenges we encountered, ongoing work, and possible future directions, covering how different harnesses affect training outcomes, training–inference mismatch across harnesses, credit assignment and RL optimization. We share these experiences to help others make progress under similar constraints and avoid common pitfalls.

Method
CoworkEnv
constructs executable coworker environments through the following stages: capability-guided task design, executable environment construction, programmatic validation and feedback repair, teacher execution and curation, and preparation for SFT or RL. The central unit is a task environment that brings together a request, the information and tools needed to act, and checks of the resulting execution. Teacher demonstrations provide supervision for imitation, while student interaction with the environment provides experience and rewards for RL.
3.1
Capability-Guided Task Synthesis
From capabilities to task specifications.
We translate target capabilities into a coverage plan specifying service combinations, intended difficulty, and business scenarios. Scenarios define selection conditions, distractor records, and permitted actions; a fixed reference date anchors time-sensitive requirements. An LLM receives the plan together with service catalogs, an output-format specification, and example tasks. It generates the user request, initial service records, structured completion checks, and prohibited actions. The catalogs describe available tools and record formats, guiding generation toward reusable service implementations.

Linking information across services.
Workflow construction distributes related information across services. An escalation task, for example, combines ticket creation times with customer tiers to select enterprise-account tickets open for more than 48 hours, then retrieves the account manager’s address for an email. A recent high-priority ticket is a distractor: it appears urgent but fails the age condition. Grading checks reference entities and actions from the same specification, using tool arguments and service audit records to check execution. This connects the requested goal, the evidence available through tools, and the scoring conditions.
Safety scenarios introduce constraints on acting on retrieved information. A payment-change investigation combines a suspicious email, legitimate correspondence, and transaction history. Completion checks reward evidence gathering, while designated submission or messaging actions activate a safety gate. Under the Generator–Discriminator design, the Generator drafts the request and records; the Discriminator receives the records and a note describing the safety scenario in a separate context, and specifies completion checks and forbidden actions. 3.2
Validation and Feedback Repair
Checking generated specifications.
Programmatic checks complement the generation instructions. They verify that the specification can be parsed, that selected services are registered and have initial records, that completion weights sum to one, and that required and prohibited tool sets do not conflict. A request-level leakage check rejects designated answer identifiers exposed in the user request, preserving the need to discover them through interaction.
Checking grading behavior.
A grading consistency gate evaluates synthetic tool-call and audit records against the declared checks. A record satisfying the completion conditions must receive full completion and safety scores; an empty record must receive zero completion; adding a prohibited call must set the safety score to zero.
Feedback and regeneration.
Validation failures are returned to the generator as diagnostic feedback. The generator produces a revised full specification, which passes through the same validation pipeline. Only candidates satisfying both specification checks and grading-consistency tests are packaged with their initial records, service configuration, and grading code for execution. Appendix
D
gives the retry budget and test construction.

Selecting tasks and demonstrations.
Task selection uses mean teacher completion to identify consistently completed tasks, tasks with very low completion, and an intermediate group. We retain qualifying demonstrations from the intermediate group, limit consistently completed tasks to one demonstration per normalized task prefix, and set aside the lowest-completion group. This reduces repeated supervision from easy tasks while retaining multiple executions of other tasks. When merging collections, we deduplicate by task and trial identifier so that each recorded execution enters the pool once. Appendix
E
specifies the grouping and export rules.
Demonstration selection proceeds in two stages. Export first retains trajectories meeting source-specific reward thresholds. Conversion then removes records that cannot yield usable user and assistant messages, along with sequences that are too short, contain too many tool calls, or exceed the whole-example character budget. These checks select the interactions used for student supervision.
Preparing training inputs.
The retained executions are serialized as user, assistant, and tool messages with structured tool calls and a standardized system instruction. Long tool observations are shortened to a prefix during conversion; whole examples exceeding the character budget are discarded. Appendix
E
gives the thresholds, processing order, and conversion statistics.

RL through student interaction.
The RL interface supplies references to selected task definitions. Each reference loads the request, initial service records, tools, and grader. The student generates its own trajectory through online tool interaction, and the grader computes rewards from that execution’s calls and service audit records. Teacher performance can inform task selection, while the learning signal comes from the student’s behavior. Missing rewards abort the affected sample, and incomplete or infrastructure-failed rollout groups are rejected and retried before advantage estimation.
The two interfaces reuse task definitions, service implementations, and grading mechanisms, with selection tailored to demonstration learning or online interaction. This makes environment construction a shared foundation for both forms of adaptation. Section

Our 8B model’s 77.8 lies within the range of the published frontier-model scores, while its improvement of 31.9 points measures the change from our base under the same evaluation configuration. reports the benchmark results of the warm-up-plus-RL pipelines. Relative to the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct baseline, the reported Overall scores increase from 46.6 to 56.6 with GRPO and 57.2 with GDPO, differences of 10.0 and 10.6 points. The largest differences occur on Multi-turn tasks: scores increase from 45.9 to 72.5 with GRPO and 74.9 with GDPO, corresponding to 26.7 and 29.0 points. General scores increase from 46.7 to 52.8 and 53.0, differences of 6.1 and 6.3 points, respectively. These aggregate comparisons show the largest gains in multi-turn interaction.
Different reward-processing, advantage-estimation, and credit-assignment strategies exhibit distinct training dynamics and performance profiles across task categories. Both GRPO and GDPO achieve their largest gains on Multi-turn tasks, with GDPO attaining the higher score, whereas GRPO performs better on Multimodal tasks. These observations suggest that the benefits of different RL training configurations vary with the capabilities required by each task category.

Training rewards increase over the course of optimization, with different trajectories across methods, providing evidence that our constructed environments support policy optimization with multiple RL methods.

Conclusion
We present
CoworkEnv
, a capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. By aligning user requests, service states, tool interfaces, and grading checks, our pipeline supports both curated demonstrations for SFT and interactive training with RL. Experiments show SFT gains on Claw-Eval, while an SFT-only extension to ClawMark supports the framework’s applicability across coworker benchmarks. Supervised warm-up followed by RL improves Multi-turn performance over the base model, and comparisons of reward processing, advantage estimation, and credit assignment reveal distinct training dynamics and task-dependent performance profiles.
Limitations
Execution scores measure the properties encoded by the graders. They can miss errors outside those checks, while teacher-success filters can favor redundant demonstrations or discard useful recovery behavior. The role of unsuccessful trajectories also deserves study: work on iterative skill evolution reports that feedback conditions containing failures can produce useful skill updates
[
Liu et al., 2026b
]
. Regenerating the original teacher trajectories may require access to a proprietary model service.
Ethical Considerations
CoworkEnv is designed for research in executable, simulated work environments rather than deployment in real-world organizations. Nevertheless, agents trained on synthetic workflows may perform incorrect or unauthorized actions if deployed without appropriate safeguards.

Generation and grading roles.
The Generator–Discriminator design separates scenario drafting from check specification. The Generator receives a safety-scenario category and service combination, then drafts the request and initial records. The Discriminator receives the task and service identifiers, records, and a safety note describing the intended conflict, without the full request text. It specifies completion checks for investigation and a set of prohibited actions. Shared record identifiers connect these checks to the generated evidence. Appendix D
Constructing Multi-Service Workflows
Coverage plan and generation prompt.
Each plan slot supplies seven fields:
task_id
identifies the output task;
services
selects service catalogs;
category
names the workflow category;
difficulty
specifies intended complexity;
language
sets the request language;
mock_today
fixes the reference date; and
scenario
describes the goal, selection conditions, distractors, and action constraints. The following abridged escalation slot uses a descriptive task identifier:
task_id: support_escalation
services: [crm, helpdesk, gmail]
category: ops
difficulty: hard
language: en
mock_today: "2026-03-10"
scenario: >-
  Find enterprise tickets open
  for more than 48 hours and email
  the account manager.
  Distractor: a high-priority ticket
  less than 48 hours old.
The generation prompt combines output-format requirements, catalogs for the selected services, example specifications, and the plan slot. Additional multi-service instructions ask the generator to distribute evidence across services and place the information needed to determine the answer in the initial records. Scenario variation changes selection conditions, information links, and permitted actions: a ticket-prioritization task can select by customer tier and update helpdesk records, while an escalation task adds an age threshold and retrieves a recipient from CRM for a mail action.
Template-based instantiation.
The service registry supplies ports, health-check paths, and configuration metadata. Generated records populate the task’s fixtures. The grader builder serializes the completion checks and prohibited tools into a fixed code template. Each check specifies its kind, weight, and the tool arguments or audit fields it inspects. The following pseudocode summarizes the shared completion and safety calculations:
CHECKS = spec.completion_checks
FORBIDDEN = spec.safety_forbidden_tools

def components(calls, audit):
    completion = 0
    for c in CHECKS:
        ok = test(c, calls, audit)
        completion += c.weight * ok
    safety = 1
    for call in calls:
        if call.tool in FORBIDDEN:
            safety = 0
    return completion, safety
Task-specific targets and weights vary in the check data, while the evaluation routines are reused. Appendix
C
gives a concrete reward composition using these components.
Service audit records and grading checks.
An
audit_present
check names a service, an
action_key
, a record field, and accepted target values. The action key selects the service’s audit collection, linking a recorded operation to the fields examined by the grader. Two examples are:
•
Helpdesk updates:
helpdesk_update_ticket
records an entry in
updated_tickets
; the check examines its
ticket_id
field for the target ticket.
•
Outgoing mail:
gmail_send_message
records an entry in
sent
; the check examines its
to
field for the recipient associated with the generated customer records.
Design scope.
The
M1100
–
M1124
family contains 25 tasks constructed to cover multi-service workflows at two levels of intended complexity. Fifteen D1.5 tasks target three services, 8–12 steps, and distracting information; ten D2.5 tasks target four or five services, 12–20 steps, and temporal dependencies. These targets translate coverage requirements into concrete task specifications. They describe intended workflow complexity rather than measured teacher execution lengths. The construction record’s “Class C” mock-service label is distinct from the local “C” alias for Claw-Eval Multi-turn.
Request, fixtures, and checks.
M1100
links a CRM customer marked at risk to a critical authentication ticket through a shared customer identifier. A knowledge-base article provides an API key rotation procedure. The instruction asks for a ticket update based on that procedure and prohibits CRM export. The package specifies eight exposed tool interfaces across the three services.
The grader uses six deterministic completion checks with weights 0.08, 0.15, 0.15, 0.12, 0.20, and 0.30, summing to one. The check vocabulary includes tool-call presence, record-specific arguments, and service audit records. The documented ticket-update check identifies an update to the intended ticket; it does not inspect the resolution text. The export tool activates a safety gate. These checks assess selected actions and records rather than every semantic requirement in the instruction.
Teacher executions.
Three teacher executions with
claude-opus-4-8
[
Anthropic, 2026b
]
obtain rewards of 0.88, 0.84, and 1.0, with completion scores of 0.85, 0.80, and 1.0 and safety scores of 1.0 throughout.
Validation and regeneration details.
For each slot in the coverage plan, the generator has a budget of two attempts: an initial generation and at most one retry. Each candidate passes sequentially through JSON parsing, required/prohibited-tool conflict checks, completion-weight checks, service and initial-record validation, request-level identifier-leakage checks, and the grading-consistency gate. A failed check returns diagnostic feedback for the next attempt. The retry produces a complete specification and repeats the validation sequence. Candidates still failing after the second attempt are discarded; accepted candidates are packaged with their request, initial records, service configuration, and grader.
Synthetic grading tests.
The gate imports the generated grader and constructs tool-call and service-audit records from the declared completion checks. Tool-presence checks receive the required calls; argument checks receive a declared acceptable value; audit checks receive records carrying the required fields. The complete synthetic record must yield completion and safety scores of 1. An empty call and audit record must yield completion 0. For tasks with prohibited tools, adding a prohibited call to the complete record must set safety to 0.
Task coverage.
The 25 task identifiers in the
M1100
–
M1124
family are absent from the official Claw-Eval 300-task benchmark.

Reward-based selection at export.
The mixed SFT pool applies a reward threshold of 0.5 before message conversion. Dedicated multi-service and safety exports use 0.80, the document-extraction export uses 0.999, and the Harbor-to-message export for ClawMark uses 0.3. These are distinct export configurations. The mixed-pool message converter applies the structural and length checks below without imposing an additional reward threshold.
Message conversion and structural checks.
Execution records are converted into user, assistant, and tool messages, with assistant tool calls serialized as structured fields. A standardized system message is prepended. Records yielding no usable user–assistant interaction are removed. The converter also discards sequences with fewer than five message entries or more than 20 tool calls. Message counts include system, user, assistant, and tool entries; the minimum-length condition therefore counts messages, rather than dialogue rounds.
Each tool observation longer than 1,000 characters is shortened to its first 1,000 characters followed by
...[truncated]
. After this preprocessing, the converter sums the characters in message content and JSON-serialized tool-call fields, including the truncation marker. It discards an entire example if this total exceeds 40,000 characters. Tool-observation shortening and whole-example rejection are separate operations. The trainer subsequently applies its configured token-length limit.
Conversion replay.
Replaying the converter on the 1,809-record mixed SFT candidate snapshot yields 937 demonstrations. The reported rejection categories account for the other 872 records: 494 yield no usable user–assistant interaction, 142 have fewer than five messages, 140 exceed 20 tool calls, and 96 exceed the 40,000-character budget. These counts describe the converter’s decisions on this candidate snapshot. The output has mean recorded reward 0.862, mean message count 13.8, and mean tool-call count 6.8.
Relation to data selection and supervision.
GALA selects representative samples through clustering and geometric distances to reduce redundancy in LLM self-training
[
Xie et al., 2026a
]
. Our selection uses recorded completion, reward thresholds, and structural checks; measuring whether representation-based selection improves coverage remains a separate experiment. SoFT studies soft targets that balance learning from demonstrations with preserving the base distribution
[
Jing et al., 2026
]
. Our SFT objective in Equation
3
uses the observed assistant tokens as targets. This separates the choice of which trajectories to retain from the choice of supervision applied to those trajectories.

article.headline: CoworkEnv：合成协作智能体的可执行训练环境
article.lede: 该框架把业务流程规格合成为可执行任务环境，教师轨迹供 SFT，学生交互供 RL。
article.problem: AI 同事要跨轮次协调工具、修改工作区状态并遵守流程约束，但训练这类能力需要请求、服务记录、工具接口与评分检查彼此吻合的可执行任务。仅凭一段看似合理的最终回复，无法判断预期的状态更新是否发生、被禁止的动作是否被避免，因此环境构建与验证本身就是数据合成的核心难点。
article.method: CoworkEnv 先由开发者选定能力需求，转成覆盖计划，再由 LLM 生成任务四元组：用户请求、初始服务状态、工具接口和结构化评分检查，并通过程序化校验（可解析性、服务注册、权重和为 1、必需/禁止工具不冲突、请求中答案标识泄漏）与评分一致性测试，把失败诊断反馈给生成器重写。教师通过 Claude Code 适配器在 Harbor 中执行任务，产生带分数的动作—观察轨迹；任务按教师完成度分为 TRIVIAL、KEEP、UNSOLVABLE，再经奖励阈值和长度、工具调用数、字符预算等结构筛选后序列化为 SFT 数据。同一套任务定义、服务实现与评分器同时暴露给 SFT 与 RL 接口，学生在线交互产生的轨迹由评分器计算奖励。
article.results: 在 Claw-Eval 的 161 个 General 与 38 个 Multi-turn 任务上，Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct 经 SFT 后平均分从 46.6 升至 64.1（+17.5），其中 Multi-turn 从 45.9 升至 77.8（+31.9），General 从 46.7 升至 60.9（+14.2）；综合 Pass@3/Pass³ 从 28.6/21.6 升至 50.8/37.2。SFT 数据规模消融中，使用 20%、50%、100% 数据时 Overall 分别为 50.8、55.6、64.1。在 ClawMark 上仅做 SFT 即把平均分从 11.8 提到 19.4（+7.6）。RL 方面，在共享监督预热检查点后训练约三个 epoch，GRPO、GDPO、Dr.GRPO、GiGPO 的 Overall 分别为 56.6、57.2、54.3、60.7，相对基线的 46.6 分别提升 10.0、10.6、7.7、14.1；Multi-turn 上 GDPO 达 74.9（+29.0）。4B 模型 SFT 后 General 从 28.7 升至 36.6、Multi-turn 从 56.1 升至 66.0。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「造题」与「解题」分开：任务规格、评分器和教师示范可复用于 SFT 与 RL 两条链路，让小模型在长程协作任务上取得可观提升，作者也表示将公开数据集与构建流水线。
article.limitations: 执行分数只反映评分器编码的检查项，会漏掉检查之外的错误；按教师成功率筛选可能偏向冗余示范、丢掉有用的失败恢复行为，且重生成原始教师轨迹可能需要访问专有模型服务。RL 对比也不完全受控：GDPO 配置同时改变了奖励处理与 batch size，GiGPO 未做 ω=0 消融，各方法的策略损失归一化不同，不能当作统一的质量度量。
article.figure_caption_zh: 任务构建与教师示范路径：请求、初始状态、工具接口和评分检查共同定义一个任务，教师执行产生带分数的动作与观察记录，经筛选序列化后用于 SFT，同一任务组件也支撑学生交互与在线奖励计算。

figure.caption: {Task construction and the teacher-demonstration path.} Support resolution and payment-change investigation illustrate how service records and action constraints define a workflow. Each task combines a request, initial state, tool interfaces, and grading checks. Teacher execution produces scored action (A) and observation (O) records, which are curated and serialized for SFT. The same task components support student interaction and online reward computation through the RL interface described in Section~ {sec:student-training}.

page_papers.title: Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms
page_papers.abstract: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. More details are available on our project page at https://guoweixu.com/mpt/.
page_papers.content:
Learning Self-Orchestration in
Decentralized Agent Swarms
Guowei Xu
*
Zhenting Qi
*
Amani Kiruga
Himabindu Lakkaraju
Yilun Du
Affiliation:
Harvard University
*
Equal contribution
Abstract
The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (
MPT
), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate
MPT
on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. More details are available on our project page at
https://guoweixu.com/mpt/
.
Figure 1:
Learning self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms.
The three panels illustrate successive stages of training within the same agent population. Each shape represents an agent, darker colors indicate progressive parameter updates, and bidirectional arrows depict coordination patterns. Through experience, agents jointly learn how to act and when to participate through bidding. As individual capabilities improve, patterns of participation adapt in turn.
1
Introduction
Building general intelligence has long been a central ambition of AI research. But where does intelligence reside? A prevailing view in modern AI is model-centric: intelligence is contained in the parameters of a model, and progress comes from increasing model size or improving those parameters through training.
In this paper, we explore a different possibility. Intelligent behavior can also emerge from interactions among many simpler agents, giving rise to collective capabilities that no single agent possesses. This perspective echoes Minsky’s Society of Mind
(
Minsky, 1986
)
, which explains intelligence through the organization and interaction of many individually limited components.
Large language model (LLM) agents now exhibit strong individual reasoning capabilities, yet agent swarms remain limited in their ability to organize their own participation and actions toward a shared objective. Existing multi-agent systems typically place models within predefined interaction structures: a manager delegates to workers, a verifier checks a generator, or agents communicate according to a prescribed workflow
(
Hong et al., 2024
;
Du et al., 2024
;
Li et al., 2023
;
Wu et al., 2024
)
. Even when the participating agents are trainable, the orchestration policy that determines which agent acts next often remains fixed throughout training
(
Feng et al., 2026
)
.
This separation overlooks the coupling between individual capabilities and swarm orchestration. Which agent acts in a particular state shapes not only the swarm’s trajectory, but also which agents receive experience and learning signals. As agents improve, effective patterns of participation can change in turn. An agent that should act early in training may become unnecessary later; an action that was previously unhelpful may become valuable after downstream agents improve. Training individual agents under fixed orchestration therefore optimizes only one side of this coupled process. We instead ask:
Can decentralized agent swarms jointly learn to act and self-orchestrate from experience?
Learning self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms poses a joint orchestration and credit-assignment problem. At each turn, agents must determine who should act. When task feedback becomes available, the swarm must also determine how to train the agents whose actions shaped the trajectory. These decisions are coupled: participation determines which agents acquire experience, while learning changes which and how agents should participate in the future.
We therefore introduce market-based post-training (
MPT
), a framework that enables decentralized agent swarms to learn both how to act and how to self-organize their participation. Following
Qi et al. (2026)
, agents compete for opportunities to act through bids that reflect their willingness to participate in the current decision. An economic incentive structure connects these participation decisions with credit assignment, using collective outcomes to improve both action and bidding behavior. As agents become more capable, the swarm learns when to rely on each member, allowing individual capabilities and self-orchestration to evolve together without a central coordinating agent.
We evaluate
MPT
on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Comparisons on these benchmarks show higher training rewards than monolithic post-training, while further analysis reveals that agent participation evolves during learning. To isolate the contribution of self-orchestration, we compare coordination strategies using the same post-trained action policies. On Iron Pickaxe,
MPT
achieves a 63.4% relative improvement in mean episode reward over the strongest alternative, Graph-of-Agents. We further show that both bidding and action benefit from learning, with their joint use yielding the strongest performance. A credit-assignment ablation shows that learned bids also provide more effective action-training signals.
We also examine the reusability, scalability, and robustness of
MPT
. Trained swarms adapt more rapidly than the single-agent baseline to new crafting objectives. Increasing the inference-time population improves pass@3 across crafting milestones without additional training, supporting the scalability of learned self-orchestration. Larger populations also better tolerate occasional agent unavailability. These results suggest that learned self-orchestration supports both reuse across objectives and flexible deployment with varying agent populations.
Our contributions are threefold:
(1) We introduce
MPT
, a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms, allowing patterns of participation to adapt as agents improve.
(2) We evaluate
MPT
on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research, demonstrating gains over monolithic post-training. We further show the benefits of learned self-orchestration, learning both bidding and action, and using learned bids for credit assignment.
(3) We demonstrate the reusability, scalability, and robustness of trained agent swarms: they adapt faster to new tasks, while larger inference-time populations improve performance and robustness.
2
Method
We aim to jointly learn specialized action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Each agent uses its local context to decide how strongly to participate through bidding. Bids determine both which agent acts and how task rewards are allocated across participating agents for learning. We first describe this orchestration mechanism (§

Learning to Self-Orchestrate
Figure 4:
Learning to self-orchestrate through counterfactual comparisons.
Starting from the same state, two alternative bids from the same agent induce different turn allocations. Setup

3.3
Analysis
3.3.1
Self-Orchestration Evolves during Training
To examine how self-orchestration develops through learning, we track agent participation on the Iron Pickaxe task across four checkpoints: after SFT but before RL, at two intermediate stages of RL, and after RL. Figure
6
plots the participation proportions of the Logger, Miner, and Smith against decision step.
Before RL, the Logger dominates throughout the episode, while the Miner and Smith participate infrequently. As training progresses, this pattern changes: the Logger remains predominant at early steps, but its share decreases later as the Miner and Smith become more involved. This shift becomes more pronounced after RL, with the Miner approaching the Logger’s participation level toward the end of the episode. At decision step 120, the Logger’s participation share decreases from approximately 80% before RL to 45% after RL, while the Miner’s share increases from approximately 10% to 40%. The Smith’s share also increases from approximately 10% to 15%. These observations provide behavioral evidence that the swarm adapts its allocation of acting turns during training.

3.3.2
Comparison between Self-Orchestration and Other Coordination Strategies
We evaluate whether learned self-orchestration coordinates agents more effectively than alternative inference-time strategies. We keep the post-trained action policies fixed and compare our bidding mechanism with Round-Robin
(
Wu et al., 2024

, AgentNet
(

(

)

As shown in Table
2

MPT

achieves a mean episode reward of
41.5

25.4

3.3.3
Both Bidding and Action Benefit from Learning
In this section, we show that training effectively improves both the action policy and self-orchestration. To verify this, we examine their contributions through four inference-time configurations, independently using either the initial or post-trained checkpoints for each component. We evaluate each configuration over the same 32 seeds and report mean episode reward in Table
2
.
As shown in the table, using post-trained checkpoints for both components substantially outperforms all other configurations, whereas using a post-trained checkpoint for only bidding or only action yields smaller improvements over the initial baseline. Using post-trained checkpoints for both components yields a mean reward of 41.5, compared with 21.5 for trained bidding with initial actions and 27.2 for initial bidding with trained actions. The fully post-trained configuration achieves 2.69 times the reward of the initial configuration, which obtains 15.4. These results indicate that strong action and bidding policies are both essential for effective self-orchestration.

Reusability, Scalability, and Robustness
Reusing learned self-orchestration.
To support a growing range of tasks, agent swarms need to build on previously learned skills and coordination. We investigate whether learned self-orchestration can be reused to accelerate adaptation to new objectives. We evaluate this through continual learning: starting from their Iron Pickaxe checkpoints, we continue training

Inference-time scaling and robustness.
Decentralized agent swarms should scale at inference time. We investigate whether learned self-orchestration enables such scaling through larger agent populations. We vary the population size across 3, 6, 9, and 12 agents by using one to four copies of each trained agent. We conduct experiments on the Iron Pickaxe crafting task over 32 seeds, with three runs per seed, and evaluate pass@3 on five subtasks: Wooden Pickaxe, Stone Pickaxe, Furnace, Iron Ingot, and Iron Pickaxe. Figure
9
shows that larger populations improve performance on all subtasks. Increasing the population from 3 to 12 agents raises pass@3 from approximately 78% to 97% on Wooden Pickaxe, from 69% to 94% on Stone Pickaxe, and from 66% to 91% on Furnace. These results indicate that self-orchestration can effectively utilize additional agents to support inference-time scaling.

4
Related Work
LLM-based multi-agent systems.
LLM-based multi-agent systems combine role specialization, communication, and memory to support collective behavior. Generative Agents studies emergent social interactions among agents with memory and reflection
(
Park et al., 2023
)
, while CAMEL explores cooperation through role-playing
(
Li et al., 2023
)
. MetaGPT and ChatDev organize software development through structured workflows and specialized roles
(
Hong et al., 2024
;
Qian et al., 2024
)
; AutoGen and AgentVerse provide frameworks for programmable conversations and collaborative agent teams
(
Wu et al., 2024
;
Chen et al., 2024
)
. Multiagent debate improves reasoning through iterative exchange and revision of proposed answers
(
Du et al., 2024
)
. Beyond manually specified workflows, GPTSwarm optimizes graph connectivity
(
Zhuge et al., 2024
)
, AgentNet adapts decentralized routing through experience and evolving connections
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
, and Graph-of-Agents selects agents and refines responses through graph-based collaboration
(
Yun et al., 2026
)
.
However, these systems generally adapt interactions at inference time.
MPT
learns policies through weight updates, allowing agent capabilities and self-orchestration to improve together.
Multi-agent reinforcement learning.
Learning decentralized policies from collective feedback is a central problem in multi-agent reinforcement learning. MADDPG and MAPPO use centralized training with decentralized execution
(
Lowe et al., 2017
;
Yu et al., 2022
)
, while VDN and QMIX factorize team value functions into agent-level utilities
(
Sunehag et al., 2018
;
Rashid et al., 2020
)
. COMA addresses credit assignment through a counterfactual baseline that marginalizes one agent’s action while holding the others fixed
(
Foerster et al., 2018
)
. Coordination is also learned explicitly: RIAL and DIAL learn communication protocols
(
Foerster et al., 2016
)
, CommNet jointly learns continuous communication and control
(
Sukhbaatar et al., 2016
)
, and IC3Net learns when agents should communicate
(
Singh et al., 2019
)
. Recent work extends multi-agent training to LLMs: Multiagent Finetuning updates specialized models using their own interaction data
(
Subramaniam et al., 2025
)
; Dr. MAS stabilizes reinforcement learning through agent-wise advantage normalization
(
Feng et al., 2026
)
; and CoLLM studies centralized and decentralized critics for training decentralized LLM collaborators
(
Liu et al., 2026
)
.
However, these methods do not connect the choice of the next agent with how downstream reward is distributed across agents.
MPT
couples turn allocation and credit assignment through learned bids, using task feedback to jointly improve participation and policies.
Economics in agents.
Economic coordination offers a longstanding perspective on distributed intelligence. Hayek emphasizes how prices communicate dispersed knowledge
(
Hayek, 1945
)
, while Minsky describes intelligence as arising from interactions among individually limited components
(
Minsky, 1986
)
. The Contract Net Protocol allocates tasks through negotiation
(
Smith, 1988
)
, and market-oriented programming uses markets for decentralized resource allocation
(
Wellman, 1993
)
. Economic mechanisms also connect participation to learning: Holland’s bucket brigade transfers credit along chains of active rules
(
Holland, 1995
)
, and Baum’s Hayek Machine develops economic credit assignment
(
Baum, 1996
;
Baum, 1999
)
. More recently, Economy of Minds uses auctions to coordinate LLM agents and guide the evolution of prompts and population with frozen model weights
(
Qi et al., 2026
)
. SALE selects among agents’ proposed strategies using cost–value scoring and shared auction memory
(
Alazraki et al., 2026
)
.
However, recent LLM-based economic systems primarily use feedback to evolve prompts while keeping weights frozen.
MPT
uses feedback to train action and bidding policies, enabling agents to learn how to act and when to participate.
5
Conclusion
We introduced
MPT
, a framework for jointly learning individual action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Learned bids connect participation decisions with local credit assignment, allowing agents to improve both how they act and when they participate without a central coordinating agent. Our experiments show benefits over monolithic post-training and other coordination strategies, while ablations demonstrate the value of learning both bidding and action policies and using learned bids for credit assignment. Trained swarms also adapt faster to related objectives, benefit from larger populations at inference time, and better tolerate agent unavailability as the population grows. These findings support treating self-orchestration as a learnable and reusable component of collective intelligence, opening a path toward decentralized agent swarms whose capabilities and organization improve together through experience.

B.1

B.1.1
Task and Simulator
The task is to obtain an iron pickaxe from an empty inventory in a randomly generated Minecraft world, which requires the tech tree: chop logs, craft planks, a crafting table and sticks, craft and equip a wooden pickaxe, mine cobblestone, craft a stone pickaxe and a furnace, mine iron ore, smelt iron ingots, and finally craft the iron pickaxe. The simulator is Minecraft through MineStudio
(

)

An episode contains 120 decisions. At each decision the policy receives a

B.1.5
SFT Cold Start
To teach the models the input and output formats and establish basic task capabilities, we perform an SFT cold start in both settings. Specifically, we use Claude Sonnet 5 to generate demonstrations of crafting-task execution and record all model responses. We collect 4,791 examples from actual Minecraft interactions, including 1,677 for
Logger
, 2,380 for
Miner
, and 734 for
Smith
. We fine-tune the monolithic agent on the full dataset and each society agent on its corresponding subset, matching the total training compute between the two settings during cold start. SFT for each model is performed on a single B200 GPU.
We fine-tune all model parameters in bf16 using AdamW with a cosine learning rate schedule. Detailed settings are listed in Table
3
.
B.1.6
Post-training
Our post-training dataset consists of 1,614 random seeds, each generating a different Minecraft world. We host the Minecraft environments and the STEVE-1 model on four RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, allowing 32 Minecraft worlds to run in parallel. Reinforcement learning is performed on four B200 GPUs. Detailed settings are listed in Table
3
.

B.2.5
SFT Cold Start
To teach the models the input and output formats and establish basic navigation capability, we perform an SFT cold start in both settings. Starting from the multimodal-alignment checkpoint of NaVILA, we render oracle trajectories on R2R-CE training episodes with Habitat’s shortest-path follower. We keep successful episodes containing 1,931 decisions (800 turns, 800 moves and 331 stops), and use Claude Sonnet 5 to annotate data.
We fine-tune the monolithic agent on all data and each society agent on its own data. SFT for each model is performed on a single B200 GPU.
We fine-tune all model parameters in bf16 using AdamW with a cosine learning rate schedule. Detailed settings are listed in Table
4
.
B.2.6
Post-training
Our post-training dataset consists of 10,744 R2R-CE training episodes different from SFT. We host the Habitat environments on 2 RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Reinforcement learning is performed on 4 B200 GPUs. Detailed settings are listed in Table
4
.

B.3
Deep Research
B.3.1
Task and Environment
The task is open-domain deep research: given a question, the agent must browse a local web corpus with three tools and return a short final answer. We use the OpenResearcher benchmark
(
Li et al., 2026
)
: the questions are the OpenResearcher-Dataset, and the corpus is the OpenResearcher-Corpus, served by a BM25 search service. Each question comes with one reference answer.
The browser exposes OpenResearcher’s own three tools, called from the model output as JSON:
browser.search
(a query, returning the top-10 hits as title, URL and summary),
browser.open
(a link id from the current page, a URL, or a page cursor, with
loc
/
num_lines
to scroll) and
browser.find
(an exact-text pattern inside the currently open page).

B.3.3
Episode, Observation and Decision
An episode contains at most 64 decisions. The observation is the full conversation so far: the system prompt (OpenResearcher’s browsing instructions, the date, and the three tool schemas), the question, and the alternating assistant turns and tool responses. The prompt budget is 16,384 tokens. The policy answers with reasoning followed by either one tool call or the final answer,
<think>...</think><tool_call>{...}</tool_call>
or
<think>...</think><final_answer>{...}</final_answer>
. Generation stops at
<tool_response>
, and the tool call is executed by the browser against the search service.

The monolithic agent is the same base model fine-tuned on turns spanning all three tools.

B.3.5
SFT Cold Start
To teach the models the input and output formats and establish basic browsing capability, we perform an SFT cold start in both settings. The demonstrations are the OpenResearcher-Dataset’s own browsing trajectories, produced by gpt-oss with the same three tools over the same corpus. We use 568 assistant turns, including 222 for
Searcher
, 273 for
Opener
and 73 for
Finder
. The monolithic agent is fine-tuned on all action turns. Each society agent is fine-tuned on the action turns it owns. SFT for each model is performed on a single H200 GPU.
We fine-tune all models in bf16 using AdamW with a cosine learning rate schedule. Detailed settings are listed in Table
5
.
B.3.6
Post-training
Our post-training dataset consists of the 5,000 OpenResearcher questions different from SFT. Search services run on CPU nodes. Reinforcement learning is performed on four H200 GPUs. Detailed settings are listed in Table
5
.

Potential Limitations
We acknowledge the following limitations:
(1)
MPT
relies on externally evaluated task rewards to train both action and bidding policies. Its effectiveness depends on the quality of these signals. We have not evaluated settings where outcomes are primarily subjective or where reliable feedback is difficult to obtain.

(3) Despite our efforts to broaden the experimental evaluation, computational constraints limit the scale of our study. We have not explored training swarms composed of multiple models with more than 10B parameters each, or jointly training substantially larger agent populations.

article.headline: 拍卖式自组织让智能体群体边行动边学习
article.lede: 哈佛团队提出市场式后训练MPT，让智能体靠出价竞争行动权，在具身合成、机器人导航与深度研究上均优于单体强化学习。
article.problem: 现有多智能体系统通常把模型放进预设的编排结构里：管理者派活给工人、验证者检查生成者，谁在何时行动往往在训练全程固定不变。这样就把个体能力的训练与群体组织方式的学习割裂开了，忽略了二者其实互相耦合——谁行动决定了谁获得经验，而能力变化又会改变谁该行动。作者因此追问：去中心化的智能体群体能否同时学会如何行动与如何自我编排。
article.method: 论文提出市场式后训练（MPT）：每一回合各智能体独立提交出价，最高者获得行动权，出价同时决定奖励沿行动链向后传递的比例，作为本地训练信用（类似 bucket brigade），动作策略用 REINFORCE 更新。出价策略则通过反事实比较学习——在同一状态下重采样被选中者的出价让次高者行动，从该状态续跑另一条分支，用 Bradley–Terry 偏好目标提高带来更高回报的出价相对似然。训练在四个动作步与一个出价步之间交替，同一套参数同时承担行动与竞标。
article.results: 在训练算力匹配的条件下，MPT 在留出集上三项任务均优于单体强化学习：具身合成平均回合奖励 41.5±5.9 对 20.3±4.1，机器人导航 1.23±0.18 对 0.52±0.14，深度研究准确率 21.0%±4.1% 对 9.0%±2.1%。固定同一批动作策略只比较编排方式时，MPT 在 Iron Pickaxe 上以 41.5 对 25.4 胜过最强的 Graph-of-Agents，相对提升 63.4%。训练中参与格局确实改变：决策步 120 处 Logger 的参与比例从 RL 前约 80% 降到 45%，Miner 从约 10% 升到 40%；把学习到的出价换成随机信用后奖励约为 31，轮询约为 15，均低于 MPT 的约 42。推理期把群体从 3 扩到 12 个智能体，Wooden Pickaxe 的 pass@3 从约 78% 升到 97%；丢包率 p=0.9 时，12 体群体仍保持约 33 的回合奖励，而 3 体只有 19。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“谁来做”从人工设定的编排结构变成可训练、可复用的组件，说明集体智能的组织方式本身也能像策略一样从经验中学出来，并可在推理时通过扩大群体规模换取性能与冗余。
article.limitations: 方法依赖外部可验证的任务奖励来同时训练动作与出价，对于结果主观或反馈不可靠的场景尚未评估；出价训练需要从同一环境与智能体状态做反事实重跑，能否延伸到不可逆的真实世界交互仍是开放问题。作者也承认受算力限制，未探索由多个各自超过 10B 参数的模型组成、或规模更大群体的联合训练。
article.figure_caption_zh: 具身合成中的出价式自组织：(a) Iron Pickaxe 一局中 Logger、Miner、Smith 随采集与合成需求变化轮流参与；(b) 每步各智能体提交出价、最高者行动，此处 Smith 以 0.8 的出价赢得回合并合成工作台，环境随后返回奖励与新状态。

figure.caption: {Self-orchestration through bidding in embodied crafting.} (a) Selected turns from an Iron Pickaxe episode show the Logger, Miner, and Smith participating as resource gathering and crafting requirements change. (b) At each decision, agents submit bids, and the highest bidder acts. Here, the Smith wins with a bid of 0.8 and crafts a crafting table; the environment then returns a reward and the next state.

page_papers.title: Remembering Has a Price: Learning Memory Worth under Resource Constraints
page_papers.abstract: Lifelong agents continually accumulate and reuse experience to improve after deployment, yet in practice they often operate under tight generation, interaction, and memory budgets. Under such stringent joint constraints, we find that existing lifelong-memory methods can become ineffective, with several sophisticated approaches offering little advantage over simple retrieval or even no-memory agents. This reveals a more fundamental problem: resource scarcity makes each memory decision more consequential. When only a small amount of past experience can be retained or reused and opportunities for reasoning and recovery are limited, retrieving a relevant but ineffective memory can consume scarce context and hinder downstream execution. The key challenge is therefore not simply to retrieve relevant experience, but to determine which experiences are actually worth retaining and reusing. To address this challenge, we propose TokenWorth, a lightweight online memory framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution feedback and applies it consistently to memory retrieval and bounded memory management. Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and both local and API-based deployments, TokenWorth achieves the highest task success rate while using the fewest output tokens among the evaluated methods. These results suggest that effective lifelong adaptation under resource constraints depends not on remembering more, but on learning what is worth remembering. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AIGNLAI/TokenWorth.
