Abstract
Lifelong agents continually accumulate and reuse experience to improve after
deployment, yet in practice they often operate under tight generation,
interaction, and memory budgets. Under such stringent joint constraints, we
find that existing lifelong-memory methods can become ineffective, with several
sophisticated approaches offering little advantage over simple retrieval or
even no-memory agents. This reveals a more fundamental problem: resource
scarcity makes each memory decision more consequential. When only a small
amount of past experience can be retained or reused and opportunities for
reasoning and recovery are limited, retrieving a relevant but ineffective
memory can consume scarce context and hinder downstream execution. The key
challenge is therefore not simply to retrieve relevant experience, but to
determine which experiences are actually worth retaining and reusing. To
address this challenge, we propose
TokenWorth
, a lightweight online
memory framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution
feedback and applies it consistently to memory retrieval and bounded memory
management. Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and both local and
API-based deployments, TokenWorth achieves the highest task success rate while
using the fewest output tokens among the evaluated methods. These results
suggest that effective lifelong adaptation under resource constraints depends
not on remembering more, but on learning what is worth remembering. Our code is publicly available at
https://github.com/AIGNLAI/TokenWorth
.
1
Introduction
Lifelong agents continually accumulate, retain, and reuse experience from an
evolving task stream, enabling continued adaptation after deployment
[
35
]
. This capability is particularly valuable for
long-running interactive agents that must adapt to changing users,
environments, and tasks
[
4
,
6
,
16
]
.
In practice, however, lifelong adaptation rarely operates with unlimited
resources. Generation is constrained by latency, computation, or inference
cost; interaction opportunities are finite; and only a bounded amount of
historical experience can be stored or supplied to the agent at each decision
step
[
8
,
11
,
29
]
. This raises a
fundamental question:
do existing lifelong-memory mechanisms remain
effective when generation, interaction, and memory resources are jointly
constrained?
Figure 1
:
Left: Representative local results with Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct under the
evaluated stringent joint resource constraints; TokenWorth remains effective
where several memory baselines do not.
Right: Resource-constrained lifelong agents operate under bounded generation,
interaction, and memory budgets.
Our evaluation reveals that they often do not. As shown in
Figure
1
(a), under stringent joint resource constraints, several
sophisticated lifelong-memory approaches provide limited improvement over
simple retrieval or even no-memory agents, and can substantially underperform
in some environments. These results highlight the need to evaluate lifelong
agents for their effectiveness under a specified joint resource budget, where
generation, interaction, and memory resources are severely limited. Importantly,
this failure cannot be attributed simply to insufficient
memory capacity: under the same resource budget, different memory policies can
lead to markedly different downstream task performance.
To study this problem systematically, we formalize
resource-constrained lifelong agents
: lifelong agents that must
continually improve from experience while operating under bounded generation,
interaction, and memory budgets. As illustrated in Figure
1
(b),
we jointly constrain the resources available for both task execution and
experience reuse. Specifically, the agent operates with a bounded output budget
and a limited number of interaction rounds, while its external memory is
constrained in capacity, the number of retrieved experiences, and the amount of
memory that can be injected at each step. These inference-time constraints leave backbone capacity unchanged, allowing us to
study lifelong adaptation under a controlled, stringent resource budget.
Why do existing memory mechanisms become fragile under such constraints? When
only a small amount of past experience can be retained or supplied to the
agent, and opportunities for reasoning and recovery are limited, each memory
decision becomes more consequential. In particular, semantic relevance alone
may be insufficient for allocating scarce memory resources: an experience can
appear relevant to the current query yet provide little downstream utility.
Conversely, a useful experience that is not retained or selected cannot be
recovered by simply injecting more context or extending the interaction.
Resource scarcity therefore turns memory allocation into a more stringent
value-estimation problem. The central challenge is no longer merely to retrieve
the most relevant past experience, but to determine which experiences are
actually
worth
retaining and reusing when memory and execution resources
are limited.
To address this challenge, we propose
TokenWorth
, a lightweight online
memory framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution
feedback. TokenWorth combines an interpretable online base scorer with a
residual Recursive Feature Machine (RFM), allowing stable global patterns of
memory usefulness to be complemented by nonlinear, query-specific corrections.
The learned worth is used to guide both memory retrieval and bounded memory-bank
management, allocating limited memory resources toward experiences that are
most useful for future tasks.
We conduct our main evaluation on three LifelongAgentBench environments
covering database interaction, operating-system tasks, and knowledge-graph
reasoning, under both local and API-based deployments. Across all six
environment–deployment combinations, TokenWorth achieves the highest task
success rate among the evaluated methods while also using the fewest output
tokens. These results show that its gains do not rely on longer generations;
instead, selecting higher-value experience allows the frozen backbone to use a
limited generation budget more effectively.
Our contributions are threefold:
•
We formulate
resource-constrained lifelong agents
and study
effectiveness under stringent joint constraints on generation, interaction,
and memory.
•
We propose
TokenWorth
, which learns query-dependent memory
worth from online execution feedback and uses it consistently for memory
retrieval and bounded memory management.
•
We evaluate TokenWorth across three LifelongAgentBench environments
under both local and API-based deployments, demonstrating improved task
success and generation efficiency under stringent resource constraints.
2
Related Work
Lifelong Language Agents.
Lifelong language agents aim to continually improve from accumulated interaction experience, enabling continued adaptation after deployment
[
6
,
35
]
. Early agent systems demonstrated that past trajectories, reflections, or reusable skills can improve future decision making, including Reflexion
[
19
]
, ExpeL
[
33
]
, Voyager
[
24
]
, and SocioDojo
[
4
]
. More recent work has developed explicit memory and skill mechanisms for continual adaptation, such as MemoryBank
[
37
]
, Mem0
[
5
]
, MemRL
[
32
]
, MemSkill
[
30
]
, and AutoSkill
[
27
]
. Meanwhile, LifelongAgentBench
[
34
]
, AgentCL
[
21
]
, SkillLearnBench
[
36
]
, and XSkill
[
10
]
provide increasingly systematic evaluation of continual adaptation in language agents. Most of these studies focus on how agents can accumulate and exploit experience to improve capability; in contrast, we study whether such memory mechanisms remain effective under stringent joint constraints on generation, interaction, and memory.
Resource-Constrained Language Agents.
Resource efficiency has been extensively studied for LLM inference and serving, including memory-efficient execution
[
11
]
and collaborative inference under computation and communication constraints
[
29
]
. More recent work has begun to examine resource constraints at the agent level.
Hajimiri et al. [9]
study whether online memory and skill modules remain beneficial under fixed inference-token budgets, while
Wu et al. [25]
investigate continual learning with a hard-bounded on-device memory. BudgetMem
[
31
]
further considers query-aware routing across runtime memory budgets, and
Chen and Cheng [3]
model agentic memory value using multiple factors for memory retention and retrieval.
These studies highlight the importance of accounting for resource cost in agent memory, but largely focus on individual resource constraints, runtime budgeting, or memory valuation in isolation. Our work instead studies lifelong adaptation under a fixed joint budget on generation, interaction, and memory resources. We identify memory-worth estimation as a central challenge and introduce
TokenWorth
, which learns query-dependent worth from streaming execution
feedback to guide retrieval and bounded memory management.

TokenWorth consists of three components. First, an interpretable linear scorer

4.2
Learning Query-Dependent Memory Worth
TokenWorth aims to determine which past experiences are worth allocating the
agent’s limited memory resources to. Unlike a fixed memory utility, the
usefulness of an experience depends on the current query and must be inferred
from sparse and indirect execution feedback. Each task is executed only once,
feedback is observed only for the memory actually used, and an execution
failure may arise from factors beyond the selected memory itself.
To balance stability and adaptivity under such feedback, TokenWorth decomposes
memory worth into two complementary components. A lightweight linear base
scorer captures stable and interpretable patterns that generalize across the
task stream, while an RFM learns nonlinear residual structure not captured by
the base scorer. The linear component is updated conservatively around an
informative prior, whereas the RFM adapts more flexibly to local
query–memory interactions.

We conduct our main evaluation on three environments from
LifelongAgentBench

These environments cover heterogeneous forms of interactive decision making

accumulated from earlier tasks can be retained and reused in subsequent
interactions. In all environments, the memory bank is initialized empty, each
task is executed once, and memory decisions depend only on experience observed

Within each environment and deployment setting, all methods process the same

6
Conclusion
We study lifelong language agents under joint constraints on generation,
interaction, and memory. We propose
TokenWorth
, a lightweight online
framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from execution feedback and
uses it for retrieval and bounded memory management. Across three
LifelongAgentBench environments and local and API-based backbones, TokenWorth
achieves the highest task success rates among evaluated methods while using the
fewest output tokens. Additional experiments show competitive performance on
coding and embodied-agent tasks. Feedback is observed only for selected
memories, so their causal contributions remain unidentified. Developing
budget-efficient credit assignment is an important direction for future work.

Additional Experimental Details
A.1
Benchmarks
Our main experiments use three environments from
LifelongAgentBench
[
34
]
: database interaction
(DB), operating-system interaction (OS), and knowledge-graph interaction (KG).
Tasks are processed sequentially, and only experience from preceding tasks may
be reused. DB requires structured database operations and answers grounded in
retrieved observations. OS requires multi-step system management through Bash
commands. KG follows an AgentBench-style protocol in which the agent interacts
with a knowledge graph through structured tool calls, while SPARQL queries
are executed by the backend. The environments thus cover heterogeneous
forms of interactive decision making under a shared online
lifelong-learning protocol.
We additionally evaluate online lifelong variants of

[
38
]
and

[
20
]
; their results are reported in

.

the impact of task ordering on continual adaptation
[

]
and the variability of performance across
evaluation sequences
[
14
]
.
These studies highlight the importance of evaluation protocols
in continual learning, while our experiments focus on online
memory adaptation under fixed resource budgets.

article.headline: 记忆有代价：资源受限下学习记忆价值
article.lede: 南大团队提出 TokenWorth，用稀疏执行反馈在线学习查询相关的记忆价值，在六种设置下成功率最高、输出 token
article.problem: 终身学习智能体在部署后不断积累经验，但现实中往往同时受到生成、交互与记忆预算的联合限制。作者发现，在这种严格约束下多种复杂记忆方法几乎不比简单检索甚至无记忆智能体更好，有时还明显更差。原因在于资源稀缺让每次记忆决策代价更高：语义相关但无用的记忆会占用宝贵上下文，而未被保留的有用经验无法靠多轮交互补救。
article.method: TokenWorth 把记忆价值拆成两部分：一个带先验正则的可解释线性基础打分器捕捉稳定的全局规律，一个基于 RFM 的残差学习器建模查询相关的非线性偏差。残差部分采用两时间尺度更新，KRR 系数快速拟合，特征度量则通过 AGOP 缓慢调整。学到的价值既用于当前查询的记忆检索，也用于有界记忆库的准入与淘汰，整个控制器不更新主干模型、不做任务回放，也不产生额外的大模型调用。
article.results: 在 LifelongAgentBench 的 DB、OS、KG 三个环境与本地 Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct、API DeepSeek-V4-Flash 两种部署共六种组合中，TokenWorth 成功率均为最高：本地 DB 达 65.0%，比最强基线 RAG 的 33.0% 高 32.0 个百分点，OS 为 59.4%（高 4.8 点），KG 为 36.7%（高 6.0 点）；API 侧 DB 为 62.2%（高 30.0 点），OS 为 73.2%（高 3.0 点），KG 为 36.7%（高 4.7 点）。输出 token 相对无记忆基线在本地的降幅为 9.3%、51.5%、18.7%，在 API 侧为 31.6%、58.3%、21.3%，六种设置均为最低。DB 本地消融显示，仅用基础打分器为 64.2%，加上固定度量的 RFM 反而降到 63.0%，启用 AGOP 特征自适应后回升到 65.0%。
article.why_it_matters: 结果提示，资源受限下的终身适应关键不在于记得更多，而在于学出哪些经验值得占用稀缺的记忆与生成预算，这为智能体记忆机制的设计提供了一个以价值估计为核心的视角。
article.limitations: 实验只覆盖一组固定的严格预算，作者明确表示不主张方法在不同预算水平下的鲁棒性；监督信号只来自被选中的那条记忆，无法识别其因果贡献。此外，在 BigCodeBench 和 ALFWorld 上的优势很小，API 版 BigCodeBench 的 50.6% 还低于 RAG 的 50.9%，超参数敏感度测试中部分设置会带来 2.4 至 3.0 个百分点的下降。

page_papers.title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs
page_papers.abstract: Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents. Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs. We introduce HarnessPro, a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Across these benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at https://github.com/pzs19/HarnessPro

Abstract
Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents.
Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs.

HarnessPro
, a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost.
In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests.
Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses.
Rather than returning a single harness,

Introduction
An agent harness is the software infrastructure that manages interactions between a large language model (LLM) and its environment
(
Grace et al., 2026
)
.
Recent work on recursive self-improvement (RSI)
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
uses past execution trajectories to diagnose problems and guide harness updates that improve performance on future tasks
(
Suzgun et al., 2026
;
Lin et al., 2026
;
Pan et al., 2026a
)
.
However, these methods often pursue performance gains through more extensive exploration and stronger verification
(
Lin et al., 2026
;
Pan et al., 2026a
)
.
These efforts improve performance, but often at the cost of higher token consumption and increased latency.
This trade-off is less appealing in practical deployment, where the execution cost and latency also matter.
We therefore ask:
Can recursive harness self-improvement deliver better performance at lower execution cost?

article.headline: 给智能体框架做帕累托自进化：性能升、成本降
article.lede: HarnessPro 用多智能体诊断执行轨迹，在无标签设定下同时优化性能与成本，在 SWE-Bench Pro 上成本更
article.problem: 现有基于递归自我改进（RSI）的 harness 优化方法，主要靠扩大探索范围和加强验证来取得性能提升，代价是 token 消耗与延迟上升。但在实际部署中，执行成本和延迟同样重要，这种「性能换成本」的取舍并不划算。作者因此提出：递归的 harness 自我改进能否在降低执行成本的同时提升性能？
article.method: HarnessPro 用多个专职 agent 把执行反馈转化为一轮轮 harness 更新：轨迹分析器检查重复 rollout，找出失败点和可避免的开销；planner 按不同的性能与成本优先级提出更新方案；再由实现 agent 落地为候选 harness。候选评估不依赖标准答案或官方测试，而由 LLM 生成的测试完成，属于无标签设定。方法最终不返回单一 harness，而是给出位于性能-成本帕累托前沿上的一组代表，供使用者按偏好挑选。
article.results: 在 SWE-Bench Pro 上，基线 RHO 的通过率从原 harness 提升到 80.0%，但单任务平均成本从 $1.88 涨到 $2.68（+42.6%）；HarnessPro-Heavy 在该基准上取得 80.7% 通过率、成本 $1.97，即性能略高而成本明显更低。在另一个基准（片段中未给出名称）上，RHO 为 76.3% 通过率、$1.09，HarnessPro-Heavy 为 80.8%、$0.72。偏向低成本的 HarnessPro-Lite 在两个基准上分别为 72.9% / $0.43 与 72.3% / $0.80，以更低通过率换取大幅成本下降。消融显示 planner 与 test synthesizer 都不可或缺：去掉 test synthesizer 后，Heavy 在两个基准上分别降到 74.6% 和 72.0%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「成本」变成 harness 自进化的一等目标，而非事后再压缩，让 agent 框架的自我改进更贴近真实部署约束。返回帕累托候选集而非单一方案的做法，也让性能与预算的取舍变得显式可调。
article.limitations: 无标签设定下以 LLM 生成测试替代官方测试，去掉 test synthesizer 后通过率明显下滑（80.8→74.6、80.7→72.0），说明结论高度依赖合成测试的质量；用于选择的核心集仅固定 10 个任务，有对选样过拟合的风险。此外成本以美元计、依赖具体 API 定价，片段中另两个基准的名称与规模、多次运行的方差均未给出。

page_papers.title: Empowering Edge Agents: A Systematic Analysis of Edge-Cloud Collaboration in LLM Agent Execution
page_papers.abstract: Edge-cloud collaboration combines the lower inference overhead and greater data locality of edge-side execution with the stronger capabilities of cloud-hosted models. However, as LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon scenarios, cloud participation becomes interleaved throughout execution rather than a one-shot decision for each query. Such interleaved participation introduces trajectory-level effects that remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we introduce EC2-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution. It provides executable digital-workspace agent tasks and a unified evaluation framework covering task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Using this benchmark, we empirically study diverse forms of edge-cloud collaboration. Our study reveals three findings. First, collaboration achieves a favorable balance among task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure compared with edge-only and cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across strategies shrink, while privacy exposure remains strongly strategy-dependent. Third, stronger edge capability shifts preferred collaboration from externally controlled cloud participation and direct cloud execution toward more edge-controlled collaboration. Further analyses identify cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction following as important edge-side abilities for effective collaboration. These findings provide a systematic understanding of edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution and insights for designing future edge agents that effectively collaborate with cloud models. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/EC2-Bench.

Abstract
Edge–cloud collaboration offers a promising way to combine the lower inference overhead and greater data locality of edge-side execution with the substantially stronger capabilities of cloud-hosted frontier models. However, as LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon scenarios, cloud participation becomes interleaved throughout execution rather than a one-shot decision for each query. Such interleaved participation introduces trajectory-level effects that remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we introduce EC
2
-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating edge–cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution. EC
2
-Bench provides executable digital-workspace agent tasks and a unified evaluation framework covering task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Using this benchmark, we empirically study diverse forms of edge–cloud collaboration. Our study reveals several key findings. First, edge–cloud collaboration provides an effective execution paradigm for long-horizon agents by achieving a favorable balance among task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure compared with edge-only and cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across collaboration strategies become smaller, while privacy exposure remains strongly dependent on the chosen strategy. Third, stronger edge capability changes the preferred collaboration mode, shifting from externally controlled cloud participation and direct cloud execution toward more edge-controlled collaboration. Further analyses identify cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction following as important edge-side abilities underlying such effective collaboration. These findings establish a systematic understanding of edge–cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution and provide insights for designing future edge models that can effectively collaborate with cloud models. All codes and resources are available at
https://github.com/OpenBMB/EC2-Bench
.
1
Introduction
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs)
(
Achiam et al., 2023
)
, together with the emergence of agent harnesses such as Claude Code
(
Anthropic, 2025
)
and OpenClaw
(
OpenClaw, 2025
)
, have shifted LLM applications from isolated prompt–response interactions toward long-horizon, goal-directed agent execution
(
Wang et al., 2024a
)
. These agents tackle complex end-to-end workflows, including software development, data analysis, information seeking, and workplace automation, through iterative interaction with external environments and tool use
(
Yao et al., 2022
;
Yang et al., 2024
;
Hu et al., 2024b
;
Shen et al., 2023
;
Zhou et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2024b
)
.
Bringing such agents to edge devices, however, remains challenging because edge platforms are inherently constrained by limited computational resources and memory
(
Qu et al., 2025
)
. Consequently, practical on-device deployment often relies on relatively small LLMs (e.g., models with
≤
\leq
10B parameters), which can struggle with demanding reasoning, planning, and tool-use tasks
(
Choi et al., 2026
)
, making reliable long-horizon execution challenging
(
Liu et al., 2024
)
. To address this limitation, recent work has explored edge–cloud LLM collaboration, where lightweight edge models are complemented by cloud-hosted frontier LLMs when additional capability is required
(
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
. This paradigm combines efficient edge-side execution with stronger cloud capabilities, but requires effective coordination of edge and cloud participation to realize these complementary benefits
(
Ding et al., 2024
;
Sun et al., 2024
;
Agrawal and Mayer,
)
.
Prior edge–cloud LLM systems largely treated collaboration as a one-shot coordination process for each query, typically through routing or escalation decisions
(
Pozi and Sato, 2025
;
Han et al., 2026
)
. In long-horizon agent execution, however, collaboration can become more interleaved, with edge and cloud models participating at different points along the trajectory as capability requirements change
(
Yi et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
. Such interleaving introduces trajectory-level dependencies: cloud participation decisions can influence subsequent execution steps, accumulate resource costs over the trajectory, and determine how much potentially sensitive information leaves the local environment. Yet existing analysis still largely focuses on isolated routing or escalation decisions at the query level, leaving these trajectory-level effects underexplored
(
Hu et al., 2024a
;
Lu et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2026a
;
Li et al., 2025
)
. To close this gap, in this paper, we conduct a systematic empirical study of edge–cloud collaboration in long-horizon agentic execution. Specifically, we organize our study around three research questions. We first ask:
does edge–cloud collaboration remain effective for realistic long-horizon agent execution?
(
RQ1
) We evaluate this question jointly in terms of task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. As edge models become more capable, more execution can be handled locally while cloud assistance is reserved for capability-demanding operations. We therefore ask:
how does increasing edge capability impact edge–cloud collaborative execution?
(
RQ2
); As increasing edge capability changes how computation is distributed between edge and cloud, collaboration strategies that are effective under one capability regime may not remain equally suitable under another. This motivates our final question:
how should edge–cloud collaboration evolve as edge capability advances?
(
RQ3
).
To provide a common empirical basis for this study, we introduce
EC
2
-Bench
(
E
dge–
C
loud
C
ollaborative Agent Benchmark), an evaluation framework that combines a diverse suite of real-world digital-workspace agent tasks with a unified execution and evaluation environment for edge–cloud collaboration.
EC
2
-Bench
characterizes each configuration along three dimensions: task performance
(
Yuan et al., 2026b
)
, resource usage
(
Fang et al., 2025
)
, and privacy exposure. We explicitly consider privacy because cloud participation may reveal sensitive workspace information encountered during agent execution, making privacy exposure an important dimension of evaluating such collaboration
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
. Using
EC
2
-Bench
, we systematically investigate edge–cloud collaboration across diverse agent tasks, collaboration strategies, and edge-capability regimes.
Our study yields three main findings. First, edge–cloud collaboration remains effective for long-horizon agents: partial cloud participation improves task performance over edge-only execution while requiring substantially less cloud resource usage and privacy exposure than cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across collaboration strategies become much smaller; however, their differences in privacy exposure remain substantial. Thus, privacy remains an important differentiator even when task performance converges. Third, the collaboration strategy that works best changes with edge capability. Weaker edge models benefit more from external routing and direct cloud execution, whereas stronger edge models benefit more from edge-controlled invocation and cloud advisory. Further analyses suggest that effective cloud-invocation decisions and instruction following are key edge-side abilities for stronger-edge collaboration modes. These findings highlight the value of optimizing future edge models for both standalone capability and effective cloud collaboration, enabling more capable edge agents.
2
Related Work
A growing body of work has investigated how edge and cloud LLMs can be coordinated to leverage their complementary capabilities and deployment characteristics, balancing overall task performance with local efficiency
(
Zhu and Yang, 2025
;
Dong et al., 2025
)
. A substantial line of work focuses on one-shot coordination for individual queries, either by routing each query to an edge or cloud model or by cascading from the local model to the cloud when additional capability is needed
(
Chen et al., 2023
;
Ong et al., 2024
;
Miao and Fang,
)
. These approaches therefore center on improving the accuracy of routing and escalation decisions
(
Ding et al., 2024
)
. More recent work has extended edge–cloud collaboration to agent execution, where edge and cloud participation can be coordinated at different steps throughout a multi-step trajectory rather than determined once for the entire query, enabling finer-grained use of their complementary capabilities. Within this setting, recent approaches have explored different designs for coordinating edge–cloud collaboration, mainly along two dimensions. Some dynamically determine when the cloud model should participate, either through dedicated rule-based controllers or routers, or by allowing the edge agent itself to decide when to invoke the cloud
(
Shao et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
;
Zeng et al., 2026b
)
. Beyond deciding when the cloud should participate, other approaches have explored complementary functional roles for edge and cloud models during execution, such as execution, planning, or providing guidance
(
Yi et al., 2025
;
Yuan et al., 2026a
)
.
Existing work has begun to develop dedicated evaluation resources for edge–cloud LLM systems. LLMSwitchBench
(
Liu et al., 2025
)
evaluates edge–cloud routing for smart-home queries, while M4A1
(
Yuan et al., 2026b
)
extends device–cloud evaluation to multimodal, multitask, and multi-turn conversations, focusing on where individual inference requests should be executed. More general LLM routing benchmarks instead abstract away from the edge–cloud setting and evaluate routing systems over heterogeneous model pools, primarily focusing on routing quality and overall cost–performance trade-offs
(
Huang et al., 2025
;
Lu et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2026b
)
. Despite this progress, existing evaluations pay more attention on routing decisions for individual queries, tasks, or turns, typically over standalone inference workloads such as knowledge, reasoning, coding, and instruction-following tasks. Our study instead treats edge–cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution as the primary object of empirical analysis, aiming to systematically characterize its effectiveness and system-level behavior across different edge capability levels and collaboration designs.
3
Preliminaries: Edge–Cloud Collaborative Execution
This section formalizes edge–cloud collaboration in agent execution, which serves as the object of study in this work. We first present a general formulation of how a collaboration strategy coordinates the participation of edge and cloud models during execution (§
3.1

3.2
). Figure

We construct

Data Collection.

We select these benchmarks because their tasks evaluate end-to-end agent execution through stateful, multi-step interactions with tools, applications, and workspace artifacts, with explicit task objectives and verifiable execution outcomes. Collectively, they cover a broad range of applications, interaction patterns, execution environments, and task difficulties, providing a diverse candidate pool for constructing

2

Task Curation.
Starting from the collected candidate pool, we further adapt and curate the tasks to construct the final task suite. Specifically, we first adapt tasks from different source benchmarks to a common execution environment and evaluation interface, enabling all tasks to be executed under the same agent runtime and evaluated under consistent conditions while preserving their original objectives, workspace states, required interactions, and success criteria. We then apply a collaboration-oriented difficulty filtering procedure to retain tasks that are informative for studying edge–cloud collaboration. We evaluate each adapted task under edge-only and cloud-only execution to characterize task difficulty at the two execution endpoints. Tasks that are consistently solved by both endpoints are removed because they provide limited opportunity to differentiate agent execution paradigms, while tasks where neither endpoint achieves meaningful completion are excluded because they provide limited basis for evaluating collaborative execution. Following these steps, we further supplement the task suite with tasks from underrepresented scenarios to maintain broad workload coverage. The resulting task suite consists of 128 executable tasks.
To measure the potential exposure of sensitive information from local workspaces to the cloud during collaboration, we further incorporate sensitivity annotations into
EC
2
-Bench
. Specifically, we first annotate sensitive information already contained in the original workspace artifacts. We then use an LLM-based approach to identify appropriate locations, generate realistic synthetic sensitive information, and insert it into relevant workspace artifacts, while preserving the original task objective, required interactions, and evaluation criteria. This process results in fine-grained sensitivity annotations for 100 tasks, where each sensitivity unit corresponds to an atomic piece of sensitive information grounded in a workspace artifact.
Detailed procedures for task adaptation, collaboration-oriented filtering, coverage supplementation, and sensitivity annotation are provided in Appendix

We first examine whether edge–cloud collaboration provides a useful execution regime between edge-only and cloud-only agents when task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure are considered jointly. As shown in Table
2
, the two execution extremes exhibit clear trade-offs. Cloud-only execution achieves the strongest task performance but incurs substantial cloud resource usage and privacy exposure, whereas edge-only execution avoids cloud usage and exposure at the cost of lower task performance. Collaborative execution occupies the space between these extremes, improving task performance over edge-only execution while substantially reducing cloud dependence relative to cloud-only execution. For example, with Qwen3.5-2B as the edge model, step-level routing improves task completion from 12.75 to 39.97 while using only 22.7% of the cloud-only cost. These results indicate that partial cloud participation can recover substantial capability without incurring the full cost of cloud-only execution.

6.2
Impact of Improving Edge Capability on Collaborative Execution (RQ2)
As edge models continue to advance rapidly
(
Xiao et al., 2025
)
, we study how improving edge capability changes edge–cloud collaborative execution. To probe how collaboration may evolve beyond current lightweight edge models, we additionally include Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.7-Plus as prospective proxies for stronger future edge models. As shown in Table
2
, stronger edge models consistently improve collaborative execution and bring its performance closer to cloud-only execution. The best available collaborative configuration increases from 39.97% completion with Qwen3.5-2B to 76.84% with Qwen3.7-Plus, approaching the 82.70% completion of cloud-only execution.
We further examine how increasing edge capability changes the variation among collaboration strategies. Specifically, for each edge model, we measure the gap between the highest and lowest completion scores and privacy exposure values. As shown in Figures
3(a)
and
3(b)
, task performance becomes substantially less sensitive to the collaboration strategy as edge capability increases. The completion gap among the evaluated strategies narrows from 25.22% with Qwen3.5-2B to 3.67% with Qwen3.7-Plus. In contrast, privacy exposure does not exhibit the same convergence, with substantial differences persisting across collaboration strategies. Notably, with Qwen3.7-Plus, the strategies differ by only 3.67% in completion but by 66.23% in privacy exposure. These results show that stronger edge capability substantially compresses performance differences across collaboration strategies, while privacy exposure remains highly differentiated.
6.3
How Does Edge–Cloud Collaboration Evolve with Edge Capability? (RQ3)
Beyond improving collaborative performance, increasing edge capability may also change effective collaboration mechanisms. We examine this shift along two dimensions: who determines cloud participation and what role the cloud plays once invoked. As shown in Table
2
, both dimensions exhibit clear shifts with improving edge capability. In terms of participation control, externally routed strategies generally outperform edge-controlled strategies with weaker edge models. For example, with Qwen3.5-2B, Per-step Routing achieves 39.97% completion, compared with 15.86% for Edge-Ctrl. Delegation. As edge capability improves, however, this pattern reverses. A similar reversal appears in the role of the cloud: weaker edge models benefit more from direct cloud execution, whereas stronger edge models favor advisory support.

Cloud-Assistance Decision Making.
The shift toward agent-controlled invocation motivates us to examine whether stronger edge models can make more effective cloud-assistance decisions. Since there is no explicit annotation indicating when cloud assistance is necessary, we compare Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation against a matched random-invocation baseline. Specifically, we preserve the same cloud-call rate as the agent-controlled strategy while randomly selecting invocation steps. As shown in Figure
4(a)

Cloud Guidance Utilization.
We next examine whether instruction-following ability is associated with improved advisory collaboration. Starting from Qwen3.5-2B, we apply targeted instruction-following training and evaluate intermediate checkpoints under a fixed cloud-advisory setting. As shown in Figure
4(b)
and Appendix
A.10
, task completion under cloud advisory consistently improves as instruction-following ability develops during training, increasing from 24.8% before training to 28.8% after 600 steps. These results suggest that instruction-following ability is associated with improved utilization of cloud-provided guidance.
7
Conclusion
In this work, we study edge–cloud collaboration for long-horizon LLM agent execution, where cloud participation is interleaved throughout the execution trajectory. To enable systematic investigation of this problem, we introduce
EC
2
-Bench
, an evaluation framework that combines executable digital-workspace agent tasks with unified measurements of task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Our findings show that edge–cloud collaboration can achieve a favorable balance between capability, cost, and privacy compared with purely edge-side or cloud-side execution. As edge models become stronger, collaborative execution increasingly approaches cloud-only performance, while privacy exposure remains highly dependent on how cloud participation is organized. We further find that stronger edge models benefit from agent-controlled cloud invocation and advisory interaction. Additional analyses suggest that effective cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction-following are important abilities for edge–cloud collaboration, motivating future work to develop more capable edge agents by strengthening their ability to collaborate with cloud models.

Ethics Statement
This work studies edge–cloud collaboration for LLM-powered agents and evaluates different collaboration strategies in terms of task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure.
EC
2
-Bench
is designed for research evaluation and responsible system development. We do not use real private user data to construct privacy-sensitive benchmark content. When additional sensitive information is required for evaluation, it is synthetically generated and does not correspond to real individuals, organizations, credentials, or financial records. Human annotation is used only to validate benchmark annotations and synthetic content; no annotator personal information is collected or analyzed. The privacy annotations in
EC
2
-Bench
are intended to support systematic evaluation of sensitive information exposed during edge–cloud collaboration and to facilitate the development of more privacy-aware agent systems.
Reproducibility Statement
We provide detailed descriptions of the benchmark construction, collaboration strategies, experimental setup, and evaluation procedures in the main paper and appendix. In particular, we document the task adaptation and filtering process, sensitivity annotation procedure and validation, implementations of the four edge–cloud collaboration strategies, model and inference configurations, and the metrics used to evaluate task performance, cloud resource usage, edge computation, and privacy exposure. We further report the experimental settings and implementation details for the analyses conducted in each research question. These details are provided to facilitate reproduction of the benchmark and the reported experimental results.

Appendix A
Appendix
A.1
License
All source benchmarks incorporated into
EC
2
-Bench
are used under their respective licenses. Claw-Eval, WildClawBench, QwenClawBench, LiveClawBench, and PinchBench are released under the MIT License, while ClawBench is released under the Apache-2.0 License. We preserve attribution to the original benchmarks for all adapted tasks and follow the redistribution and usage requirements specified by their licenses.
A.2
Detailed Comparison with Prior Benchmarks
We provide additional details on how
EC
2
-Bench
differs from representative benchmarks for LLM routing and edge–cloud collaboration. Overall, prior benchmarks primarily study model allocation over queries or conversational turns and evaluate task quality together with inference-related costs, whereas
EC
2
-Bench
extends the evaluation to long-horizon agent execution, broader collaboration mechanisms, and trajectory-level privacy exposure. We next compare these benchmarks along three aspects: evaluation scenario, collaboration mode, and evaluation dimension.
Evaluation Scenario.
Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate routing over conventional LLM queries or conversational interactions, while
EC
2
-Bench
focuses on long-horizon agent execution in interactive environments. RouterBench
(
Hu et al., 2024a
)
evaluates routing across a collection of general LLM tasks. LLMRouterBench
(
Li et al., 2026b
)
further broadens the task coverage to include software-engineering and tool-use benchmarks in addition to conventional reasoning, knowledge, and code-generation tasks. LLMSwitchBench
(
Liu et al., 2025
)
focuses on independent smart-home queries spanning binary, multiple-choice, and open-ended formats. M4A1
(
Yuan et al., 2026b
)
considers multi-modal and multi-task interactions within multi-turn conversations. In comparison,
EC
2
-Bench
evaluates collaboration over multi-step agent trajectories, where models repeatedly interact with tools, applications, and persistent workspace states.
Collaboration Modes.
Prior benchmarks predominantly study routing-based collaboration, whereas
EC
2
-Bench
additionally considers collaboration in which the edge agent itself controls cloud participation. RouterBench, LLMRouterBench, and LLMSwitchBench formulate model allocation primarily as query routing, where each input query is assigned to a selected model. M4A1 allows device–cloud placement to be reconsidered for different tasks throughout a multi-turn conversation.
EC
2
-Bench
includes both Query Routing and Per-Step Routing, and further considers two edge-controlled modes. Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation allows the edge agent to decide when to delegate the next execution step to the cloud, while Edge-Controlled Cloud Advisory lets the edge agent request cloud guidance while retaining responsibility for subsequent action generation.
Evaluation Dimensions.
Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate task quality and inference-related efficiency, while
EC
2
-Bench
additionally quantifies privacy exposure over the complete execution trajectory. RouterBench focuses on task performance and economic cost, while LLMRouterBench evaluates performance-oriented and performance–cost routing and additionally provides latency-aware analysis. M4A1 jointly considers response quality, latency, and usage cost in device–cloud offloading. LLMSwitchBench incorporates privacy-sensitive queries and privacy-aware routing mechanisms, including local execution and masking before cloud inference, while its main routing evaluation reports task-quality metrics and inference cost. In
EC
2
-Bench
, privacy exposure is directly quantified by tracking which annotated sensitive information from the local workspace becomes visible to the cloud during execution. Resource usage is likewise measured over the complete trajectory, including cloud-side token consumption and monetary cost as well as edge-side computation.
A.3
Task Suite Construction and Statistics
This section provides additional details on the construction and composition of the
EC
2
-Bench
task suite, including collaboration-oriented difficulty filtering, coverage supplementation, and task statistics.
We first collect candidate tasks from multiple Claw-style executable-workspace agent benchmarks and adapt them to the
EC
2
-Bench
execution environment following the protocol in Appendix
A.4
. We then perform collaboration-oriented difficulty filtering to retain tasks that provide meaningful room for edge–cloud collaboration. All filtering runs are conducted on the adapted task instances in the standardized
EC
2
-Bench
environment, using the same workspace states, tool interfaces, and task-specific evaluation checks defined after adaptation. Specifically, each task is evaluated under three endpoint configurations, using Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-9B as representative edge models and GLM-5.3 as the cloud model. We use the resulting task completion scores as the filtering signal to characterize whether a task is already handled by edge-only execution, can be completed by cloud-only execution, or remains challenging for both endpoints.

We remove tasks that are consistently completed by both edge-only and cloud-only execution, since such tasks provide limited opportunity to differentiate execution paradigms. We also exclude tasks where neither endpoint achieves meaningful completion, since such tasks provide limited basis for evaluating collaborative execution. The resulting task suite focuses on scenarios where edge-only, cloud-only, and collaborative execution can exhibit meaningful differences. Importantly, this criterion does not require all edge models to fail: tasks that are challenging for Qwen3.5-2B but can be handled by Qwen3.5-9B are retained, as they remain informative for studying how collaboration evolves with increasing edge capability.

A.4
Task Adaptation Protocol
This section describes how tasks collected from heterogeneous executable-workspace benchmarks are adapted into standardized executable instances for
EC
2
-Bench
. The adaptation protocol consists of three components: standardizing task execution, standardizing task evaluation, and validating that the resulting instances preserve comparable task difficulty. We then illustrate the resulting task format and execution workflow with a representative
EC
2
-Bench
instance.
Standardization and Fidelity Check.
Inspired by the task format used in
Ding et al. (2026)
, we first standardize task execution by organizing each task into a unified configuration and workspace structure. Each task is converted into a unified configuration format specifying its prompt, workspace paths, tools, environment settings, and other execution requirements. Task-relevant files and resources are organized into a common workspace structure, while tool and skill settings are aligned across tasks so that instances from different sources can follow the same agent loop and logging mechanism. We next standardize task evaluation while preserving the original success criteria of each task. The original verification logic is converted into a set of task-specific evaluation checks compatible with
EC
2
-Bench
, including rule-based validation, file or application-state auditing, command-output inspection, and rubric-based LLM-as-a-judge verification when semantic judgment is required. The resulting check scores are aggregated into the task completion score defined in Section
4.2
.
To validate adaptation fidelity, we examine whether the adapted instances preserve comparable execution and evaluation outcomes. For each task, we execute both the original and adapted versions with Qwen3.5-9B and compare their average completion scores over three independent runs. Tasks whose absolute difference in average completion score exceeds 0.3 are discarded. This validation helps identify substantial behavioral or scoring shifts introduced during adaptation.

This subsection describes how sensitivity-unit annotations are constructed in
EC
2
-Bench
. Since privacy-relevant information in digital workspaces can be distributed across heterogeneous files, application states, and other task artifacts, we adopt an LLM-based annotation process to identify and annotate sensitive information from two sources: information already present in the task environment and realistically synthesized sensitive content introduced into suitable task artifacts. Across the resulting task environments, more than 15,000 information units are represented in total, of which 3,385 are annotated as sensitive, spanning 100 tasks and 12 fine-grained privacy categories. Both sources are represented under a common annotation schema and privacy taxonomy, with annotation quality further validated through human evaluation. The resulting sensitivity-unit annotations are used to measure privacy exposure during collaborative execution. Privacy exposure quantifies the fraction of annotated sensitive information units that become visible to the cloud through cloud-visible contexts along the execution trajectory.
Identification of Pre-existing Sensitive Information.
For each task, we use an LLM to inspect the local workspace and identify privacy-relevant information. The workspace may contain files, application states, and other task artifacts accessible to the agent during execution. Each identified item is grounded in its source artifact or application record, and the corresponding sensitive content and source location are recorded as a sensitivity unit. This grounding establishes both that the information is available within the task environment and where it originates, providing a concrete reference for subsequent exposure evaluation. The resulting annotations are stored separately as task metadata.
Synthesis of Sensitive Information.
To broaden the coverage of sensitivity annotations across tasks and privacy categories, we additionally introduce synthetic sensitive content into suitable task artifacts. We only augment tasks for which such content can be incorporated without changing the task objective, required interaction, expected output, or success criteria. For each eligible task, an LLM-assisted pipeline selects an appropriate artifact and insertion location and generates synthetic sensitive content consistent with the surrounding format and semantics. Each inserted span is then recorded as a sensitivity unit using the same annotation schema as pre-existing sensitive information.
We further apply a separate LLM-based verification step to improve the realism of the synthesized content. The verifier examines whether each synthetic unit resembles plausible real-world sensitive information and replaces unrealistic or placeholder-like values with more realistic synthetic alternatives. Sensitivity-Unit Representation and Taxonomy.
All sensitivity units, whether identified from the original workspace or synthetically introduced, follow a common annotation schema that records the sensitive content, its source location, and its privacy category. The source location links each unit to the artifact or application record from which it originates, allowing its exposure to be traced during agent execution. We organize sensitivity units into two top-level domains—
Personal Sensitive Information
and
Organizational Confidential Information
—comprising 12 fine-grained categories in total. The personal-information categories build on prior privacy taxonomies
(

)

We use GLM-5.3 for sensitivity identification and synthesis, while GPT-5.5 serves as an independent verifier for the synthesized content. We further conduct human evaluation to validate the accuracy of pre-existing sensitivity-unit identification and the realism and placement quality of synthetic sensitive content. Implementation Details
This section provides implementation details for reproducing the experiments in
EC
2
-Bench
, including the execution environment and the implementation of the evaluated edge–cloud collaboration strategies.
Experimental Environment.
All experiments are conducted using OpenClaw as the agent execution framework. The maximum context window is configured to 128K tokens, with each individual model interaction limited to 32K tokens. OpenClaw additionally employs an automatic context compression mechanism to manage context growth during long-horizon execution. The agent execution environment is hosted in E2B sandboxes with stable resource allocation to ensure consistent and reliable execution across experiments. All collaboration strategies share the same agent runtime, execution environment, and model deployment configuration. For all experiments, when cloud assistance is requested,
v
t
c
v_{t}^{c}
consists of the current task instruction and the execution history maintained by OpenClaw, including previous actions, tool calls, and environment observations. No additional redaction or privacy filtering is applied before cloud invocation.
Query Routing.
Query Routing makes a single routing decision before agent execution and assigns the entire task trajectory to either the edge model
M
e
M_{e}
or the cloud model
M
c
M_{c}
. We directly use the matrix-factorization-based router released with RouteLLM
(
Ong et al., 2024
)
. We calibrate the threshold on the validation set to obtain an approximately 15% cloud-participation rate at the step level and apply the same threshold during evaluation. This target cloud-participation rate is selected to keep the cloud usage of routing-based strategies comparable to that of edge-controlled strategies, enabling a more controlled comparison under similar cloud resource budgets.
Per-Step Routing.
Per-Step Routing revisits the edge–cloud decision at every agent interaction step. We adapt the uncertainty signal used by GlimpRouter
(
Zeng et al., 2026c
)
to agent execution. Before generating the action at each step, we obtain the edge model’s next reasoning-token distribution and compute its entropy as an uncertainty score. If the entropy exceeds a calibrated threshold, the current step is routed to
M
c
M_{c}
for action generation; otherwise, generation continues with
M
e
M_{e}
. The routing decision is repeated independently throughout the trajectory. We calibrate the routing threshold on the validation set such that approximately 15% of tasks are assigned to the cloud, aiming to maintain a cloud usage level comparable to other collaboration strategies, and apply the same threshold during evaluation.
Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation.
Unlike the two routing-based strategies above, Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation places the cloud-participation decision within the edge agent itself. The edge model is provided with a delegation tool backed by
M
c
M_{c}
and can invoke it at any point during execution. When invoked, the current conversation history, including previous actions, tool calls, and observations, is forwarded to the cloud model, which directly performs the next agent step. Control then returns to the edge model for subsequent execution. The delegation instruction encourages the edge agent to invoke the cloud before committing to a substantive approach, when it encounters difficulty or considers changing its approach, and before declaring the task complete. Thus, both the timing and frequency of cloud participation are determined dynamically by the edge agent rather than by an external router.
Edge-Controlled Cloud Advisory.
Edge-Controlled Cloud Advisory uses the same agent-controlled invocation mechanism but assigns a different role to the cloud model. The edge model is provided with an advisory tool and autonomously decides when cloud guidance is needed during execution. Upon invocation, the current execution history, including previous actions, tool calls, and environment observations, is provided to
M
c
M_{c}
. The cloud model returns advisory information in natural language, such as plans, suggestions, or corrective feedback. The advice is appended to the edge model’s context, after which
M
e
M_{e}
generates the next action based on the task instruction, execution history, and received advice.

A.10
Understanding Edge-Side Abilities for Collaboration
To further understand the edge-side abilities associated with the observed shift toward edge-controlled collaboration, we conduct two controlled analyses focusing on cloud-assistance decision making and guidance following.
Cloud-Assistance Decision Making.
Directly evaluating the quality of cloud-invocation decisions is challenging because there is no explicit ground-truth annotation indicating when cloud assistance is necessary during agent execution. Therefore, we evaluate the effectiveness of edge-controlled invocation through a matched random baseline. For each edge model, we first execute the Edge-Controlled Cloud Delegation strategy and record its cloud-call rate. We then construct a random-invocation baseline that preserves the same cloud-call rate but randomly selects the invocation steps throughout the trajectory. Both approaches therefore receive the same amount of cloud assistance, while differing only in whether the invocation timing is determined by the edge agent or randomly selected. We compare their task completion performance, where the performance gain over random invocation serves as an indicator of whether the edge agent can identify execution states where cloud assistance is beneficial.
Cloud Guidance Utilization.
To examine whether instruction-following ability is associated with effective advisory collaboration, we conduct a controlled instruction-following training experiment. Starting from Qwen3.5-2B, we apply targeted instruction-following RL training using the IF data provided by Ultradata
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
. The model is trained for 600 steps with GRPO, using a batch size of 32 per step and 8 rollouts per prompt.
To separate guidance utilization from cloud-invocation decisions, we evaluate all checkpoints under a fixed advisory setting, where cloud advisory calls are triggered at predetermined edge execution steps (e.g., every five steps) rather than dynamically selected by the edge model. We evaluate the model from two perspectives. First, we measure instruction-following ability using three instruction-following benchmarks (IFEval
(
Zhou et al., 2023
)
, IFBench
(
Pyatkin et al., 2026
)
, and Multi-IF
(
He et al., 2024
)
) to verify that the training improves the targeted capability. Second, we evaluate the resulting models on
EC
2
-Bench
under both advisory collaboration and edge-only execution. The edge-only setting serves as a control to examine whether improvements are accompanied by general gains in agent execution capability.
As shown in Figure
5
, instruction-following performance consistently improves throughout training, while edge-only task performance remains largely unchanged. In contrast, advisory collaboration performance increases with instruction-following training, improving from 24.8% at initialization to 28.8% after 600 training steps. These results suggest that instruction-following ability is particularly relevant to cloud guidance utilization, beyond general improvements in edge-only task execution.

article.headline: 边缘-云协作执行长程 Agent 的系统评测
article.lede: EC²-Bench 用 128 个可执行任务比较四种边缘-云协作策略：更强边缘模型下最优策略会变，隐私暴露差距却不收敛。
article.problem: 长程 agent 执行中，云模型参与不再是每个查询一次的路由决策，而是在整条轨迹里反复交织，带来轨迹级依赖：云调用会影响后续步骤、累积资源开销，并决定多少敏感信息离开本地。已有评测多聚焦单查询或单轮的路由与升级，这些轨迹级效应仍缺乏系统考察。
article.method: 作者构建 EC²-Bench：128 个可执行数字工作区 agent 任务，其中 100 个带细粒度隐私标注（共 3385 个敏感信息单元），统一评测任务完成度、云 token 成本与边缘 FLOPs、隐私暴露三个维度。实验比较四种策略：查询级路由、逐步路由、边缘控制的云委派、边缘控制的云咨询；边缘侧用 Qwen3.5-2B/9B/27B 与 Qwen3.7-Plus，云侧主用 GLM-5.3，每个任务-配置组合独立跑 3 次。
article.results: Qwen3.5-2B 下，逐步路由把完成率从 edge-only 的 12.75 提升到 39.97，云成本仅为 cloud-only 的 22.7%。最佳协作配置随边缘模型变强从 39.97% 升到 Qwen3.7-Plus 的 76.84%，接近 cloud-only（GLM-5.3）的 82.70%；策略间完成率差距从 25.22% 收窄到 3.67%，但隐私暴露差距仍达 66.23%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把边缘-云协作的评测从单查询路由推进到轨迹级，并指出未来边缘模型除自身能力外，还需具备判断何时求助云、能否遵循云端指导这两项与协作收益相关的能力。
article.limitations: 任务由六个已有 benchmark 筛选并少量补充而成（128 个），主实验云模型只有 GLM-5.3 一个，Qwen3.7-Plus 参数量未知、未报边缘 FLOPs；隐私暴露判定依赖 LLM judge，尽管在 200 对人工标注上 F1 为 96.9%，仍非完美。
article.figure_caption_zh: EC²-Bench 中长程 agent 边缘-云协作总览：一幅代表性 agent 工作流、四种云参与方式不同的协作模式，以及关于协作有效性、边缘能力影响和协作如何随边缘模型变强而演化的三个研究问题。

figure.caption: Overview of edge--cloud collaboration for long-horizon agent execution in {}. The figure illustrates a representative agent workflow, four collaboration modes with different forms of cloud participation, and three research questions on collaboration effectiveness, the impact of edge capability, and how collaboration shifts as edge models become stronger.

page_papers.title: CoworkEnv: Synthesizing Training Environments for Long-Horizon Cowork Agents
page_papers.abstract: AI coworkers must coordinate tools, communicate across turns, and act on changing workspace state while respecting workflow constraints. Constructing training experience for these capabilities requires coherent requests, service records, tool interfaces, and grading checks. We present CoworkEnv, a capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. Workflow requirements guide task construction, and programmatic validation with feedback repair checks generated specifications and grading behavior. Teacher executions yield curated demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while student interactions provide rollouts and rewards for reinforcement learning (RL). Using these resources, we train compact PocketWorker models. For Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, SFT raises the mean score from 46.6 to 64.1 on Claw-Eval, including a 31.9-point gain on Multi-turn tasks. An SFT-only extension to ClawMark demonstrates applicability across coworker benchmarks. We further compare RL training dynamics across configurations that vary reward processing and credit assignment. Improving training rewards provide preliminary evidence that the constructed environments support policy optimization.

\setheadertext

CoworkEnv: Synthesizing Training Environments for Long-Horizon Cowork Agents
Zhongwei XIE
Yiming DU
Jiaxin BAI
Baixuan XU
Chunyang LI

{zxiebk, zwanggy}@connect.ust.hk

*
Corresponding author:
zwanggy@connect.ust.hk
Abstract
AI coworkers must coordinate tools, communicate across turns, and act on changing workspace state while respecting workflow constraints. Constructing training experience for these capabilities requires coherent requests, service records, tool interfaces, and grading checks. We present
CoworkEnv
, a capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. Workflow requirements guide task construction, and programmatic validation with feedback repair checks generated specifications and grading behavior. Teacher executions yield curated demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while student interactions provide rollouts and rewards for reinforcement learning (RL). Using these resources, we train compact
PocketWorker
models. For Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, SFT raises the mean score from 46.6 to 64.1 on Claw-Eval, including a 31.9-point gain on Multi-turn tasks. An SFT-only extension to ClawMark demonstrates applicability across coworker benchmarks. We further compare RL training dynamics across configurations that vary reward processing and credit assignment. Improving training rewards provide preliminary evidence that the constructed environments support policy optimization.
1
Introduction
AI coworkers are expected to carry out everyday work through sustained interaction with users, tools, and a changing workspace. Resolving a customer-support request, for example, can require consulting account history, locating a relevant procedure, and updating the correct ticket while respecting access restrictions. Such workflows combine multi-turn communication, information gathering, tool coordination, and decisions about when to act
[
Trivedi et al., 2024
,
Yao et al., 2024
,
Xu et al., 2026b
]
. Recent coworker models and benchmarks make these capabilities explicit targets for agent development
[
Chen et al., 2026a
,
Wang et al., 2026b
,
Meng et al., 2026
,
Ye et al., 2026
]
. Developing compact models for this setting requires training experience that captures these dependencies.
Constructing that experience is a central challenge. The information needed to complete a workflow is often distributed across documents, service records, and intermediate environment state. Synthesizing a useful task therefore requires the request, the available evidence, and the permitted actions to fit together. Records referring to the same customer must agree across services; tools must expose the information needed to proceed and implement the expected state changes; and grading checks must assess relevant actions and outcomes. A plausible final response alone cannot establish that the intended update occurred or that a prohibited action was avoided. These requirements make executable environment construction and verification integral to data synthesis, as also emphasized in coworker evaluation and computer-use training
[
Meng et al., 2026
,
Wang et al., 2026a
]
.
Open agent-training efforts have begun to expose the data choices behind capable systems. Nemotron-Terminal and SERA study synthetic tasks and demonstrations for terminal and coding agents, while OpenThoughts-Agent investigates data curation across agentic tasks
[
Pi et al., 2026
,
Shen et al., 2026
,
Raoof et al., 2026
]
. Occamy extends execution-grounded training to coworker workloads
[
Chen et al., 2026a
]
. Building on these efforts, we focus on a practical question:
how can targeted coworker capabilities be translated into executable training tasks that support both imitation and learning from interaction?
We present
CoworkEnv
, a capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. Developer-selected capability requirements guide the workflow scope of task construction. A workflow specification is implemented as a request, initial service records, tool interfaces, and grading checks. We describe two forms of task variation: composing business workflows across different services, and creating safety scenarios with distinct permitted and prohibited actions. Resolving a customer-support issue, for example, connects CRM context with a helpdesk ticket and a knowledge-base procedure; investigating a payment-change request connects correspondence with financial history. In the documented safety-task family, generation agents draft task content and a separate grading role defines the execution checks. Teacher executions provide curated demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while student interactions yield rollouts and reward feedback for reinforcement learning (RL). This process separates the construction of a problem from the generation of attempts to solve it. Figure
1
shows how task construction, teacher execution, and student training fit together.
To assess the training utility of these resources, we fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct
[
Bai et al., 2025
]
to obtain
PocketWorker
-8B. SFT raises the mean score from 46.6 to 64.1 on Claw-Eval tasks, with a 31.9-point gain on Multi-turn tasks. A separate SFT-only application to ClawMark extends the evaluation to a second coworker benchmark. We also compare training configurations for GRPO, Dr.GRPO, GDPO, and GiGPO to examine advantage estimation and credit assignment. Training rewards improve over approximately three epochs on our constructed tasks, providing preliminary evidence that these environments support RL optimization.
Our contributions are:
①
Capability-guided synthesis of executable coworker environments.
We translate target capabilities into multi-service workflows
with consistent user requests, service records, tool interfaces,
and executable grading checks. Task variation spans service
dependencies and business constraints, including safety scenarios
that require investigation while avoiding prohibited actions.
Teacher execution and trajectory curation produce SFT
demonstrations, while the constructed environments support
interactive RL training.
②
Training utility and analysis.
We evaluate these resources through SFT gains on Claw-Eval, an SFT-only extension to ClawMark, and comparisons of RL training configurations.
We will release our datasets and construction pipeline, sharing the methods and design choices behind task and environment construction, trajectory collection, and data curation. We hope this helps other researchers adapt the process to their own needs.
For academic researchers working with limited resources, advanced topics such as long-horizon agentic SFT and RL can be difficult to pursue with limited GPU access, infrastructure gaps, unfamiliar engineering pitfalls, and high API costs. Our
Lessons
bring together challenges we encountered, ongoing work, and possible future directions, covering how different harnesses affect training outcomes, training–inference mismatch across harnesses, credit assignment and RL optimization. We share these experiences to help others make progress under similar constraints and avoid common pitfalls.
2
Related Work
Agent post-training.
Open post-training efforts make training data and recipes available for study
[
Lambert et al., 2024
]
. AgentTuning develops general agent abilities through instruction tuning, while Nemotron-Terminal, OpenThoughts-Agent, and SERA investigate task generation and trajectory curation for terminal, coding, and broader agentic behavior
[
Zeng et al., 2024
,
Pi et al., 2026
,
Raoof et al., 2026
,
Shen et al., 2026
]
. Related recipes extend trajectory-based training to research, data analysis, and GUI workflows
[
Fang et al., 2025
,
Qiao et al., 2026
,
Ding et al., 2026
]
. AgentGym-RL and RAGEN study learning through sequential interaction, while ToolRL examines reward design for tool use
[
Xi et al., 2025
,
Wang et al., 2025
,
Qian et al., 2026
]
. slime provides a post-training framework with customizable data generation for RL scaling
[
Zhu et al., 2025
]
. Agent harnesses organize execution and interaction interfaces
[
Xie et al., 2026b
,
Huang et al., 2026
]
, with LEGO-RL connecting native coding-agent harnesses to policy-gradient training
[
Du et al., 2026
]
. Polar provides asynchronous rollouts over existing agent harnesses, reconstructing training trajectories from proxied model API calls
[
Xu et al., 2026a
]
. Building on PPO and GRPO
[
Schulman et al., 2017
,
Shao et al., 2024
]
, subsequent methods explore advantage and loss normalization, reward-component normalization, and finer-grained credit assignment
[
Liu et al., 2025c
,
Liu et al., 2026a
,
Feng et al., 2025
,
Wei et al., 2025
]
. Our framework connects executable task construction, curated demonstrations, and interactive RL for compact coworkers.
Executable task synthesis and demonstration curation.
Task synthesis couples generated requests with interaction settings and completion criteria. AgentGen and MATRIX construct environments or simulated scenarios
[
Hu et al., 2025
,
Tang et al., 2025
]
; APIGen-MT links task blueprints to multi-turn interactions, and CUA-Gym jointly constructs instructions, environments, and rewards
[
Prabhakar et al., 2026
,
Wang et al., 2026a
]
. CuES generates executable tasks by exploring existing tool environments
[
Mai et al., 2025
]
. Verification and refinement further shape training data: ToolACE verifies generated tool-use dialogues, while AgentRefine studies refinement-oriented demonstrations
[
Liu et al., 2025b
,
Fu et al., 2025
]
. Complementary approaches obtain training experience through environment models and adaptive generation: DreamGym and Qwen-AgentWorld simulate environment dynamics, PatchWorld induces executable world-model programs with counterexample-driven repair, and AgentEvolver combines task generation with experience-guided exploration
[
Chen et al., 2026b
,
Zuo et al., 2026
,
Bai et al., 2026
,
Zhai et al., 2025
]
. Concurrent work includes Cowork-Gym
[
Zou et al., 2026
]
, which explores large-scale synthesis of interactive work environments. Our construction jointly specifies cross-service records, tools, and grading checks, then validates tasks and curates teacher executions for SFT while retaining environments for RL.
Coworker agents and evaluation.
Occamy studies coworker specialization through execution-grounded data and staged post-training
[
Chen et al., 2026a
]
. AppWorld,
τ
\tau
-bench, TheAgentCompany, and AutomationBench evaluate multi-application work, user interaction, and workflow constraints
[
Trivedi et al., 2024
,
Yao et al., 2024
,
Xu et al., 2026b
,
Shepard and Salimans, 2026
]
, while GDPval evaluates economically valuable professional tasks
[
Patwardhan et al., 2026
]
. ClawMark emphasizes persistent workflows and evolving service state, and Claw-Eval evaluates task completion, safety, and robustness
[
Meng et al., 2026
,
Ye et al., 2026
]
. AgentDojo and ToolEmu assess risks from prompt injection and agent actions
[
Debenedetti et al., 2024
,
Ruan et al., 2024
]
; Terminal-Bench and CyberGym provide execution-based evaluation in terminal and software-security settings
[
Merrill et al., 2026
,
Wang et al., 2026c
]
. We evaluate SFT on Claw-Eval and ClawMark and compare RL configurations on Claw-Eval to study learning for coworker workflows.
3
Method
CoworkEnv
constructs executable coworker environments through the following stages: capability-guided task design, executable environment construction, programmatic validation and feedback repair, teacher execution and curation, and preparation for SFT or RL. The central unit is a task environment that brings together a request, the information and tools needed to act, and checks of the resulting execution. Teacher demonstrations provide supervision for imitation, while student interaction with the environment provides experience and rewards for RL.
3.1
Capability-Guided Task Synthesis
From capabilities to task specifications.
We translate target capabilities into a coverage plan specifying service combinations, intended difficulty, and business scenarios. Scenarios define selection conditions, distractor records, and permitted actions; a fixed reference date anchors time-sensitive requirements. An LLM receives the plan together with service catalogs, an output-format specification, and example tasks. It generates the user request, initial service records, structured completion checks, and prohibited actions. The catalogs describe available tools and record formats, guiding generation toward reusable service implementations.

Programs instantiate the specification: service configurations are populated from a registry, and structured completion checks and prohibited actions are inserted into a fixed grader template. Shared services expose the generated records and support state-changing actions. Task variation thus changes the scenario, records, and checks while reusing the execution and grading implementations. Linking information across services.
Workflow construction distributes related information across services. An escalation task, for example, combines ticket creation times with customer tiers to select enterprise-account tickets open for more than 48 hours, then retrieves the account manager’s address for an email. A recent high-priority ticket is a distractor: it appears urgent but fails the age condition. Grading checks reference entities and actions from the same specification, using tool arguments and service audit records to check execution. This connects the requested goal, the evidence available through tools, and the scoring conditions.
Safety scenarios introduce constraints on acting on retrieved information. A payment-change investigation combines a suspicious email, legitimate correspondence, and transaction history. Completion checks reward evidence gathering, while designated submission or messaging actions activate a safety gate. Under the Generator–Discriminator design, the Generator drafts the request and records; the Discriminator receives the records and a note describing the safety scenario in a separate context, and specifies completion checks and forbidden actions. Appendices
C
and
D
describe the role inputs and workflow examples.
3.2
Validation and Feedback Repair
Checking generated specifications.
Programmatic checks complement the generation instructions. They verify that the specification can be parsed, that selected services are registered and have initial records, that completion weights sum to one, and that required and prohibited tool sets do not conflict. A request-level leakage check rejects designated answer identifiers exposed in the user request, preserving the need to discover them through interaction.
Checking grading behavior.
A grading consistency gate evaluates synthetic tool-call and audit records against the declared checks. A record satisfying the completion conditions must receive full completion and safety scores; an empty record must receive zero completion; adding a prohibited call must set the safety score to zero.
Feedback and regeneration.
Validation failures are returned to the generator as diagnostic feedback. The generator produces a revised full specification, which passes through the same validation pipeline. Only candidates satisfying both specification checks and grading-consistency tests are packaged with their initial records, service configuration, and grading code for execution. Appendix
D

Selecting tasks and demonstrations.
Task selection uses mean teacher completion to identify consistently completed tasks, tasks with very low completion, and an intermediate group. We retain qualifying demonstrations from the intermediate group, limit consistently completed tasks to one demonstration per normalized task prefix, and set aside the lowest-completion group. This reduces repeated supervision from easy tasks while retaining multiple executions of other tasks. When merging collections, we deduplicate by task and trial identifier so that each recorded execution enters the pool once. Appendix
