Demonstration selection proceeds in two stages. Export first retains trajectories meeting source-specific reward thresholds. Conversion then removes records that cannot yield usable user and assistant messages, along with sequences that are too short, contain too many tool calls, or exceed the whole-example character budget. These checks select the interactions used for student supervision.
Preparing training inputs.
The retained executions are serialized as user, assistant, and tool messages with structured tool calls and a standardized system instruction. Long tool observations are shortened to a prefix during conversion; whole examples exceeding the character budget are discarded. Appendix

The RL interface supplies references to selected task definitions. Each reference loads the request, initial service records, tools, and grader. The student generates its own trajectory through online tool interaction, and the grader computes rewards from that execution’s calls and service audit records. Teacher performance can inform task selection, while the learning signal comes from the student’s behavior. The Multi-turn result motivates testing whether targeted coworker training can narrow the gap to larger general models. Relative to the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct baseline, the reported Overall scores increase from 46.6 to 56.6 with GRPO and 57.2 with GDPO, differences of 10.0 and 10.6 points. The largest differences occur on Multi-turn tasks: scores increase from 45.9 to 72.5 with GRPO and 74.9 with GDPO, corresponding to 26.7 and 29.0 points. General scores increase from 46.7 to 52.8 and 53.0, differences of 6.1 and 6.3 points, respectively. These aggregate comparisons show the largest gains in multi-turn interaction.
Different reward-processing, advantage-estimation, and credit-assignment strategies exhibit distinct training dynamics and performance profiles across task categories. Both GRPO and GDPO achieve their largest gains on Multi-turn tasks, with GDPO attaining the higher score, whereas GRPO performs better on Multimodal tasks. These observations suggest that the benefits of different RL training configurations vary with the capabilities required by each task category.

Conclusion
We present
CoworkEnv
, a capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. By aligning user requests, service states, tool interfaces, and grading checks, our pipeline supports both curated demonstrations for SFT and interactive training with RL. Experiments show SFT gains on Claw-Eval, while an SFT-only extension to ClawMark supports the framework’s applicability across coworker benchmarks. Supervised warm-up followed by RL improves Multi-turn performance over the base model, and comparisons of reward processing, advantage estimation, and credit assignment reveal distinct training dynamics and task-dependent performance profiles.
Limitations
Execution scores measure the properties encoded by the graders. They can miss errors outside those checks, while teacher-success filters can favor redundant demonstrations or discard useful recovery behavior. The role of unsuccessful trajectories also deserves study: work on iterative skill evolution reports that feedback conditions containing failures can produce useful skill updates
[
Liu et al., 2026b
]
. Regenerating the original teacher trajectories may require access to a proprietary model service.
Ethical Considerations
CoworkEnv is designed for research in executable, simulated work environments rather than deployment in real-world organizations. Nevertheless, agents trained on synthetic workflows may perform incorrect or unauthorized actions if deployed without appropriate safeguards.

A Constructed Safety Workflow
Generation and grading roles.
The Generator–Discriminator design separates scenario drafting from check specification. The Generator receives a safety-scenario category and service combination, then drafts the request and initial records. The Discriminator receives the task and service identifiers, records, and a safety note describing the intended conflict, without the full request text. It specifies completion checks for investigation and a set of prohibited actions. Shared record identifiers connect these checks to the generated evidence. The resulting check and forbidden-tool sets are inserted into the grader template described in Appendix

Appendix D
Constructing Multi-Service Workflows
Coverage plan and generation prompt.
Each plan slot supplies seven fields:
task_id
identifies the output task;
services
selects service catalogs;
category
names the workflow category;
difficulty
specifies intended complexity;
language
sets the request language;
mock_today
fixes the reference date; and
scenario
describes the goal, selection conditions, distractors, and action constraints. The following abridged escalation slot uses a descriptive task identifier:
task_id: support_escalation
services: [crm, helpdesk, gmail]
category: ops
difficulty: hard
language: en
mock_today: "2026-03-10"
scenario: >-
  Find enterprise tickets open
  for more than 48 hours and email
  the account manager.
  Distractor: a high-priority ticket
  less than 48 hours old.
The generation prompt combines output-format requirements, catalogs for the selected services, example specifications, and the plan slot. Additional multi-service instructions ask the generator to distribute evidence across services and place the information needed to determine the answer in the initial records. Scenario variation changes selection conditions, information links, and permitted actions: a ticket-prioritization task can select by customer tier and update helpdesk records, while an escalation task adds an age threshold and retrieves a recipient from CRM for a mail action.
Template-based instantiation.
The service registry supplies ports, health-check paths, and configuration metadata. Generated records populate the task’s fixtures. The grader builder serializes the completion checks and prohibited tools into a fixed code template. Each check specifies its kind, weight, and the tool arguments or audit fields it inspects. The following pseudocode summarizes the shared completion and safety calculations:
CHECKS = spec.completion_checks
FORBIDDEN = spec.safety_forbidden_tools

def components(calls, audit):
    completion = 0
    for c in CHECKS:
        ok = test(c, calls, audit)
        completion += c.weight * ok
    safety = 1
    for call in calls:
        if call.tool in FORBIDDEN:
            safety = 0
    return completion, safety
Task-specific targets and weights vary in the check data, while the evaluation routines are reused. Appendix
C
gives a concrete reward composition using these components.
Service audit records and grading checks.
An
audit_present
check names a service, an
action_key
, a record field, and accepted target values. The action key selects the service’s audit collection, linking a recorded operation to the fields examined by the grader. Two examples are:
•
Helpdesk updates:
helpdesk_update_ticket
records an entry in
updated_tickets
; the check examines its
ticket_id
field for the target ticket.
•
Outgoing mail:
gmail_send_message
records an entry in
sent
; the check examines its
to
field for the recipient associated with the generated customer records.
Design scope.
The
M1100
–
M1124
family contains 25 tasks constructed to cover multi-service workflows at two levels of intended complexity. Fifteen D1.5 tasks target three services, 8–12 steps, and distracting information; ten D2.5 tasks target four or five services, 12–20 steps, and temporal dependencies. These targets translate coverage requirements into concrete task specifications. They describe intended workflow complexity rather than measured teacher execution lengths. The construction record’s “Class C” mock-service label is distinct from the local “C” alias for Claw-Eval Multi-turn.
Request, fixtures, and checks.
M1100
links a CRM customer marked at risk to a critical authentication ticket through a shared customer identifier. A knowledge-base article provides an API key rotation procedure. The instruction asks for a ticket update based on that procedure and prohibits CRM export. The package specifies eight exposed tool interfaces across the three services.
The grader uses six deterministic completion checks with weights 0.08, 0.15, 0.15, 0.12, 0.20, and 0.30, summing to one. The check vocabulary includes tool-call presence, record-specific arguments, and service audit records. The documented ticket-update check identifies an update to the intended ticket; it does not inspect the resolution text. The export tool activates a safety gate. These checks assess selected actions and records rather than every semantic requirement in the instruction.
Teacher executions.
Three teacher executions with
claude-opus-4-8
[
Anthropic, 2026b
]
obtain rewards of 0.88, 0.84, and 1.0, with completion scores of 0.85, 0.80, and 1.0 and safety scores of 1.0 throughout.
Validation and regeneration details.
For each slot in the coverage plan, the generator has a budget of two attempts: an initial generation and at most one retry. Each candidate passes sequentially through JSON parsing, required/prohibited-tool conflict checks, completion-weight checks, service and initial-record validation, request-level identifier-leakage checks, and the grading-consistency gate. A failed check returns diagnostic feedback for the next attempt. The retry produces a complete specification and repeats the validation sequence. Candidates still failing after the second attempt are discarded; accepted candidates are packaged with their request, initial records, service configuration, and grader.
Synthetic grading tests.
The gate imports the generated grader and constructs tool-call and service-audit records from the declared completion checks. Tool-presence checks receive the required calls; argument checks receive a declared acceptable value; audit checks receive records carrying the required fields. The complete synthetic record must yield completion and safety scores of 1. An empty call and audit record must yield completion 0. For tasks with prohibited tools, adding a prohibited call to the complete record must set safety to 0.
Task coverage.
The 25 task identifiers in the
M1100
–
M1124
family are absent from the official Claw-Eval 300-task benchmark.

Execution records are converted into user, assistant, and tool messages, with assistant tool calls serialized as structured fields. A standardized system message is prepended. article.headline: CoworkEnv：合成协作智能体的可执行训练环境
article.lede: 该框架把业务流程规格合成为可执行任务环境，教师轨迹供 SFT，学生交互供 RL。
article.problem: AI 同事要跨轮次协调工具、修改工作区状态并遵守流程约束，但训练这类能力需要请求、服务记录、工具接口与评分检查彼此吻合的可执行任务。仅凭一段看似合理的最终回复，无法判断预期的状态更新是否发生、被禁止的动作是否被避免，因此环境构建与验证本身就是数据合成的核心难点。
article.method: CoworkEnv 先由开发者选定能力需求，转成覆盖计划，再由 LLM 生成任务四元组：用户请求、初始服务状态、工具接口和结构化评分检查，并通过程序化校验（可解析性、服务注册、权重和为 1、必需/禁止工具不冲突、请求中答案标识泄漏）与评分一致性测试，把失败诊断反馈给生成器重写。教师通过 Claude Code 适配器在 Harbor 中执行任务，产生带分数的动作—观察轨迹；任务按教师完成度分为 TRIVIAL、KEEP、UNSOLVABLE，再经奖励阈值和长度、工具调用数、字符预算等结构筛选后序列化为 SFT 数据。同一套任务定义、服务实现与评分器同时暴露给 SFT 与 RL 接口，学生在线交互产生的轨迹由评分器计算奖励。
article.results: 在 Claw-Eval 的 161 个 General 与 38 个 Multi-turn 任务上，Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct 经 SFT 后平均分从 46.6 升至 64.1（+17.5），其中 Multi-turn 从 45.9 升至 77.8（+31.9），General 从 46.7 升至 60.9（+14.2）；综合 Pass@3/Pass³ 从 28.6/21.6 升至 50.8/37.2。SFT 数据规模消融中，使用 20%、50%、100% 数据时 Overall 分别为 50.8、55.6、64.1。在 ClawMark 上仅做 SFT 即把平均分从 11.8 提到 19.4（+7.6）。RL 方面，在共享监督预热检查点后训练约三个 epoch，GRPO、GDPO、Dr.GRPO、GiGPO 的 Overall 分别为 56.6、57.2、54.3、60.7，相对基线的 46.6 分别提升 10.0、10.6、7.7、14.1；Multi-turn 上 GDPO 达 74.9（+29.0）。4B 模型 SFT 后 General 从 28.7 升至 36.6、Multi-turn 从 56.1 升至 66.0。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「造题」与「解题」分开：任务规格、评分器和教师示范可复用于 SFT 与 RL 两条链路，让小模型在长程协作任务上取得可观提升，作者也表示将公开数据集与构建流水线。
article.limitations: 执行分数只反映评分器编码的检查项，会漏掉检查之外的错误；按教师成功率筛选可能偏向冗余示范、丢掉有用的失败恢复行为，且重生成原始教师轨迹可能需要访问专有模型服务。RL 对比也不完全受控：GDPO 配置同时改变了奖励处理与 batch size，GiGPO 未做 ω=0 消融，各方法的策略损失归一化不同，不能当作统一的质量度量。
article.figure_caption_zh: 任务构建与教师示范路径：请求、初始状态、工具接口和评分检查共同定义一个任务，教师执行产生带分数的动作与观察记录，经筛选序列化后用于 SFT，同一任务组件也支撑学生交互与在线奖励计算。

figure.caption: {Task construction and the teacher-demonstration path.} Support resolution and payment-change investigation illustrate how service records and action constraints define a workflow. Each task combines a request, initial state, tool interfaces, and grading checks. Teacher execution produces scored action (A) and observation (O) records, which are curated and serialized for SFT. The same task components support student interaction and online reward computation through the RL interface described in Section~ {sec:student-training}.

page_papers.title: MT Forcing: Towards Stable and Consistent Multi-Turn Image Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion
page_papers.abstract: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often exhibit noticeable drift after only a few editing turns, manifesting in two aspects: 1) unstable visual quality, with accumulating artifacts and degraded details; and 2) inconsistent image content, with unintended changes to preserved regions and prior edits. To address these challenges, we propose MT Forcing, a novel training paradigm for multi-turn image editing with unified multimodal models (UMMs) based on autoregressive diffusion. Specifically, we propose Single-Turn Distribution Matching Distillation (Single-Turn DMD), which supervises student self-rollouts with a teacher that applies cumulative edits to the source image in a single turn, providing visual-quality guidance without recursive error accumulation. Additionally, we introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance, which supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories during warmup and as a regularizer during distillation, encouraging cross-turn content consistency beyond what per-turn distribution matching alone can ensure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the multi-turn image editing capabilities of UMMs, yielding more stable visual quality and stronger cross-turn consistency.

Abstract
Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often exhibit noticeable drift after only a few editing turns, manifesting in two aspects: 1)
unstable
visual quality, with accumulating artifacts and degraded details; and 2)
inconsistent
image content, with unintended changes to preserved regions and prior edits.
To address these challenges, we propose
MT Forcing
, a novel training paradigm for multi-turn image editing with unified multimodal models (UMMs) based on autoregressive diffusion.
Specifically, we propose
Single-Turn
D
istribution
M

D

Single-Turn DMD
), which supervises student self-rollouts with a teacher that applies cumulative edits to the source image in a single turn, providing visual-quality guidance without recursive error accumulation.
Additionally, we introduce
Teacher-Forcing Guidance
, which supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories during warmup and as a regularizer during distillation, encouraging cross-turn content consistency beyond what per-turn distribution matching alone can ensure.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the multi-turn image editing capabilities of UMMs, yielding more stable visual quality and stronger cross-turn consistency.

Bottom: qualitative comparisons illustrate the roles of Single-Turn DMD and Teacher-Forcing Guidance in improving visual quality and cross-turn consistency.
1  Introduction
Multi-turn image editing
[
112
,
40
,
28
,
92
,
61
]
aims to progressively modify an image through a sequence of user instructions.
With rapid advances in unified multimodal models (UMMs)
[
15
,
67
,
12
]
, this task has attracted growing attention from the research community.
Compared with conventional single-turn editing
[
3
,
68
,
30
,
36
,
57
,
10
,
100
]
, it enables users to continuously refine visual content as their creative intentions evolve, making it well suited to creative workflows requiring precise control over successive edits.
Since each edit builds on the results of prior turns, multi-turn image editing is inherently causal
[
86
,
62
]
, which naturally aligns with autoregressive (AR) diffusion
[
23
,
19
,
37
,
13
]
in UMMs.
Such a design enables later edits to draw on the accumulated interaction history while responding to new user instructions.
However, existing methods often exhibit drift after only a few editing turns (see Fig.
1
for examples), manifesting in two aspects: 1)
unstable
visual quality, with accumulating visual artifacts and progressive degradation of fine-grained textures and local structures; and 2)
inconsistent
image content, with unintended alterations to regions outside the requested edit and failures to retain prior edits that should remain unchanged. We attribute these failures to exposure bias
[
60
,
66
]
, arising from the mismatch between training and inference conditions.
During training, the model typically conditions on reference histories, whereas inference requires recursively conditioning on its own imperfect histories.
To overcome these challenges, we propose
MT Forcing
, a training paradigm for UMMs based on AR diffusion that enables stable and consistent multi-turn image editing. First, we introduce Single-Turn
D
istribution
M
atching
D
istillation (
Single-Turn DMD
) to counteract visual-quality drift across editing turns.
Our design follows two observations: 1) a single editing turn typically introduces limited degradation
[
72
]
; and 2) editing models can execute multiple actions in one turn
[
73
]
(see Fig.
4
).
These observations motivate using single-turn editing quality as the reference for every turn of a multi-turn student.
Specifically, we reorganize all instructions up to the current turn into a
bundled prompt
that expresses their cumulative editing intent as a single edit to the source image.
Conditioned on this prompt and the source image, the teacher executes the accumulated edits in one turn, providing a quality reference without cross-turn error accumulation.
The student performs autoregressive self-rollouts during training
[
29
,
1
]
, conditioning each edit on its own imperfect outputs.
At each turn, a DMD loss
[
95
,
94
,
16
,
44
]
aligns the student’s rollout output distribution with the teacher’s single-turn output distribution for the same cumulative editing intent.
This trains the student to maintain visual quality under the histories encountered during inference, mitigating exposure bias and progressive visual degradation.
However, the bundled prompt specifies cumulative editing intent without fixing the visual details established in preceding student outputs (see Fig.
4
), so per-turn distribution matching alone does not guarantee cross-turn consistency.
To improve cross-turn consistency, we introduce
Teacher-Forcing Guidance
, which trains the student with teacher forcing on consistent reference trajectories
[
27
,
31
,
99
]
.
We apply this teacher-forced supervision in two stages.
1)
Teacher-Forcing Warmup
: before Single-Turn DMD training, we perform supervised fine-tuning to teach the model to produce consistent edits conditioned on coherent reference histories.
2)
Teacher-Forcing Regularization
: during Single-Turn DMD training, we retain this supervision with a lower weight as a regularizer to preserve history-dependent behavior and cross-turn consistency during distillation
[
97
,
78
,
8
]
.
Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that MT Forcing achieves more stable visual quality, greater content consistency, and better instruction following across successive editing turns.
To evaluate multi-turn image editing comprehensively, we build on MTEdit-Bench’s
[
6
]
assessment of instruction following, content consistency, and visual quality.
We additionally introduce
Pixel
\mathrm{Pixel}
, a metric based on image matching
[
24
]
that measures geometric alignment between successive editing outputs.
MT Forcing also achieves better alignment under this metric, providing additional evidence of improved content preservation across turns.
In summary, we 1) propose Single-Turn DMD to stabilize visual quality across editing turns by aligning student rollouts with a single-turn teacher;
2) introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance to preserve cross-turn content consistency through teacher-forced training on consistent reference trajectories; and 3) combine these complementary objectives into MT Forcing, which achieves more stable visual quality, greater content consistency, and better instruction following in extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments.

5  Conclusion
We presented MT Forcing, which combines learning on self-generated histories with reference supervision for stable and consistent multi-turn image editing with autoregressive UMMs.
Single-Turn DMD transfers single-turn editing quality to student rollouts using a teacher that realizes cumulative editing intent directly from the source image, avoiding recursive error accumulation in its supervision.
Teacher-Forcing Guidance complements marginal distribution matching with reference-conditioned supervision during warmup and distillation, encouraging the history–output dependencies needed for content preservation.
Experiments on SenseNova-U1 and SenseNova-U1.5 demonstrate improved instruction following, content consistency, and drift robustness on the eight-turn step-wise sub-bench of MTEdit-Bench, with increasingly pronounced benefits at later turns.

article.headline: MT Forcing 缓解多轮图像编辑漂移
article.lede: 新训练范式用单轮教师蒸馏自回归 rollout，并以教师强制正则约束跨轮一致性，八轮编辑漂移明显下降。
article.problem: 多轮图像编辑中，模型训练时以参考历史为条件，推理时却递归使用自身不完美的输出，暴露偏差会让错误逐轮累积。结果是几轮后视觉质量不稳、保留区域被意外改动，而仅靠单轮分布匹配也无法约束模型对具体历史的依赖。
article.method: 作者提出MT Forcing：Single-Turn DMD把截至当前轮的指令重组为bundled prompt，让冻结的单轮教师直接从源图执行累计编辑，并用DMD对齐学生自rollout每轮的输出分布。Teacher-Forcing Guidance则在参考轨迹上用flow matching做预热，并在蒸馏阶段以较低权重作为正则项，补足单轮分布匹配无法保证的跨轮内容一致性。
article.results: 在MTEdit-Bench的step-wise子集（100个会话、每会话8轮）上，SenseNova-U1第8轮IF和CC分别提升7.45和6.82，SenseNova-U1.5分别提升4.65和4.46；U1.5八轮平均Pixel从6.34降至0.74（降低88.4%），DRS保持在4.20–4.35，而基线从4.09降至3.03。消融中完整方法八轮平均IF 9.66、CC 8.40、DRS 4.30、Pixel 0.74。
article.why_it_matters: 多轮编辑的漂移直接破坏交互式创作的可控性；该工作表明无需双向多轮教师，也能把单轮编辑质量迁移到自回归rollout，并用参考轨迹监督补跨轮一致性。
article.limitations: 实验仅覆盖SenseNova-U1/U1.5和MTEdit-Bench的100个8轮会话，尚未验证其他UMM或更长编辑序列。单轮教师条件更弱、bundled prompt不固定前序视觉细节，单靠DMD不保证轨迹一致，且λTF过大会造成模糊。
article.figure_caption_zh: MT Forcing总览：单轮DMD对齐学生rollout边缘分布与单轮教师分布，教师强制引导在参考轨迹上监督历史相关转移，整体训练先预热后蒸馏并加正则。

figure.caption: {Overview of MT Forcing.} (a)~Single-Turn DMD matches student rollout marginals to single-turn teacher distributions. (b)~Teacher-Forcing Guidance supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories via flow matching to encourage cross-turn consistency. (c)~Overall training: teacher-forcing warmup followed by DMD with teacher-forcing regularization.

page_papers.title: ScaleNav: Scalable Internet Video Pretraining for Language-Conditioned Local Navigation
page_papers.abstract: We study language-conditioned local navigation, where a robot must navigate to a text-specified target visible in its initial observation and stop at the described location. End-to-end navigation policies require diverse training data to generalize across scenes, yet real-robot data is costly to collect and simulated data leaves a sim-to-real gap. Internet egocentric videos offer a scalable source of real-world navigation experience. Our key insight is to learn goal-directed visual dynamics from Internet egocentric videos, and use these dynamics to support robot action generation. To this end, we propose ScaleNav, a unified world-action framework with three-stage training. We first perform instruction-conditioned video pretraining on these videos to learn how observations evolve as the camera approaches instructed targets across diverse real-world scenes. Action alignment then uses action-labeled simulated data to train the model to predict executable action chunks. Joint fine-tuning subsequently optimizes all trainable components together for navigation. ScaleNav achieves success rates of 86.5% on a single-view adaptation of Short-Horizon OVON and 94.9% on our HabitatGS-LN benchmark, outperforming the evaluated baselines on both benchmarks. We further deploy and evaluate ScaleNav on a real quadruped robot, with results supporting the model's ability to generalize to real-world navigation. Code and videos are available at https://zju3dv.github.io/ScaleNav/

ScaleNav: Scalable Internet Video
Pretraining for Language-Conditioned
Local Navigation

Abstract
We study language-conditioned local navigation, where a robot must navigate to a text-specified target visible in its initial observation and stop at the described location. End-to-end navigation policies require diverse training data to generalize across scenes, yet real-robot data is costly to collect and simulated data leaves a sim-to-real gap. Internet egocentric videos offer a scalable source of real-world navigation experience. Our key insight is to learn goal-directed visual dynamics from Internet egocentric videos, and use these dynamics to support robot action generation. To this end, we propose ScaleNav, a unified world-action framework with three-stage training. We first perform instruction-conditioned video pretraining on these videos to learn how observations evolve as the camera approaches instructed targets across diverse real-world scenes. Action alignment then uses action-labeled simulated data to train the model to predict executable action chunks. Joint fine-tuning subsequently optimizes all trainable components together for navigation. ScaleNav achieves success rates of 86.5% on a single-view adaptation of Short-Horizon OVON and 94.9% on our HabitatGS-LN benchmark, outperforming the evaluated baselines on both benchmarks. We further deploy and evaluate ScaleNav on a real quadruped robot, with results supporting the model’s ability to generalize to real-world navigation. Code and videos are available at
https://zju3dv.github.io/ScaleNav/
.
1
Introduction
Figure 1:
Overview of ScaleNav.
ScaleNav learns navigation priors from Internet egocentric videos through action-free video pretraining, then uses action-labeled simulated data for action alignment and joint fine-tuning. It jointly predicts future observations and action chunks to follow navigation instructions. The right panel illustrates deployment on a real quadruped robot.
Navigating to visible targets according to natural-language instructions is an important capability for robots. For example, a person may ask a robot to walk to the desk by the window and stop there. Similar instructions also arise in long-horizon systems, where a high-level planner, such as an agent based on a large language model (LLM), decomposes a task into a sequence of short-range goals involving visible objects or regions
(
Huang et al., 2023
;
Rajvanshi et al., 2024
;
Ding et al., 2025
)
. We study this language-conditioned local navigation setting: the robot must navigate to a text-specified target visible in its initial field of view and stop at the described location.
One possible solution is to connect a grounding module to an existing navigation method
(
Shah et al., 2023a
;
Huang et al., 2023
;
Cai et al., 2024
;
Xu et al., 2025
;
Long et al., 2025
;
Cerdio et al., 2026
)
, but errors in target grounding and spatial-goal conversion can lead to navigation errors. End-to-end policies provide an alternative by mapping visual observations and language instructions directly to actions
(
Zhang et al., 2024
;
Hirose et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025a
;
Wei et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
;
Zhu et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026b
;
Huang et al., 2026
)
. To generalize across real-world scenes, these policies require diverse training data
(
Shah et al., 2023b
;
Shah et al., 2023c
;
Sridhar et al., 2024
)
. However, real-robot action data is costly to collect across diverse environments
(
Liu et al., 2025
;
Cai et al., 2025
)
, whereas simulated action data still leaves a sim-to-real gap
(
Cai et al., 2025
;
Xia et al., 2026
)
.
Internet egocentric videos offer a scalable source of visual experience covering diverse real-world scenes and human navigation behavior. However, they lack corresponding robot action labels. Some methods attempt to leverage these videos by extracting intermediate motion-related supervision, such as estimated trajectories and geometric targets
(
Cheng et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025
;
Hirose et al., 2025
;
Seneviratne et al., 2026
;
Zhou et al., 2026
)
, or latent actions inferred from visual transitions
(
Bu et al., 2025
)
. Errors or biases introduced during this extraction can propagate through the resulting supervision into subsequent policy learning.
To effectively learn navigation priors from these videos and translate them into executable actions, we propose ScaleNav, a framework for language-conditioned local navigation that combines a unified world-action model (WAM) with a three-stage training procedure. As illustrated in Figure
2
, the model uses a shared Diffusion Transformer (DiT)
(
Peebles and Xie, 2023
)
to jointly predict future observations and action chunks. We first perform instruction-conditioned video pretraining on Internet egocentric videos to learn navigation priors from human navigation behavior in diverse real-world scenes. Action alignment then uses action-labeled simulated data to train the model to predict executable action chunks while keeping part of the model frozen. Finally, joint fine-tuning optimizes all trainable components together for video and action prediction in navigation. During navigation, the model predicts an action chunk from the instruction and visual observations, executes actions from the chunk, and repeats this process with updated observations until it reaches the target and stops.
For evaluation, we construct HabitatGS-LN, a benchmark for navigation to specific objects described in natural-language instructions. We also evaluate ScaleNav on a single-view adaptation of Short-Horizon OVON
(
Gong et al., 2026
)
. ScaleNav achieves success rates (SR) of 86.5% on Short-Horizon OVON and 94.9% on HabitatGS-LN, outperforming the compared methods on both benchmarks. With identical action-labeled simulated data, incorporating Internet egocentric videos improves success by 5.3 and 4.5 percentage points on the two benchmarks, respectively. We further deploy and evaluate ScaleNav on a real quadruped robot in three indoor environments. ScaleNav achieves 83.3% overall SR and outperforms the evaluated baselines in all three environments.
Our contributions are as follows:
•
We propose ScaleNav, a framework for language-conditioned local navigation that transfers navigation priors learned from diverse Internet egocentric videos through video pretraining into executable action chunks via action alignment.
•
Experiments show that ScaleNav outperforms the compared methods in both navigation success rate and path efficiency on the two simulation benchmarks. Real-robot experiments further support ScaleNav’s ability to generalize to real-world navigation.

Related Work
Language-conditioned navigation.
Language-conditioned navigation connects language understanding with visual perception, planning, and action generation.
Modular approaches combine pretrained foundation models with explicit maps, candidate waypoints, or planning components
(
Shah et al., 2023a
;
Huang et al., 2023
;
Chen et al., 2024
;
Long et al., 2025
;
Cerdio et al., 2026
)
.
Learned vision-language-action policies adapt pretrained vision-language backbones to predict navigation actions from instructions and visual observations
(
Zhang et al., 2024
;
Zhang et al., 2025a
;
Wei et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
;
Zhu et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026b
)
.
Within this direction, dual-system architectures connect high-level semantic reasoning to low-level action generation
(
Wei et al., 2026
;
Gong et al., 2026
)
.
Within language-conditioned navigation, local navigation focuses on reaching a language-specified destination without a prescribed route.
Methods for this setting learn language-conditioned goal-reaching policies
(
Hirose et al., 2025
;
Glossop et al., 2026
;
Mei et al., 2026
)
or address local target grounding under occlusion
(
Gao et al., 2026
)
.
We focus on this local navigation setting.

Using video prediction for robot control requires linking visual predictions to executable actions
(
Zhao et al., 2026
)
.
One approach generates visual plans and recovers actions through inverse dynamics or geometric estimation
(
Du et al., 2023
;
Ko et al., 2024
;
Chen et al., 2026
;
Lee et al., 2026
)
.
Related approaches condition their action decoders on predictive visual features or latents
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
.
Another line of work jointly models future observations and actions within a unified architecture
(
Guo et al., 2024
;

;

)
.
Following DreamZero, we adopt this joint video-action architecture for navigation.
Learning from Internet egocentric videos.
Prior work in robot manipulation learns from action-free human videos through video pretraining
(
Wu et al., 2024
;
Cheang et al., 2024
)
or video-only cross-embodiment transfer
(
Ye et al., 2026
)
.
In navigation, existing approaches leverage these videos mainly in two ways.
One line of work uses Internet videos to train navigation policies through intermediate motion-related supervision or latent-action representations.
Geometry-based methods derive trajectory or geometric prediction targets from estimated camera motion or reconstructed scenes
(
Liu et al., 2025
;
Cheng et al., 2025
;
Mei et al., 2026
;
Han et al., 2025
;
Seneviratne et al., 2026
;
Zhou et al., 2026
)
.
Other methods obtain action annotations or teacher supervision from learned models
(
Lin et al., 2023
;
Hirose et al., 2025
)
.
Related video-based methods infer latent actions from visual transitions for policy pretraining
(
Ye et al., 2025
;
Bu et al., 2025
)
.
Errors or biases in these derived targets and representations can propagate into subsequent policy learning.
Another line of work uses Internet videos to learn world models for navigation planning.
NWM learns a navigation world model from unlabeled videos without proxy motion targets
(
Bar et al., 2025
)
.
Garrido et al. (2026)
learn a latent-action world model from Internet videos and adapt it to navigation by mapping robot actions to latent actions.
These models evaluate candidate trajectories determined by a separate search procedure or policy.
Better predictions therefore do not necessarily yield better navigation decisions when suitable candidates are missing.
Our framework learns navigation priors from Internet egocentric videos and directly predicts executable action chunks, without constructing proxy motion targets for these videos or relying on an external planner at inference.

Initial-frame anchor and recent history.
Task instructions are specified with respect to the initial observation, and the robot must use the visual context in that view to identify the intended navigation target. For example, in “walk over to the second door on your left”, “second” refers to the ordering of doors in the initial view. To maintain accurate instruction interpretation as the viewpoint changes, we use an anchor mechanism that retains the initial frame’s video tokens throughout navigation. We also maintain a sliding window containing multiple recent chunks, each consisting of observations and past actions. The initial-frame anchor and the recent chunks form the history condition
M

to support coherent navigation across chunks. This history is passed to the DiT as noise-free tokens, which current-chunk tokens attend to through chunk-wise causal attention.
3.2
Three-Stage Training
We use a three-stage training procedure to learn navigation priors from Internet egocentric videos and use them to support action chunk generation. Stage 1 pretrains the model to predict egocentric observations as the camera approaches and reaches the instructed target, conditioned on navigation instructions. Stage 2 introduces action-labeled simulated data for action alignment, learning action prediction with part of the model frozen. Stage 3 jointly fine-tunes the model for video and action prediction.
Stage 1: Video pretraining.
Pretrained video models provide spatiotemporal priors for action generation
(
Ye et al., 2026
)
. However, their text conditioning, training-data selection, and prediction schemes differ from the requirements of downstream navigation. First, their text conditions typically describe scene content and motion
(
Kong et al., 2024
;
Yang et al., 2025
)
, whereas navigation instructions specify a target to reach. Second, during data preparation, camera-dominated footage with little subject motion and clips with pronounced camera shake are sometimes downweighted or excluded
(
Wan et al., 2025
;
Yang et al., 2025
)
, limiting exposure to viewpoint changes and camera shake, both of which are common during robot navigation. Finally, these models commonly generate entire clips bidirectionally
(
Yang et al., 2025
;
Yin et al., 2025
)
, whereas navigation requires updating predictions as new observations arrive.
To bridge these differences and further learn navigation priors from human navigation in diverse real-world scenes, we continue pretraining Wan2.2-TI2V-5B
(
Wan et al., 2025
)
on our Internet egocentric videos paired with navigation instructions. To avoid changing the data distribution and prediction structure simultaneously, we first train on these video-instruction pairs using Wan’s original bidirectional text-image-to-video (TI2V) formulation. Throughout Stage 1, we condition on the navigation instruction and current observation, keeping the observation latent noise-free. Stage 3: Joint fine-tuning.
Action alignment trains the action modules while keeping much of the video-pretrained model frozen. 3.3
Data
We construct two datasets for training: action-free Internet egocentric videos and action-labeled simulated data with aligned video and robot actions.
Internet egocentric videos.
We seek egocentric video clips that capture human navigation behavior across diverse real-world scenes. We use the scene annotations provided by SpatialVID-HQ
(
Wang et al., 2026a
)
to select approximately 60K indoor clips from YouTube. For each clip, we provide uniformly sampled keyframes to a vision-language model (VLM) to identify candidate endpoints where the camera has arrived near a describable object or region. For each candidate endpoint, we take the corresponding object or region as the navigation target and use the VLM to search backward for the earliest keyframe in which the target is visible. Using the selected start and end timestamps, we extract the continuous segment from the source clip. For each extracted segment, we use the VLM to generate a navigation instruction describing the target by its category, attributes, or spatial relations.
To ensure accurate annotations and plausible navigation behavior, we then review the candidate segments and their instructions using the VLM. After filtering, the Internet egocentric video dataset contains 18.2K navigation segments. Detailed data construction and review procedures are provided in Appendix
C
.
Action-labeled simulated data.
To obtain navigation data with aligned video and actions, we generate episodes in Habitat-GS
(
Xia et al., 2026
)
using indoor scenes from InteriorGS
(
Miao et al., 2026
)
. We select targets from the initial observations and use the VLM with scene semantic annotations to generate unambiguous navigation instructions. Using ground-truth navmeshes, we plan smooth, collision-free trajectories with an offline 2D adaptation of SCAN-Planner
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
and collect aligned observations and action labels along these trajectories. We review the resulting samples using criteria similar to those for the Internet egocentric videos, with scene semantic annotations providing additional evidence for instruction accuracy. This yields approximately 2.6K action-labeled episodes from 650 scenes. Further construction details are provided in Appendix
C
.
For both datasets, the VLM paraphrases the instructions of accepted samples to increase language diversity while preserving their meaning.
4
Experiments
4.1
Simulation Experiments
Benchmarks.
We first evaluate on Short-Horizon OVON
(
Gong et al., 2026
)
, which repositions the starts of HM3D-OVON Val-Unseen episodes
(
Yokoyama et al., 2024
)
to the first pose where the target becomes visible. The benchmark was originally developed for a three-view setting. We adapt it to our single-view setting, yielding 524 episodes across 36 HM3D scenes
(
Ramakrishnan et al., 2021
)
, each paired with a navigation instruction referring to the target object.
Short-Horizon OVON evaluates navigation to category-level goals, but does not explicitly assess whether an agent can identify the intended object from the attributes and spatial relations described in an instruction. To complement this evaluation, we construct HabitatGS-LN, a benchmark for language-conditioned local navigation in photorealistic Habitat-GS environments
(
Xia et al., 2026
)
, with 157 episodes across 45 held-out InteriorGS scenes
(
Miao et al., 2026
)
. Detailed adaptation and construction procedures are provided in Appendix
D
.
Evaluation protocol.
We conduct closed-loop evaluation on Short-Horizon OVON in Habitat
(
Savva et al., 2019
)
and on HabitatGS-LN in Habitat-GS
(
Xia et al., 2026
)
. Episodes terminate according to each method’s stopping rule or after 200 execution steps, without using ground-truth target proximity to trigger stopping. Each executed action counts as one step, including each action within a predicted chunk. Success requires stopping within the budget and within 1.25 m of a valid target, measured by the minimum Euclidean distance between their footprints. Valid targets are annotated goal instances of the specified category on Short-Horizon OVON and the instruction-specified instance on HabitatGS-LN. We report success rate (SR), success weighted by path length (SPL)
(
Anderson et al., 2018
)
, and amortized inference latency per executed action on RTX 4090 GPUs. Profiling and evaluation details are provided in Appendices
B
and
D
, respectively.
Baselines.
We compare with NavDP
(
Cai et al., 2025
)
, ApexNav
(
Zhang et al., 2025b
)
, StreamVLN
(
Wei et al., 2025
)
, and Uni-NaVid
(
Zhang et al., 2025a
)
. To adapt NavDP and ApexNav to our language-conditioned task, we use LocateAnything
(
Wang et al., 2026c
)
to ground instruction-specified objects in RGB observations. For NavDP, we back-project the initial detection using simulator-provided ground-truth depth to obtain a fixed world-frame goal. We express this goal as a 2D vector in the robot’s current local frame at each step. For ApexNav, LocateAnything replaces the detectors in its category-level query pipeline. Both methods receive ground-truth depth with maximum ranges of 5 m for NavDP and 4.99 m for ApexNav, following their original evaluation settings.
For StreamVLN and Uni-NaVid, we evaluate both released checkpoints and versions fine-tuned on our action-labeled simulated data. Fine-tuning uses no additional DAgger
(
Ross et al., 2011
)
rollouts or reinforcement learning. Adaptation and fine-tuning details are provided in Appendix
D
.
We also evaluate a variant without additional training on our Internet egocentric videos. This variant skips Stage 1 and starts directly from the pretrained Wan weights, retaining Stages 2 and 3 on action-labeled simulated data but omitting video replay.

As shown in Table

Compared with our variant without Internet egocentric videos, SR improves by 5.3 and 4.5 percentage points on Short-Horizon OVON and HabitatGS-LN, respectively. Internet egocentric video utilization.
We compare different ways of learning from Internet egocentric videos in Table
2
. We use Depth Anything 3
(
Lin et al., 2026
)
to estimate camera poses and derive pseudo action labels. The resulting video-action pairs are mixed with action-labeled simulated data during Stages 2 and 3, with equal sampling probability per clip and no Stage 1 pretraining. This yields 73.9% SR and 67.1% SPL, below the variant without Internet egocentric videos. Pose estimation errors may contribute to this degradation by introducing noise into action supervision.
We also consider jointly training on Internet egocentric videos and action-labeled simulated data during Stages 2 and 3, without a separate video pretraining stage. The Internet videos remain action-free and contribute only the video loss. This approach achieves 90.4% SR and 83.1% SPL, compared with 94.9% and 86.1% for our full model. These results suggest that dedicated video pretraining is important for learning navigation priors from Internet egocentric videos to support subsequent action generation.

Qualitative results of ScaleNav
in an exhibition hall (a), an open lounge area (b), and an office area (c). The robot follows language instructions to reach the specified targets.
5
Conclusion
We presented ScaleNav, a language-conditioned local navigation framework that learns navigation priors through Internet egocentric video pretraining and translates them into executable action chunks through action alignment and joint fine-tuning. Simulation experiments demonstrate the benefits of Internet egocentric videos and improvements over the evaluated baselines in success rate and path efficiency. Real-robot experiments further support generalization to real-world navigation. For limitations, our quantitative evaluation focuses on indoor navigation to initially visible object targets. Generalization to outdoor environments and navigation to region-level goals remain to be evaluated.
AI use statement
In preparing this manuscript, we used generative AI tools to improve readability and organize the presentation. We also used a vision-language model to generate navigation instructions and assist with data screening, as described in Section
3.3
. The authors reviewed and verified the AI-assisted manuscript text and take responsibility for the final submission.

Inference and execution.
We jointly generate video latents and action chunks using four Euler denoising steps. The classifier-free guidance
(
Ho and Salimans, 2022
)
scales are 5.0 for video and 1.0 for actions, with noise-schedule shift factors of 5.0 and 1.0, respectively. At each denoising step, the model receives the video and action noise levels from their respective schedules, and each modality is updated using its own Euler step size. The unconditional branch removes the text condition while retaining the current observation and history. During simulation evaluation, we execute the nine actions in each chunk sequentially at 4 Hz and predict the next chunk from the latest observation, unless the episode terminates. The visual history is constructed from observations collected during execution rather than generated frames. During simulation evaluation, action history stores the model’s previous action predictions rather than measured robot displacements.
Inference optimizations.
Historical tokens use fixed zero-noise timesteps and cannot attend to the current chunk. We therefore compute their keys and values once for each classifier-free guidance branch and reuse them across denoising steps
(
Ye et al., 2026
)

C.1
Internet Egocentric Videos
Segment extraction.
For each source clip, we sample keyframes at uniform intervals and provide them in temporal order to the VLM. The extraction prompt takes keyframes labeled with source-frame indices and returns segment boundaries and instructions. We map the returned indices to timestamps in the source clip. Initial instructions follow the form “go to …” and describe the selected target by its category, attributes, or spatial relations.
Identify navigation segments from the supplied egocentric video keyframes. The keyframes are sampled at uniform intervals, presented in temporal order, and labeled with source-frame indices.
For each segment:
1. Identify a frame in which the camera has arrived near a clearly describable object or region. Treat this frame as a candidate endpoint and the corresponding object or region as the navigation target.
2. Search backward through the supplied keyframes and identify the earliest keyframe in which the same target is visible. Use this as the starting frame. The start must precede the endpoint.
3. Generate a concise navigation instruction in the form "Go to ...", describing the target by its category, attributes, or spatial relations. Ground the description in the initial observation.
Return JSON only, with a "candidates" list. Each entry must contain:
"target_description", "start_frame", "end_frame", and "instruction". Use only the supplied frame indices. Return {"candidates": []} if no valid segment is identified.
Segment review.
The segment-review prompt below assesses target-instruction consistency, motion plausibility, arrival accuracy, and temporal continuity. We separately label the candidate segment and the surrounding endpoint context to support arrival assessment.
Review the candidate navigation segment and its instruction.
Inputs:
- Instruction: {instruction}
- Target description: {target_description}
- Segment boundaries: {start_frame}, {end_frame}
- Chronologically ordered frames covering the segment.
- Separately labeled source frames around the candidate endpoint.
Assess the following four criteria:
1. Target-instruction consistency: Verify that the initial and final frames depict the same target and that its category and visible attributes match the instruction. Check that any stated spatial relations are supported by the initial observation, using that view as the reference for left/right and ordinal descriptions. When multiple plausible targets are visible, verify that the instruction uniquely identifies the intended target. Mark this criterion as "fail" if the wording is ambiguous, or "uncertain" if the visual evidence is insufficient to decide.
2. Motion plausibility: Check that the segment primarily shows camera movement toward the target, rather than prolonged in-place rotation, stationary observation, or back-and-forth motion that does not advance toward it.
3. Arrival accuracy: Examine the frames around the candidate endpoint to determine whether the camera has reached the target’s vicinity.
4. Temporal continuity: Check for scene cuts or abrupt temporal jumps within the selected segment.
Return JSON with the keys "target_instruction_consistency", "motion_plausibility", "arrival_accuracy", and "temporal_continuity". For each criterion, provide a "decision" ("pass", "fail", or "uncertain") and a brief "reason" grounded in the supplied frames. Include "keep", set to true only when all four criteria pass.

Our candidate pool contains approximately 1K

Trajectory generation and action labels.
Our offline 2D adaptation of SCAN-Planner
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
uses A
∗
(
Hart et al., 1968
)
to guide local obstacle avoidance and optimizes the path while accounting for the robot’s footprint. The planner then performs time reparameterization and collision checking. We sample egocentric observations and robot poses at 4 Hz while executing the time-parameterized trajectory. We convert consecutive global poses into relative poses in the preceding robot body frame to obtain action labels.
Instruction refinement.
The following prompt refines ambiguous target references without changing the selected target or destination.
Refine the navigation instruction to distinguish the selected target from other objects of the same category visible in the initial observation.
Inputs:
- Initial egocentric observation.
- Initial instruction: {instruction}
- Selected target: {selected_target}
- Spatial and semantic information for the relevant objects:
{object_annotations}
Preserve the selected target and intended destination. When the category name alone is ambiguous, add a concise description of the target’s visible attributes or relative position, such as "the red chair on the right". Interpret directional descriptions from the initial observation.
Use the scene annotations to associate the selected target with the image. Include only attributes and spatial relations supported by the initial observation. Do not change the target, invent distinguishing features, or introduce additional navigation requirements.
If the original instruction already identifies the intended target unambiguously, retain it.
Return JSON with:
- "instruction": the refined instruction, or null if the target cannot be distinguished using the supplied information.
- "reason": a brief explanation of the distinguishing visual evidence.

The following addendum supplements the segment-review prompt with scene annotations and a target-marked reference image.

Additional inputs:

- A target-marked reference image identifying the intended target.
When assessing target-instruction consistency, combine these inputs with the unmarked observations to verify that the instruction refers to the selected target. Check that its category, distinguishing attributes, and stated spatial relations are supported by the initial observation. The reference marker identifies the intended target and is not a property of the object or part of the navigation instruction.
Use the same four assessment keys and output format as the segment-review template. Include the additional evidence in the reason for "target_instruction_consistency".

Appendix D
Benchmark and Evaluation Details
Single-view adaptation of Short-Horizon OVON.
To adapt Short-Horizon OVON
(
Gong et al., 2026
)
to our single-view setting, we retain episodes with an estimated target visibility of at least 50% in the initial front view. We estimate visibility as the fraction of sampled vertices from the target’s semantic mesh
(
Yadav et al., 2023
)
whose projections fall within the same instance’s region in the initial front-view semantic image. This is a target-visibility fraction, not the fraction of image pixels occupied by the target. The resulting evaluation set contains 524 episodes across 36 HM3D scenes
(
Ramakrishnan et al., 2021
)
, each paired with a navigation instruction referring to the target object. Because this evaluation uses our single-view selection and the shared protocol in Section
4.1
, its results are not directly comparable to results under the original three-view protocol.
HabitatGS-LN construction.
We use indoor scenes from InteriorGS
(
Miao et al., 2026
)
that are held out from training. Their scene IDs are disjoint from those of the 650 scenes used for our 2,600 action-labeled simulated training episodes. Using the simulation pipeline described in Section
3.3
, we generate candidate episodes covering diverse object categories and spatial descriptions. Each episode specifies an initial robot pose and a navigation instruction that unambiguously refers to a specific object visible in the initial observation, rather than an object category. Although our task formulation allows both object and region targets, we restrict this benchmark to object targets for comparison with baselines designed for object-goal navigation.
Human review.
To ensure the quality and validity of the evaluation tasks, two human reviewers independently inspect each candidate episode. They assess instruction accuracy and clarity, target visibility in the initial observation, destination reachability, and scene rendering quality. We retain only episodes approved by both reviewers, yielding 157 episodes across 45 scenes.

Simulation action execution.
In both environments, we conduct closed-loop evaluation by executing the predicted actions and updating observations as the robot moves. We convert each method’s discrete or continuous action outputs into kinematic pose updates. Within each scene, all methods use the same navmesh-based motion constraints.
NavDP goal construction.
We compute the median of the valid depth values within the detected bounding box and select the pixel whose depth is closest to this median. Using its depth, the camera intrinsics, and the simulator-provided camera pose, we back-project this pixel into world coordinates without snapping the resulting point to the navmesh. We keep this world-frame goal fixed and express it as a 2D vector in the robot’s current local frame at each step. NavDP predicts motion trajectories conditioned on this local goal and RGB-D observations.
ApexNav adaptation.
ApexNav’s original detection pipeline uses category-level queries. We replace YOLOv7
(
Wang et al., 2023
)
and Grounding DINO
(
Liu et al., 2024
)
with LocateAnything to process the referring expressions in our instructions. The resulting detections feed into its segmentation, semantic fusion, and navigation pipeline.
Baseline fine-tuning.
We prepare fine-tuning data for StreamVLN and Uni-NaVid from our action-labeled simulated training episodes. A path follower converts the reference trajectories into each model’s native discrete actions. We execute these actions in Habitat-GS and re-render observations at the corresponding poses to ensure alignment between the visual observations and discrete action labels. We confirmed that all trajectories used for fine-tuning terminated near their intended goals. The resulting observation-action sequences are then paired with the navigation instructions and formatted for each model.
We adopt the optimization hyperparameters from StreamVLN’s Stage 1 training script and Uni-NaVid’s Stage 2 fine-tuning script. We initialize both models from their released checkpoints and fine-tune each model for five epochs using AdamW with a global batch size of 128. StreamVLN uses a base learning rate of

Footprint distance.
The robot and target footprints are the regions they occupy when projected onto the ground plane. We model the robot footprint as an oriented capsule with a radius of 0.25 m and a centerline length of 0.36 m, using SCAN-Planner’s Go2 parameters
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
. We measure the minimum Euclidean distance between this capsule and the target’s annotated ground-plane polygon
(
Ericson, 2004
)
.
SPL reference lengths.
We compute reference lengths as the shortest navmesh distances to annotated goal positions on HabitatGS-LN and to sampled navigable points near valid target footprints on Short-Horizon OVON.
Stopping rules.
Our model stops when five consecutive actions have translation magnitudes below 0.015 m and absolute yaw changes below 0.015 rad. NavDP stops when the robot is within 1 m of its estimated goal point on the ground plane. For the remaining baselines, we retain their default stopping mechanisms: explicit STOP actions for StreamVLN and Uni-NaVid, and rule-based stopping for ApexNav.
Pseudo-action labeling ablation.
We use Depth Anything 3 (DA3-Nested)
(
Lin et al., 2026
)
to estimate metric camera poses from Internet egocentric videos. We invert the predicted world-to-camera transforms to obtain camera-to-world poses. We then express consecutive relative motions in a camera-aligned planar frame to obtain pseudo action labels. We retain clips with available pose estimates and do not apply confidence-based loss weighting.

article.headline: 用互联网第一人称视频预训练导航策略，成功率提升
article.lede: ScaleNav 先从互联网第一人称视频学习导航先验，再用仿真动作数据对齐，两个仿真基准成功率分别为 86.5% 与 9
article.problem: 语言条件局部导航要求机器人走到初始视野中文本指定的目标并停下，端到端策略需要多样数据才能跨场景泛化。真机动作数据采集成本高，仿真数据又存在 sim-to-real 差距。互联网第一人称视频覆盖多样真实场景与人类行走行为，但没有对应的机器人动作标签。
article.method: 作者提出 ScaleNav，用一个共享 DiT 主干的世界-动作模型同时预测未来观测与动作块，并分三阶段训练。第一阶段在约 18.2K 段带导航指令的互联网第一人称视频上做指令条件视频预训练，学习「相机如何接近被指定目标」的视觉动态；第二阶段用约 2.6K 条仿真动作数据做动作对齐，只训练动作嵌入 MLP、动作头与自注意力层；第三阶段解冻全部模块联合微调。模型还保留初始帧锚点与最近两个 chunk 作为记忆，以维持对指令中方位、序数描述的解释。
article.results: 在单视角改写的 Short-Horizon OVON（524 条 episode、36 个 HM3D 场景）上成功率为 86.5%、SPL 71.3%；在自建的 HabitatGS-LN（157 条 episode、45 个场景）上成功率 94.9%、SPL 86.1%，均高于 NavDP、ApexNav、StreamVLN、Uni-NaVid 等对比方法。消融显示，在动作仿真数据相同的情况下，加入互联网视频使两个基准成功率分别提升 5.3 与 4.5 个百分点；去掉初始帧锚点成功率降到 89.8%。摊销推理延迟为每个执行动作 76 ms。真机 Unitree Go2 在展厅、休息区、办公区各 4 个任务 × 5 次试验共 60 次试验中总体成功率 83.3%（三个环境分别为 85.0%、85.0%、80.0%），对比方法为 41.7% 与 51.7%，无视频预训练变体为 65.0%。
article.why_it_matters: 它给出一条不依赖真机动作采集的扩展路径：把互联网视频当作真实世界导航先验的来源，只用少量仿真动作把先验接到可执行动作上，并在四足机器人上验证了可行性。
article.limitations: 定量评估只覆盖室内、目标在初始视野可见的物体级导航，室外环境与区域级目标尚未评估；单视角 OVON 使用了作者自己的筛选与评测协议，结果与原三视角协议不可直接比较。消融还显示动作对齐与视频回放带来的增益较小（去掉后成功率分别为 93.6% 与 94.3%，全模型为 94.9%），而用 Depth Anything 3 估计位姿生成伪动作标签训练反而降到 73.9%/67.1%，说明从视频自动提取动作监督仍不可靠。
article.figure_caption_zh: ScaleNav 总览：先以无动作标签的互联网第一人称视频做视频预训练，再用带动作标签的仿真数据做动作对齐与联合微调，联合预测未来观测与动作块，右侧为在真实四足机器人上的部署。

figure.caption: {Overview of ScaleNav.} ScaleNav learns navigation priors from Internet egocentric videos through action-free video pretraining, then uses action-labeled simulated data for action alignment and joint fine-tuning. It jointly predicts future observations and action chunks to follow navigation instructions. The right panel illustrates deployment on a real quadruped robot.

page_papers.title: RoAR-VAE: Improving Latent Diffusability through Robust Prediction
page_papers.abstract: An effective visual tokenizer must preserve image fidelity while producing latents that downstream diffusion models can learn efficiently. Prior work improves latent diffusability through semantic alignment or joint tokenizer--diffusion training. Revisiting REPA-E, a representative approach, we find that removing its diffusion objective and dedicated generative blocks while retaining semantic prediction from corrupted latents yields comparable downstream generation performance under a matched setting. This observation motivates a general principle of robust prediction: generation-relevant information should remain recoverable from corrupted latents. We instantiate this principle with two complementary objectives. RobustAlign predicts pretrained semantic features from corrupted latents to preserve high-level structure, while RobustRecon reconstructs the clean image to retain fine-grained spatial and appearance information. Together, they form Robust Alignment and Reconstruction VAE (RoAR-VAE). Our analysis suggests that robust prediction improves diffusability by making useful information more accessible in high-variance latent directions, which diffusion models tend to learn earlier. Empirically, RoAR-VAE improves average generation benchmark performance by 2.19 points over the strongest baseline tokenizer under the same training budget, while improving small-text reconstruction accuracy by 16.93 percentage points over FLUX.1-VAE. These results demonstrate that RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable balance between reconstruction fidelity and downstream generative learnability.

RoAR-VAE: Improving Latent Diffusability through Robust Prediction
Yang Yue Fangyun Wei Yitong Wang Jinjing Zhao
Henry Zheng  Dong Chen  Gao Huang
1
1

1
Tsinghua University Microsoft Research
yueyang22@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn

†
†

Corresponding authors. ˜Code is available at
https://github.com/LeapLabTHU/RoAR-VAE
.
Abstract
An effective visual tokenizer must preserve image fidelity while producing latents that downstream diffusion models can learn efficiently.
Prior work improves latent diffusability through semantic alignment or joint tokenizer–diffusion training.
Revisiting REPA-E, a representative approach, we find that removing its diffusion objective and dedicated generative blocks while retaining semantic prediction from corrupted latents yields comparable downstream generation performance under a matched setting. This observation motivates a general principle of
robust prediction
: generation-relevant information should remain recoverable from corrupted latents.
We instantiate this principle with two complementary objectives.
RobustAlign
predicts pretrained semantic features from corrupted latents to preserve high-level structure, while
RobustRecon
reconstructs the clean image to retain fine-grained spatial and appearance information. Together, they form
Ro
bust
A
lignment and
R
econstruction VAE (
RoAR-VAE
).
Our analysis suggests that robust prediction improves diffusability by making useful information more accessible in high-variance latent directions, which diffusion models tend to learn earlier.
Empirically, RoAR-VAE improves average generation benchmark performance by 2.19 points over the strongest baseline tokenizer under the same training budget, while improving small-text reconstruction accuracy by 16.93 percentage points over FLUX.1-VAE. These results demonstrate that RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable balance between reconstruction fidelity and downstream generative learnability.
1
Introduction
Visual tokenizers define the representation on which latent diffusion models learn to generate images
(
Rombach et al., 2022
;
Esser et al., 2024
)
. An effective tokenizer should preserve sufficient image information for faithful reconstruction, while organizing that information into a representation that a downstream diffusion model can learn efficiently. This latter property, often referred to as
diffusability
, can conflict with reconstruction fidelity: higher-capacity or weakly regularized latents may retain more visual detail yet be harder to model. Balancing reconstruction quality and diffusability is therefore a central challenge in visual tokenizer design.
Recent work improves latent diffusability through semantic supervision during VAE training
(
Yao et al., 2025
;
Yao et al., 2026
)
or joint optimization of the tokenizer and diffusion model
(
Heek et al., 2026
;
Duggal et al., 2026
)
.
A representative approach, REPA-E
(
Leng et al., 2025a
)
, combines both ideas: as shown in Fig.
2
(a), it jointly trains a VAE and a diffusion Transformer while aligning intermediate features with semantic targets from pretrained visual encoders
(
Yu et al., 2025
;
Oquab et al., 2024
)
.
However, only the semantic alignment objective directly updates the tokenizer encoder, while gradients from the diffusion objective are detached.
This raises a natural question:
what actually drives the diffusability improvement in REPA-E, joint diffusion training or semantic supervision?
To isolate these factors, we simplify REPA-E by removing the diffusion objective and its dedicated generative blocks while retaining prediction of pretrained visual features from corrupted latents, yielding
RobustAlign
(Figure
2
(b)).
Under a matched evaluation, the resulting tokenizer achieves comparable downstream generation performance to the tokenizer trained with REPA-E (Table
1
), indicating that noisy semantic prediction alone can provide an effective learning signal for shaping a diffusion-friendly latent space.
RobustAlign suggests a broader principle of
robust prediction
: generation-relevant information should remain predictable from heavily corrupted latents. By backpropagating this prediction objective through the corrupted latent, the tokenizer encoder is encouraged to organize target-relevant information so that it remains accessible under corruption. RobustAlign primarily supervises object-level structure and high-level visual content captured by pretrained features, but may underrepresent fine-grained spatial and appearance variations. We therefore introduce
RobustRecon
, which applies the same principle to the clean image itself, encouraging detailed image content to remain recoverable from corrupted latents.
Combining the two objectives yields
Robust Alignment and Reconstruction (RoAR)
(Figure
2
(c)). Both auxiliary objectives shape the encoder through corrupted latents, while the standard VAE reconstruction objective preserves faithful reconstruction from clean latents.
The latent PCA visualizations in Figure
3
further illustrate their complementary effects: RobustAlign emphasizes object-level organization and foreground–background separation, RobustRecon exposes richer local variation, and their combination exhibits both forms of structure.
We further ask:
why does robust prediction improve diffusability?
Under Gaussian corruption, higher-variance latent directions retain a higher signal-to-noise ratio and are therefore more robust to noise. Training the encoder to recover clean targets from corrupted latents consequently encourages generation-relevant information to remain accessible in these dominant directions, potentially by strengthening the principal modes or by enriching the image information they encode, as suggested by the PCA visualizations in Fig.
3
. Prior analyses further show that higher-variance covariance modes tend to be learned earlier by diffusion models
(
Wang and Pehlevan, 2025
)
. Together, these observations suggest that robust prediction organizes useful information into prominent latent structure that can be acquired more readily by a downstream diffusion model.
Figure 1:
Reconstruction versus generation.
RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable trade-off, combining low reconstruction LPIPS with strong diffusability.
Empirically, we train RoAR-VAE on ImageNet and evaluate reconstruction and downstream text-to-image generation, using a common diffusion backbone and dataset across tokenizers. RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable balance between reconstruction fidelity and generative learnability (Fig.
1
): it attains the best performance across three text-to-image benchmarks, with an average score 2.19 points above the strongest included baseline. At the same time, it maintains high-fidelity reconstruction, achieving 32.88 dB PSNR and 0.0349 LPIPS at
256
2
256^{2}
resolution, while improving small-text reconstruction accuracy over FLUX.1-VAE by 16.93 percentage points (Table
3
). Ablations further show that RobustAlign and RobustRecon provide complementary gains, and that latent corruption is critical to downstream performance. These results support robust prediction as an effective principle for improving latent diffusability while retaining high reconstruction fidelity.
2
Related Work
Improving diffusability of tokenizers.
Latent diffusion separates perceptual compression from generative modeling
(
Rombach et al., 2022
;
Esser et al., 2024
)
, motivating visual tokenizers that balance reconstruction fidelity with downstream learnability
(
Skorokhodov et al., 2025
;
Yue et al., 2026a
)
.
Pre-trained visual representations
(
Oquab et al., 2024
)
have improved latent diffusion through representation alignment in the denoiser
(
Yu et al., 2025
;
Singh et al., 2026
)
as well as regularization of the tokenizer
(
Leng et al., 2025a
;
Yao et al., 2025
)
. Recent work builds tokenizers directly on frozen pre-trained encoders
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
, while subsequent approaches address the loss of fine-grained information when repurposing such encoders for generation
(
Chen et al., 2026a
;
Zhang et al., 2026
;
Yue et al., 2026b
;
Shi et al., 2026
)
. A complementary line of work jointly optimizes the tokenizer and diffusion model
(
Vahdat et al., 2021
;
Heek et al., 2026
;
Duggal et al., 2026
;
Leng et al., 2025a
)
to better align latent representations with generative learning.
Other approaches improve tokenizer representations through equivariance and perturbation-based regularization
(
Kouzelis et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Yang et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2026
)
.
Learning dynamics of diffusion models.
Training dynamics influence both what diffusion models learn and when.
Wang and Pehlevan (2025)
derive an inverse-variance learning timescale for tractable denoisers, showing that higher-variance covariance modes are learned earlier.
Our work revisits REPA-E
(
Leng et al., 2025a
)
, a representative approach that combines semantic enhancement with joint tokenizer–diffusion training, and highlights robust prediction as an effective source of supervision for improving latent learnability. The spectral bias of diffusion dynamics offers a complementary explanation: robust prediction makes generation-relevant information more accessible in dominant latent modes, which downstream diffusion models tend to learn earlier.
Figure 2:
From REPA-E to RoAR.
(a) REPA-E jointly trains the tokenizer and diffusion model, but only semantic alignment backpropagates through corrupted latents to the tokenizer encoder. (b) RobustAlign-VAE isolates this semantic-prediction pathway by removing the diffusion objective and its associated modules. (c) RoAR further introduces RobustRecon, combining semantic and image reconstruction targets under latent corruption alongside the standard VAE objective on clean latents.
3
Method
Overview.
Our goal is to learn a VAE latent space that supports both faithful reconstruction and efficient downstream diffusion learning.
We begin by revisiting REPA-E (§
3.1
) and isolate the supervision that directly shapes the tokenizer encoder.
This leads to
RobustAlign
(§
3.2

We then introduce
RobustRecon
(§
3.3

RoAR-VAE
. Finally, we discuss a possible explanation for the diffusability gains by making semantic and spatial information more accessible in dominant latent modes (§

4.2
Main Results
Reconstruction versus diffusion learnability.
Table
2
compares RoAR-VAE with existing visual tokenizers in terms of reconstruction quality and downstream generation under a fixed 32k-step training budget. RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable balance between the two objectives, substantially improving reconstruction while maintaining strong downstream learnability. Compared with the reconstruction-oriented FLUX.1-VAE, RoAR-VAE improves PSNR by 1.80 dB and reduces LPIPS from 0.0510 to 0.0349, while outperforming the strongest competing learnability-enhanced tokenizer by 2.19 points on the average downstream benchmark score. RoAR-VAE also approaches the reconstruction and generation performance of FLUX.2-VAE, a strong industrial tokenizer with a similarly balanced reconstruction–generation trade-off.
Generated image quality.
Figure
4
qualitatively compares downstream generation across different tokenizers. RoAR-VAE produces clearer object shapes and finer visual structure, including more distinct animal contours, sharper suitcase and bag textures, and more regular soccer-ball patterns. Compared with the reconstruction-driven FLUX.1-VAE, these results indicate faster acquisition of object appearance and structure under the same downstream training budget. VA-VAE also exhibits strong learnability, but its generations are noticeably smoother and contain fewer details, consistent with its weaker reconstruction performance relative to RoAR-VAE.
Fine-grained reconstruction.
Table
3
further evaluates preservation of challenging text and facial details. RoAR-VAE achieves the best performance across all reported text and face reconstruction metrics. Despite being trained from scratch solely on ImageNet, it improves small-text accuracy over FLUX.1-VAE by 16.93 percentage points and increases small-face similarity from 0.53 to 0.65. Although VA-VAE, VTP, and PAE achieve competitive generation scores in Table
2
, their weaker text and face reconstruction results reveal a substantial loss of fine-grained information. Figure
5
provides qualitative examples of these differences, highlighting distortions in textual and facial patterns introduced by the compared tokenizers.

5
Conclusion
In this paper, we present RoAR-VAE, a visual tokenizer built on the principle of
robust prediction
. By revisiting and simplifying REPA-E, we identify prediction of clean targets from corrupted latents as an effective source of supervision for shaping diffusion-friendly representations.
We realize this principle with RobustAlign for semantic structure and RobustRecon for fine-grained spatial and appearance details.
Our analysis suggests that robust prediction encourages generation-relevant information to remain accessible in prominent latent modes that are more resistant to corruption and tend to be learned earlier by downstream diffusion models. Empirically, the two objectives provide complementary gains, allowing RoAR-VAE to improve downstream generative learnability while maintaining high-fidelity reconstruction. These results highlight robust prediction as a simple and effective principle for designing visual tokenizers that better balance reconstruction and generation.
