article.headline: 损坏潜变量仍可预测，提升 VAE 可扩散性
article.lede: 清华与微软提出 RoAR-VAE，把「从损坏潜变量预测干净目标」当作训练原则，生成基准均分超最强基线 2.19 分。
article.problem: 视觉 tokenizer 既要保真重建，又要让下游扩散模型好学（可扩散性），两者常相互冲突。REPA-E 把 tokenizer 与扩散模型联合训练，但流匹配损失对编码器的梯度被 detach，真正回传到编码器的只有语义对齐项，因此「联合训练」还是「语义监督」在起作用并不清楚。
article.method: 作者删掉 REPA-E 的扩散目标和仅用于生成预测的模块，只保留从损坏潜变量预测冻结 DINOv2-B 特征，得到 RobustAlign，在与 REPA-E 匹配的设置下下游表现相当。再用 RobustRecon 让辅助解码器从损坏潜变量重建干净图像（L1 与 LPIPS），补足语义特征缺失的细粒度细节。两者与标准 VAE 目标相加构成 RoAR-VAE，tokenizer 约 84M 参数、8× 下采样、32 通道。
article.results: 在 ImageNet 256² 上，RoAR-VAE 重建达 32.88 dB PSNR、0.0349 LPIPS、0.9258 SSIM、rFID 0.1309；在 GenEval、GenEval2、DPG-Bench 三项 32k 步下游生成评测上分别为 62.22、51.79、77.56，均分 63.86，比最强基线 REPA-E-FLUX 的 61.45 高 2.19 分。TokBench 上小文字重建准确率比 FLUX.1-VAE 高 16.93 个百分点（69.00 对 52.07），小尺度人脸相似度由 0.53 升至 0.65。消融显示去掉潜变量加噪后均分从 63.86 降到 58.47，RobustAlign 与 RobustRecon 单独使用分别为 62.49 和 59.38。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明提升可扩散性不必把扩散模型拉进 tokenizer 训练，只需从损坏潜变量预测干净目标，因而可缓存潜变量、降低训练成本。作者还给出一种解释：加噪下高方差主模态信噪比更高，该目标把有用信息推向扩散模型较早学到的主导方向。
article.limitations: 高方差模态的解释只是「possible explanation」，论文未做因果验证；tokenizer 仅在 ImageNet 256² 上训练，下游模型也只有约 0.8B 参数，规模与分辨率都有限。作为参考的 FLUX.2-VAE 在 rFID（0.1085 对 0.1309）上仍优于本文，但其训练数据与配方未公开，无法公平比较。
article.figure_caption_zh: 从 REPA-E 到 RoAR：(a) REPA-E 联合训练 tokenizer 与扩散模型，但只有语义对齐经损坏潜变量回传到编码器；(b) RobustAlign-VAE 去掉扩散目标及相关模块，隔离出该通路；(c) RoAR 进一步加入 RobustRecon，在潜变量损坏条件下同时预测语义特征并重建图像。

figure.caption: {From REPA-E to RoAR.} (a) REPA-E jointly trains the tokenizer and diffusion model, but only semantic alignment backpropagates through corrupted latents to the tokenizer encoder. (b) RobustAlign-VAE isolates this semantic-prediction pathway by removing the diffusion objective and its associated modules. (c) RoAR further introduces RobustRecon, combining semantic and image reconstruction targets under latent corruption alongside the standard VAE objective on clean latents.

page_papers.title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?
page_papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference. This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a fixed noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training. Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training. Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at $256 \times 256$ resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of $1.19$ among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming.
page_papers.content:
Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?
Woobin Park
Jaeyeon Kim
Yilun Du
Sitan Chen
Bohyung Han

Abstract
Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference.
This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce
Priming Models
, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a
fixed
noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training.
Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training.
Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at
256
×
256
256\times 256
resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of
1.19
1.19
among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at
https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming
.
Figure 1:
Priming Models
dramatically improve the training compute vs. FID trade-off on ImageNet (
left
). Simple reconstruction pretraining provides an effective initialization that makes subsequent distributional post-training substantially more efficient (
right
).
1
Introduction
A central goal of generative modeling is to achieve high sample quality with efficient training and inference. Diffusion and flow-based models
(
Song et al., 2020
;
Ho et al., 2020
;
Lipman et al., 2022
;
Albergo et al., 2025
)
have demonstrated remarkable generative capabilities and now serve as backbones for several domains
(
Ho et al., 2020
;
Abramson et al., 2024
;
Chi et al., 2025
)
, but they rely on iterative sampling with multiple network evaluations.
This has motivated considerable effort toward one- and few-step generation
(
Salimans and Ho, 2022
)
. Much of this progress builds on diffusion and flow formulations, including consistency-based modeling
(
Song et al., 2023
;
Lu and Song, 2025
)
, flow-map learning
(
Boffi et al., 2024
;
Geng et al., 2026a
;
Geng et al., 2026b
)
, and distributional distillation
(
Luo et al., 2023
;
Yin et al., 2024a
;
Yin et al., 2024b
)
. While promising, these approaches require a considerable amount of extra machinery to work, like specialized stabilization strategies, Jacobian–vector products, classifier-free guidance, a teacher to distill from, etc.
A complementary approach is to train a generator by directly matching its output distribution to the data distribution. This naturally supports generation in a single network evaluation and has a long history in GANs
(
Goodfellow et al., 2014
)
and maximum mean discrepancy-based generators
(
Li et al., 2015
;
Li et al., 2017
)
. Translating these objectives into effective training, however, requires significant engineering effort
(
Gulrajani et al., 2017
;
Mescheder et al., 2018
)
.
This latter approach has seen a recent resurgence of interest, with Drifting Models
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
and W-Flow
(
Han et al., 2026
)
demonstrating that direct distributional learning can produce high-quality one-step generators at scale. Their training recipes nevertheless rely on longer training-time schedules and subtle tricks like style-conditioning
(
Karras et al., 2019
)
. Thus, the simplicity of one-step inference still comes at the cost of substantial complexity in getting these models to train.
In this work, we therefore ask:
Does training a one-step generator need to be this complicated?
We introduce
Priming Models
, a drastically more straightforward framework for one-step generative modeling with just two basic components:
[Stage 1] Reconstruction pretraining:
We pretrain the network with a simple reconstruction objective – in fact, even denoising at a
fixed
corruption level suffices.
[Stage 2] Distributional post-training:
We use the pretrained network directly as a one-step
generator that maps Gaussian noise to samples, then
refine it by matching generated and real distributions
in feature space, e.g., using an optimal transport loss.
Empirically,
Priming Models
achieve strong performance with substantially reduced training compute across three visual domains:
•
ImageNet
: Priming Models achieve state-of-the-art FID (
1.19
)
1
1
1
FD-loss
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
reports FID 0.72 for pixel MeanFlow by directly optimizing Fréchet Distance. We exclude this configuration from comparison and revisit this in Section
4.2
.
and Fréchet distances across other feature spaces among one-step generators, outperforming Pixel MeanFlow
(
Lu et al., 2026b
)
, Drifting
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
, and even multistep diffusion baseline JiT
(
Li and He, 2026
)
, with approximately
10
×
10\times
less compute than Drifting (Figure
1
, left).
•
Text-to-Image
: Priming Models substantially outperform one-step MeanFlow on GenEval and DPG, while reducing training compute by a factor of
1.9
.
•
World models
: Priming Models outperform the Drifting baseline
(
Lu et al., 2026a
)
with approximately half the training compute, while also achieving performance comparable to the (multi-step) flow matching baseline.
A key factor behind our strong empirical results is that
reconstruction pretraining substantially accelerates distributional post-training
(Figure
1
, right). Without the former, even when the distributional objective provides useful correction directions, the network’s Jacobian may hinder how effectively the parameters update to realize these improvements. Through controlled experiments, we demonstrate that reconstruction pretraining ameliorates this by aligning the Jacobian and shaping how readily the model’s outputs can be refined.
Together, our findings suggest a surprisingly minimal design principle for generative modeling: use reconstruction pretraining to
prepare
a generator for distributional post-training. Priming Models realize this principle, enabling high-quality one-step generators to be efficiently trained from scratch.

;

;

More recently, Drifting Models

1,280

We find that fixing these style embeddings yields only marginal differences between images
across different Gaussian noises
(Figure
3
), although varying the style embeddings still produces diverse samples. This suggests that style conditioning is an important source of sample diversity in this setting. Taken together, these observations suggest that optimizing distributional objectives from scratch, especially without these tweaks, remains challenging. This leads us to ask:
Question:
Can a suitable initialization make distributional post-training more effective?
Our intuition is that distributional training is challenging from scratch because at the start, the network has no information about the structure of natural images. To that end, we seek to first learn a related capability: recovering clean-image structure from corrupted inputs. Denoising reconstruction provides a natural way to learn this capability. Corrupted inputs retain information about the underlying images to guide recovery, while their clean counterparts provide direct supervision.
Our hypothesis is that learning to reconstruct provides a useful initialization for subsequent distributional optimization. This motivates
reconstruction pretraining
as a
first stage
toward learning the full noise-to-image mapping.

Fréchet distance

5
Conclusion
In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generative models end-to-end. Reconstruction pretraining prepares the generator for efficient distributional post-training, enabling strong empirical performance across multiple visual domains.
That said, our work leaves several open questions. Priming Models rely on pretrained feature encoders. Although we demonstrate our method with multiple sets of feature encoders, this dependence raises the question of whether it can be eliminated. The relationship between reconstruction pretraining and Jacobian alignment also warrants deeper investigation. Finally, closing the remaining performance gap with multi-step diffusion and flow models remains an important challenge.
Outlook.
More broadly, our results suggest that we may be overthinking the problem: the specialized formulations and elaborate training machinery used in prior work are not the only path to train one-step generators. We hope our work opens the door to simpler and more scalable approaches to one-step generative modeling.

Appendix A
Related Work
In this section, we review prior work on one- and few-step generative modeling, organized by their methodological category.
Category 1: Trajectory straightening and flow-map learning.
These lines of work obtain few-step generative models by learning from a diffusion or probability-flow trajectory. Progressive distillation repeatedly compresses a teacher sampler into fewer steps
(
Salimans and Ho, 2022
)
. Consistency Models instead enforce agreement among predictions made at different points along the same trajectory
(
Song et al., 2023
)
, while subsequent work improves their stability and scaling or extends consistency to trajectory segments
(
Geng et al., 2025
;
Song and Dhariwal, 2024
;
Lu and Song, 2025
;
Kim et al., 2024
)
. Rectified Flow and reflow
(
Liu et al., 2023a
;
Liu et al., 2023b
)
seek straighter transport paths that are easier to integrate in few steps. These straightening methods modify the coupling and resulting trajectory so that coarse numerical integration can accurately reach its endpoint.
A related but distinct family learns the finite-time transition across an interval of a flow-matching trajectory, such as a flow map or average velocity. This includes Flow Map Matching, Shortcut Models, MeanFlow, Improved MeanFlow, and Inductive Moment Matching
(
Boffi et al., 2024
;
Frans et al., 2025
;
Geng et al., 2026a
;
Geng et al., 2026b
;
Zhou et al., 2025
)
. These methods differ in their targets and training estimators, but generally supervise a particular time-dependent transport or consistency relation.
Priming:
Priming Models do not attempt to recover a prescribed trajectory or flow map: reconstruction pretraining provides an initialization for the network, which we then directly use as a one-step generator.
Category 2: Teacher-guided distillation.
Another line of work distills a pretrained diffusion teacher into a one-step student, with much of the focus on designing effective distillation objectives. Diff-Instruct
(
Luo et al., 2023
)
uses score-based distributional objectives derived from a diffusion teacher, while DMD and DMD2
(
Yin et al., 2024b
;
Yin et al., 2024a
)
optimize the student using the difference between teacher and student score estimates. Score Identity Distillation
(
Zhou et al., 2024
)
provides a related score-based formulation. Adversarial Diffusion Distillation combines score distillation with an adversarial objective to improve fidelity in the low-step regime
(
Sauer et al., 2024
)
.
Priming:
These approaches inherit the cost and machinery required to obtain and query that teacher. In contrast, Priming Models are trained from scratch and therefore do not require a pretrained teacher.
Category 3:Distributional loss (from scratch).
Directly matching a generator distribution to the data distribution has a long history. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) learn a one-pass generator through an adversarially trained discriminator
(
Goodfellow et al., 2014
)
, with Wasserstein objectives and regularization improving the geometry and stability of training
(
Arjovsky et al., 2017
;
Gulrajani et al., 2017
;
Mescheder et al., 2018
)
. Generative Moment Matching Networks use maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) in place of adversarial discrimination, while MMD-GANs further learn the MMD kernel adversarially
(
Li et al., 2015
;
Li et al., 2017
)
.
Genevay et al. (2018)
trains implicit generative models directly using a Sinkhorn divergence. These works, however, are limited in empirical scope and, more importantly, differ from Priming Models in that we apply the distributional objective after a reconstruction pretraining stage.
Recent works revisit direct one-step learning at a more practical scale. YOSO
(
Luo et al., 2024
)
stabilizes adversarial one-step training through a self-cooperative diffusion GAN, while Adversarial Flow
(
Lin et al., 2025
)
trains with an adversarial objective but constrains the generator to learn the deterministic transport map associated with flow matching.
Priming:
Priming Models share the goal of direct distribution matching, but do not optimize it from random initialization: reconstruction pretraining first teaches the generator to correct corrupted inputs toward clean images, after which a distributional objective refines it into a one-step generator.
Category 3-1: Drifting Models.
Drifting Models
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
construct an attraction-repulsion field using a normalized Laplacian kernel and train the generator to match stop-gradient targets obtained by displacing its generated features along this field. W-Flow
(
Han et al., 2026
)
derives a training-time velocity field from the Wasserstein gradient flow of the Sinkhorn divergence, using barycentric projections computed from entropic optimal transport plans.
Van Assel et al. (2026)
additionally examine how the choice of frozen feature space affects transport stability in distribution matching.
Priming:
Priming Models introduce reconstruction pretraining before distributional optimization, and this stage is key to our strong compute vs. quality trade-off.
Our implementation also seeks to dispense with the additional engineering machinery used in these works. Both reported ImageNet architectures include learned random style embeddings, and both frameworks support classifier-free guidance; Drifting additionally normalizes its constructed drift field. Priming does not use these additional mechanisms and instead optimizes an OT-based distributional surrogate. All four models reported in Section
3
share exactly the same post-training configuration, further illustrating the simplicity of our approach.
This suggests that reconstruction pretraining can make distributional optimization more efficient while supporting a simpler training recipe. We hypothesize that this initialization reduces the need for additional training mechanisms, although our experiments do not isolate their individual contributions.
Category 4: Distributional loss (fine-tuning).
Distributional objectives have also been used to adapt pretrained generative models. MMD-DDM
(
Aiello et al., 2023
)
fine-tunes pretrained diffusion models with MMD to improve quality under a restricted sampling-step budget. DiffRatio
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
estimates the density ratio between noisy real and generated distributions to train a one-step model without a teacher score. FD-loss
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
makes feature-space Fréchet distance practical as a training objective by maintaining population-level feature statistics, and applies it to pretrained one- and multi-step generators. More recently, iRDM
(
Feng et al., 2026
)
scales MMD-based post-training across multiple pretrained representation spaces.
Most closely related to our work, D2O
(
Zheng and Yang, 2025
)
shows that adversarial fine-tuning alone can convert a pretrained diffusion model into a one-step generator, while
Yang et al. (2026, Section 4.3)
show that FD-loss can convert JiT, a multi-step diffusion model, into a competitive one-step generator.
Priming:
Priming Models build on the perspective that pretraining can prepare a network for subsequent distributional optimization. We investigate how simple this pretraining task can be, showing that reconstruction—even denoising at a single fixed noise level without noise-level conditioning—can provide an effective initialization for our distributional training, despite poor initial one-step samples (Figure
1
, right). We further examine alternative pretraining tasks (Section
4.1
) within the same framework.
Finally, viewing reconstruction pretraining and distributional post-training as a complete training procedure also enables comparisons with prior methods based on total training compute across both stages, measured in EFLOPs.

article.headline: 先重建再分布微调：一步生成训练更省算力
article.lede: Priming Models 先做简单重建预训练，再做特征空间分布后训练，在 ImageNet 一步生成取得 FID 1
article.problem: 扩散与流匹配通常需要多次网络评估；现有的一步或少步生成方法多依赖一致性模型、流图学习、蒸馏或复杂的稳定化技巧。直接匹配生成分布虽天然支持一步采样，但从零训练对优化很敏感、工程负担重。论文因此追问：训练一步生成器是否真的需要如此复杂？
article.method: Priming Models 分两阶段训练同一网络：先用重建目标预训练，主实验甚至在固定噪声水平 s=0.8 下做像素去噪，也可替换为掩码重建或 RAE 表示蒸馏。随后把网络直接当作从高斯噪声到图像的一步生成器，在冻结特征空间用最优传输（Sinkhorn）等分布损失做后训练。该框架不依赖预设扩散轨迹、教师蒸馏或分类器无引导，也不使用风格嵌入等额外组件。
article.results: ImageNet 256×256 上，Priming-L（160 epoch 预训练）取得 FID 1.19、FDr5 7.10，总训练算力 238.95 EFLOPs；表 1 中 Drifting-L 为 FID 1.61、1476.39 EFLOPs。文本到图像上，固定 s=0.8 的 200k 版本 GenEval 0.740、DPG-Bench 81.30，总算力 293.53 EFLOPs，约为 MeanFlow 基线 546.64 EFLOPs 的 1/1.86；logit-normal 290k 版本为 GenEval 0.818、DPG-Bench 82.16，算力 420.16 EFLOPs。世界模型 RT-1 上，Priming 用 12.37 EFLOPs，较 DriftWorld 的 30.71 少 59.7%，SSIM 0.878、FID 3.16；Bridge-V2 用 9.50 EFLOPs，较 37.05 少 74.4%。消融中，去掉感知损失使 FID 从 1.38 升至 2.07；固定噪声 s=0.8 在 80 epoch 预训练、12.5k 后训练更新后 FID 为 1.65，而 s=1.0 为 65.08。
article.why_it_matters: 若这一设计具有可扩展性，一步生成器不必依赖复杂蒸馏或轨迹学习，简单重建预训练就能显著降低分布后训练的门槛与算力。
article.limitations: 作者承认方法依赖冻结的预训练特征编码器，且与多步扩散/流模型仍有性能差距；Jacobian 对齐解释主要是相关性证据，ConvNeXt 的全局均值特征并不遵循同一趋势。另外，摘要称约为先前方法十分之一算力，但表 1 中相对 Drifting-L 的 1476.39 对 238.95 EFLOPs 约为 6.2 倍差距，具体倍数取决于基线与可比 FID 的口径。
article.figure_caption_zh: Priming Models 显著改善 ImageNet 上训练算力与 FID 的权衡（左）；简单重建预训练提供有效初始化，使后续分布后训练更高效（右）。

figure.caption: {Priming Models} dramatically improve the training compute vs. FID trade-off on ImageNet ( {left}). Simple reconstruction pretraining provides an effective initialization that makes subsequent distributional post-training substantially more efficient ( {right}).

page_papers.title: GAD: Geometry Attention Distillation for Consistent Video Generation
page_papers.abstract: Video diffusion models generate visually compelling short-term sequences but often struggle to preserve scene geometry and object structure over time. In this paper, we first demonstrate that current video attention cannot identify reliable correspondences across frames, with responses dispersed across multiple regions even after recognizable scene structure has emerged. We argue that reliable cross-frame associations are essential for information exchange as scene structure forms in video generation. Thus, we introduce Geometry Attention Distillation (GAD), which transfers correspondences from a frozen geometry model's attention to video attention. Extracted from clean videos, these correspondences link the same static surface or moving object across frames. Since structure formation begins in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise, we apply attention distillation at a student layer selected according to the noise timestep. After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding locations. Experiments across all three video backbones demonstrate improved long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency, with geometric gains across generation lengths. On Wan2.2 5B, GAD improves cross-frame matching accuracy by at least 30% over the Wan baseline on both long-range benchmarks. Notably, GAD achieves these gains without additional inference modules, offering a promising approach to efficient and consistent video-based world simulation. Project page: https://fantasy-amap.github.io/GAD/.

Abstract
Video diffusion models generate visually compelling short-term sequences but often struggle to preserve scene geometry and object structure over time.
In this paper, we first demonstrate that current video attention cannot identify reliable correspondences across frames, with responses dispersed across multiple regions even after recognizable scene structure has emerged.
We argue that reliable cross-frame associations are essential for information exchange as scene structure forms in video generation.
Thus, we introduce Geometry Attention Distillation (
GAD
), which transfers correspondences from a frozen geometry model’s attention to video attention.
Extracted from clean videos, these correspondences link the same static surface or moving object across frames.
Since structure formation begins in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise, we apply attention distillation at a student layer selected according to the noise timestep.
After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding locations.
Experiments across all three video backbones demonstrate improved long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency, with geometric gains across generation lengths.
On Wan2.2 5B,
GAD
improves cross-frame matching accuracy by at least 30% over the Wan baseline on both long-range benchmarks.
Notably,
GAD
achieves these gains without additional inference modules, offering a promising approach to efficient and consistent video-based world simulation.

1  Introduction
Recent video diffusion models
[

generate visually compelling sequences from text and images, yet struggle to preserve scene geometry over time and maintain coherent object structure during motion. Such consistency is essential for interactive world modeling
[
68

49
]
, robotic planning
[
17
,
32
]
, and autonomous driving simulation
[
21
,
64
]
, where generated videos must represent temporally coherent environments.
To improve consistency, existing approaches employ camera-aware positional encoding
[
36
,
72
]
, explicit geometric conditioning
[
53
,
6
,
25
]

[
37
,
78

[
65
,
23
]
.
However, such guidance does not ensure that video models reliably associate observations of the same scene element across frames, a capability essential for consistent video generation.
To understand how cross-frame associations develop, we examine attention patterns in video models and the emergence of scene structure across noise levels and network depths.
Our analysis shows that video attention cannot reliably identify the same scene element across frames: its responses are often dispersed across multiple regions, even after recognizable scene structure has emerged.
Such ambiguous associations can mix information from unrelated regions, undermining the preservation of scene geometry and object structure across frames.
Ideally, cross-frame attention should connect observations of the same scene element, enabling information exchange that supports consistent structure formation. We further observe that recognizable scene structure begins to emerge in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise. This suggests guiding video attention where structure and cross-frame associations are beginning to form, with the guidance depth adapted to the noise level. For a source of this guidance, we turn to geometry foundation models
[
35
,
58
]
with promising multi-view matching capabilities.
Probing VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
[
59
]
reveals attention responses that associate the same static surface or moving object across frames, providing geometric correspondence targets for guiding video attention.
Building on these insights, we introduce Geometry Attention Distillation (
GAD
), an attention distillation framework that guides cross-frame associations during structure formation. During training, we extract correspondence targets from the attention of a frozen geometry model on clean videos. The total attention each source token assigns to a target frame serves as a reliability cue for weighting its supervision. We select the student layer for attention distillation according to the noise timestep, guiding cross-frame associations as scene structure forms. At the selected layer, pairwise supervision encourages spatial discrimination within frame pairs, while trackwise supervision extends temporal coverage by matching a common source to multiple target frames. These complementary distillation objectives are optimized jointly with the original video generation loss, transferring cross-frame relations while preserving the flexibility of video representations. After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding regions across frames, while generated videos better preserve scene geometry and moving-object structure.
We evaluate
GAD
on camera-controlled video generation using RealEstate10K and DL3DV-10K for long-range scene consistency and OmniWorld-Game for dynamic consistency.
Across all three video backbones,
GAD
improves geometric consistency in long-range generation and temporal consistency in dynamic generation.
Geometric improvements across generation lengths further support the applicability of
GAD
across backbone configurations and video durations.
Notably, with Wan2.2 5B,
GAD
delivers at least a 30% relative improvement in cross-frame matching accuracy on both long-range benchmarks, without additional inference modules or computations.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We analyze cross-frame associations in video models, revealing persistent geometric ambiguities in attention and a noise-dependent shift in the depth at which scene structure begins to form. These observations motivate geometry attention distillation at layers where structure is emerging.
•
We propose
GAD
, an attention distillation framework that transfers geometric correspondence knowledge to video attention for improved cross-frame consistency.
•
Extensive experiments demonstrate that
GAD
improves long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency across all three video backbones, with consistent improvements across generation lengths and no additional inference modules.

3  Analysis and Motivation
3.1  Attention Patterns in Video Models
Cross-frame consistency requires associating the same scene element across viewpoint changes or object motion. We examine how video attention establishes these associations across noise levels and network depths.
In
Fig.
2(a)
, we fix a source query and a target frame within a single video generation trajectory, and visualize the target frame’s intermediate token features using PCA alongside query-to-target attention responses. The PCA visualizations reveal recognizable scene structure, while the attention maps show whether responses concentrate near the reference correspondence or favor other regions. Further visualization details are provided in
Section
E.1
.
This joint analysis reveals two key findings. First, video attention cannot reliably identify the same scene element across frames. Its responses can remain dispersed across multiple regions, including those with similar appearance or semantics, even after recognizable scene structure has emerged in the PCA features. Second, the emergence of scene structure and cross-frame associations depends on both noise level and network depth. We distinguish three qualitative regimes.
In the
noise-dominated region
, PCA features show little recognizable scene structure, while attention responses remain scattered rather than concentrated around the corresponding region.
In the
structure-formation region
(red boxes in
Fig.
2(a)
), recognizable scene structure begins to emerge, and attention starts to respond to corresponding regions across frames, although competing responses remain. This region occurs in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise.
In the
structure-established region
, scene layout is more clearly defined in the PCA features and cross-frame associations are more apparent, but they are not necessarily geometrically accurate.
These observations motivate explicitly guiding video attention toward geometrically corresponding regions to help preserve scene and object structure across frames.
Furthermore, the three observed regimes suggest that the placement of this guidance matters. In the noise-dominated region, weak structural evidence may make correspondence supervision difficult to exploit; in the structure-established region, additional guidance may have less opportunity to shape associations that have already formed.
The structure-formation region offers an intermediate stage where correspondence learning has a structural basis while the associations are still developing. We therefore hypothesize that geometric guidance is most effective in this region. Since this region emerges at different depths depending on noise, we adapt the supervision layer to the noise timestep.

5.3  Ablations
Using Wan2.2 5B on DL3DV-10K, we ablate the noise-timestep routing schedule, confidence-aware teacher weighting, and pairwise and trackwise supervision to assess their contributions.
Noise-dependent supervision.
As shown in
Table
4
, fixed-layer supervision (R2–R4) already improves geometric metrics over the Wan baseline (R1), while the proposed noise-timestep routing (R8) outperforms all other configurations (R1–R7); complete metrics appear in
Table
6
. Thus, correspondence targets are useful on their own, while their placement determines how effectively they guide generation. The lower performance of R5–R7 compared with R2–R4 further suggests that varying supervision with noise is insufficient without an appropriate layer choice.
These results support the motivation in
Section
3
: supervision should adapt to the noise timestep to target the structure-formation region rather than constrain a fixed layer throughout denoising.
Contributions of distillation components.
Table
5
shows that transferring teacher correspondences indiscriminately is insufficient: without confidence weighting, matching hit rate falls below the Wan baseline despite modest improvements in camera error. This supports accounting for uncertainty in teacher matches rather than treating every target equally. With confidence weighting, either pairwise or trackwise supervision improves all geometric metrics, while their combination performs best across all seven metrics. The joint gains are consistent with their complementary roles: pairwise supervision discriminates spatial matches within a target frame, whereas trackwise supervision extends correspondence coverage across time.
6  Conclusion
We have presented
GAD
, an attention distillation framework that transfers geometric correspondence knowledge from a frozen geometry teacher to video attention.
Motivated by geometric ambiguities in video attention and the noise-dependent emergence of scene structure,
GAD
guides cross-frame associations during structure formation while preserving the video model’s representational flexibility.
Experiments show that
GAD
consistently focuses attention on corresponding regions and improves long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency across all three video backbones, with geometric improvements across generation lengths. These gains require no additional inference modules. Our findings highlight geometric correspondence transfer through attention as a promising approach to consistent video generation and video-based world simulation.

Appendix A
Loss and Sampling Details
Sampling source–target relations.
Pairwise supervision samples valid directed frame pairs without replacement, excluding pairs within the same frame. Within each selected pair, source tokens are sampled uniformly without replacement from those with valid cached correspondences. Each selected query is compared with all spatial keys in its target frame. If fewer valid pairs or queries are available than the sampling budget, the remaining entries are masked out.
Trackwise supervision first samples one source frame containing eligible source tokens, then samples tokens that have valid correspondences in at least two other frames. Each source is matched to all of its valid target frames, excluding its own frame. For each target frame, the candidate set contains the Gaussian positive neighborhood and uniformly sampled spatial negatives without replacement from outside that neighborhood. Both schemes resample their relations during training; confidence weights affect the loss reduction rather than the probability of selecting a valid relation.

Appendix B
Implementation Details
B.1  Teacher Targets and Alignment
Reference correspondences for head selection.
We select the teacher layer–head pair using reference correspondences from both static and dynamic scenes. For the static set, we randomly sample 50 DL3DV scenes and estimate per-view depth and camera parameters with VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
, retaining only high-confidence depth estimates. Inspired by CAMEO
[
34
]
, we construct correspondence labels through cycle projection. A sampled source pixel is unprojected into 3D using its depth and camera parameters, then projected into a target view and assigned to a target token. We unproject the center of that target token using the target-view depth and project it back into the source view. A correspondence is retained only if the projections remain in bounds, the projected and estimated depths agree in both directions, and the return location is sufficiently close to the source sample. When multiple samples within a source token pass these checks, we retain the correspondence with the smallest cycle error. These are geometry-derived reference labels, rather than manually annotated ground truth. For the dynamic set, we use the provided ground-truth point correspondences from 30 dynamic scenes in TAPVid-DAVIS
[
15
]
.
Layer–head evaluation and selection.
We randomly sample query tokens from the input frame of each video and examine every global-attention layer–head pair. For each query, we extract the maximum-response location in each subsequent view and its target-frame attention mass, following
Eq.
1
. We compare the predicted locations with the reference correspondences to measure correspondence error and examine the associated attention masses as reliability cues. Considering correspondence consistency across both static and dynamic tokens, we select layer 13, head 10, which provides the best overall performance in this evaluation. All layer and head indices here are zero-based, and this single pair is used for training-label extraction in all experiments.
The evaluation also reveals substantial specialization across heads. For example, layer 13, head 0 captures static-token correspondences well but fails to reliably associate dynamic tokens, whereas layer 12, head 12 captures dynamic-token correspondences well but performs poorly on static tokens. Other pairs exhibit little correspondence consistency for either type of token. These observations motivate selecting a pair using both static and dynamic scenes, rather than relying on either set alone.
Limitations of projection-based labels.
The depth-and-camera cycle projection above assumes a static scene and therefore cannot directly recover correspondences for moving scene elements. We also observe substantial errors around thin structures and closely spaced surfaces, where depth errors and token discretization can associate different surfaces. These limitations can affect methods that rely on such projection-derived supervision, including CAMEO. Extracting correspondences from VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
attention instead exploits the model’s learned cross-view consistency without imposing a static-scene projection constraint. In our observations, this alleviates these failure cases and also supports correspondences for dynamic scene elements.

Human visibility annotations.
We determine the sigmoid mapping from human visibility annotations on DL3DV, using attention labels computed in an 81-frame teacher context. Of 803 judgments, we exclude 230 uncertain cases and retain 573 source-token/target-frame pairs, comprising 401 visible and 172 not-visible cases. These labels assess visibility rather than the localization accuracy of the attention maximum.

Dynamic generation.
The OmniWorld-Game adapters cover the same 0–5-second interval. Voyager and Uni3C use one 81-frame segment, with Voyager retaining its internal prefix mechanism. Camera-scale adaptation.
Warping-based methods are sensitive to camera scale because their explicit scene initialization and geometric conditioning depend on depth estimated from the first frame. Camera translations must therefore be expressed at a scale consistent with this depth; a mismatch produces an inconsistent initial scene and incorrect warps, which can propagate errors into subsequent predictions. This dependence on depth–camera scale calibration is a practical limitation of these explicit geometric methods. To provide suitable geometric inputs for a fair comparison, we carefully align camera translations with the depth scale used by each baseline, using the dataset- and model-specific corrections described below. PCA projection.
For each inspected layer and denoising step, we collect the target frame’s block-output features and project the spatial tokens onto three principal components. PCA is fitted independently for each layer–step pair, with a fixed random seed and deterministic component signs. Each projected channel is scaled using its first and 99th percentiles for RGB display. Because each projection is fitted independently, we compare the spatial organization of regions within each visualization rather than matching colors across cells. As discussed in
Section
3.1
, these maps reveal where recognizable scene structure emerges across noise levels and network depth: little coherent structure is visible in the noise-dominated region, scene regions begin to take shape in the structure-formation region, and the scene layout becomes more clearly defined in the structure-established region. The onset of recognizable structure occurs in deeper layers at higher noise and in shallower layers at lower noise. Viewed alongside the attention maps, the PCA features help distinguish the emergence of scene structure from the development of cross-frame associations, showing that attention can still favor competing regions even when the scene layout is recognizable. This joint analysis motivates placing correspondence supervision near the structure-formation stage and adapting the supervised layer to the noise timestep.
Attention readout.
At the same layer and step, we extract queries and keys after normalization and rotary positional encoding. For the fixed source query, each head’s dot-product scores are softmax-normalized over all video keys. We then retain the target-frame slice and average the resulting probabilities over heads. This readout differs from both the block-output features used for PCA and the learned aggregation MLP used during training. Target-frame responses are displayed after normalization by each map’s maximum, with color mapping and interpolation used only for visualization. Thus, the color scale indicates relative spatial response within a map, not an absolute probability shared across layers or noise levels.
The denoising axis uses the actual model noise timesteps along the sampled inference trajectory. The noise-dependent shift in structure formation motivates our layer-routing schedule, whose generation performance is evaluated against fixed-layer and alternative schedules in

Our results demonstrate that attention distillation with geometric correspondence targets improves video consistency. The current implementation extracts these targets from VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
attention, making their quality dependent on the teacher’s matching ability and spatial resolution. This raises a natural question: can more reliable correspondences further improve the effectiveness of attention distillation? Stronger correspondence estimators or complementary sources of matching evidence could provide more accurate and complete supervision, particularly for ambiguous appearance, occlusion, and moving objects. The correspondence-based formulation of
GAD
provides a basis for exploring such alternatives to the current geometry teacher.
Adaptive supervision placement.
Our noise-timestep routing improves geometric metrics over fixed-layer supervision, demonstrating the value of adapting supervision depth to the denoising state. The current layer assignment depends only on the noise timestep and remains fixed throughout training. As the video model learns, the layers that benefit most from correspondence supervision may also change. Conditioning routing jointly on noise timestep and training progress could better match supervision to the model’s evolving representations, extending the current mechanism while preserving the original inference procedure.
Extension to autoregressive video generation.
GAD
improves static and dynamic consistency in Wan’s bidirectional video models. Autoregressive video generation offers a natural next setting, where preserving scene identity over long rollouts and maintaining coherent object motion remain important challenges. The principle of guiding attention with correspondences also applies to associations between newly generated content and preceding frames. Adapting the distillation objectives to the available temporal context under causal attention could help autoregressive models retain scene structure and moving-object identity as generation proceeds. This offers a promising route to extending the benefits demonstrated here to autoregressive generation.

article.headline: 几何注意力蒸馏改善视频生成一致性
article.lede: GAD 在训练时把冻结几何模型的跨帧对应蒸馏进视频注意力，推理流程不变。
article.problem: 视频扩散模型能生成视觉上吸引人的短片段，但跨帧难以保持场景几何和物体结构。作者分析发现，视频注意力即使在场结构已经显现后，对同一场景元素的响应仍分散在多个区域，无法可靠建立跨帧对应。
article.method: GAD 从冻结的 VGGT-Ω 几何教师模型的注意力中提取干净视频的跨帧对应，并用目标帧注意力质量加权，构造软对应目标。训练时根据噪声时间步把蒸馏路由到不同深度的学生层，在结构形成阶段用成对和轨迹两种对应损失约束视频注意力；推理阶段不增加模块或计算。
article.results: 在 Wan2.2 5B 上，RealEstate10K 的跨帧匹配命中率从 0.263 升至 0.350，DL3DV-10K 从 0.257 升至 0.335，原文称两个长程基准相对提升至少 30%。OmniWorld-Game 上主体一致性由 0.825 升至 0.853，背景一致性由 0.900 升至 0.913；推理峰值显存保持 34.85 GB，运行时间 69.60 s 对 70.44 s。
article.why_it_matters: 无需改变推理流程就能把几何基础模型的对应先验注入视频扩散训练，为长时视频世界模拟和相机控制生成提供低成本一致性方案。
article.limitations: 对应目标的质量受 VGGT-Ω 匹配能力和空间分辨率限制，且层路由仅由噪声时间步决定、训练中固定；方法也只在 Wan 的双向视频模型上验证，尚未扩展到自回归生成。
article.figure_caption_zh: 冻结几何教师从干净视频提取的对应关系在去噪过程中引导视频模型注意力；该监督只在训练时加入，不改变推理流程。

page_papers.title: Spark-0: Scaling Spatially Aligned Tactile Pretraining for Robot Dexterous Manipulation
page_papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies benefit from large-scale visual pretraining but often struggle with contact-rich dexterous manipulation, where force, compliance, and incipient slip are hard to observe from images. We present Spark-0, a spatially aligned vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) model that uses touch in two complementary ways. During pretraining, image-space contact maps derived from tactile gloves, together with features from a frozen 3D geometry teacher, supervise the visual tokens; these objectives are removed at inference. In parallel, a tactile pathway encodes regional force histories and 3D taxel states to condition the action expert. A single checkpoint therefore supports both vision-only and tactile-conditioned deployment. To scale this supervision, we build HumanTouch, a 1,000-hour dataset of full-hand tactile human manipulation, and pretrain Spark-0 on it together with egocentric video, robot data, and simulation. We also release SparkArena, which pairs vision-only simulated tasks with tactile-conditioned real-robot tasks on one dexterous embodiment. Spark-0 achieves the highest mean success rate on both SparkArena tracks and ranks first on all eight aggregate metrics of the Ego Humanoid Manipulation Benchmark. Compared with vision-only pretraining on the same data and compute with touch discarded, retaining the touch of 1,000 hours of HumanTouch raises vision-only success on Ego Humanoid from 52.5% to 71.7%, and success on SparkArena-Real, where touch is also used at deployment, from 44.0% to 52.0%, indicating that touch serves not only as a policy input but also as scalable supervision for dexterous visuomotor pretraining. The Website is available at: https://xsparkai.com/Spark-0.

article.headline: 用触觉做预训练：Spark-0 提升灵巧操作
article.lede: 把触觉同时当作监督信号和策略输入，Spark-0 在视觉-触觉-语言-动作预训练上验证了这条路线。
article.problem: 通用机器人策略受益于大规模视觉预训练，但在接触密集的灵巧操作中仍显吃力：力、柔顺性和初始滑移这些关键量很难从图像中观测到。现有视觉预训练没有为这类接触信息提供监督信号，导致模型在需要精细力控的任务上表现受限。
article.method: 作者提出 Spark-0，一个空间对齐的视觉-触觉-语言-动作模型，用两种互补方式利用触觉。预训练阶段，由触觉手套得到的图像空间接触图，以及一个冻结的 3D 几何教师特征，共同监督视觉 token，这些目标在推理时被移除；同时一条独立的触觉通路编码分区力历史和 3D taxel 状态，用来条件化动作专家，因此单个 checkpoint 同时支持纯视觉和触觉条件部署。为支撑这一监督规模，团队构建了 1,000 小时全手触觉人类操作数据集 HumanTouch，并与第一人称视频、机器人数据和仿真数据联合预训练，另发布 SparkArena 基准，在同一灵巧本体上把纯视觉仿真任务与触觉条件真机任务配对。
article.results: Spark-0 在 SparkArena 两个赛道均取得最高平均成功率，并在 Ego Humanoid Manipulation Benchmark 的全部八项汇总指标上排名第一（论文未给出具体数值）。在与相同数据、相同算力但丢弃触觉的纯视觉预训练对比中，保留 1,000 小时 HumanTouch 的触觉使 Ego Humanoid 的纯视觉成功率从 52.5% 提升到 71.7%；在部署阶段同样使用触觉的 SparkArena-Real 上，成功率从 44.0% 提升到 52.0%。架构上，每只手使用 320 个 taxel 的 3D 状态与分区力流，最终压缩为 24 个触觉 token。
article.why_it_matters: 结果表明触觉不只是部署时的策略输入，还可以作为一种可扩展的监督信号，用于灵巧视觉运动预训练。这为「接触密集任务需要额外模态预训练」提供了一个可复用的数据与训练范式。
article.limitations: 主要证据来自作者自建的 HumanTouch 与 SparkArena，触觉监督源自手套采集的人类数据，到机器人本体存在具身差距；论文也未给出 SparkArena 平均成功率的具体数值和跨本体迁移的定量结果。
article.figure_caption_zh: Spark-0 架构：Qwen3-VL 条件化流匹配动作专家，偶数层对 VLM 做交叉注意力、奇数层在状态-触觉-动作 token 上自注意力，所有层使用力条件 AdaLN，原始触觉绕过 VLM 经独立通路生成 24 个触觉 token。

figure.caption: {Spark-0 architecture.} {(a)} Qwen3-VL conditions a flow-matching action expert; train-only objectives align visual tokens, and raw touch bypasses the VLM. {(b)} Even layers cross-attend to the VLM; odd layers self-attend over State--Tactile--Action tokens. All layers use force-conditioned AdaLN. {(c)} Regional force and 3D taxel ($320$ per hand) streams yield $24$ tactile tokens. {(d)} The VLM column is even-layer cross-attention, including the training shortcut; the other columns are odd-layer self-attention. Details are in Appendix~ {app:architecture_details}.

page_papers.title: SPARC: Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus
page_papers.abstract: Speech anonymization has focused on the acoustic signal, leaving open how much speaker information the transcribed words themselves retain. In this work, we study pairwise speaker and demographic-attribute verification from transcribed speech. We introduce SPARC (Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus), a benchmark built from two podcast corpora comprising over 12,500 speakers, 1.5M quality-filtered utterances, and speaker-level inferred or source-provided labels for sex, age, and accent, and evaluate five attribution models and three LLMs on identity- and attribute-verification trials with episode- and metadata-based topic proxies. LLM adversaries distinguish same-speaker pairs from text alone. Attribute-label agreement is harder to verify, but LLMs perform sex- and accent-label verification above chance. Finally, releasing only short probe texts (50 words) degrades the strongest adversaries the most, offering a partial reduction in observed linkage.
page_papers.content:
SPARC: Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus
Efthymios Tsaprazlis  Bowen Yi   Tiantian Feng
Email:
tsaprazl@usc.edu
Junghwan Kim   David Jurgens   Shrikanth Narayanan
University of Southern California   University of Michigan
Abstract
Speech anonymization has focused on the acoustic signal, leaving open how much speaker information the transcribed words themselves retain. In this work, we study pairwise speaker and demographic-attribute verification from transcribed speech. We introduce
SPARC
(Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus), a benchmark built from two podcast corpora comprising over 12,500 speakers, 1.5M quality-filtered utterances, and speaker-level inferred or source-provided labels for sex, age, and accent, and evaluate five attribution models and three LLMs on identity- and attribute-verification trials with episode- and metadata-based topic proxies. LLM adversaries distinguish same-speaker pairs from text alone. Attribute-label agreement is harder to verify, but LLMs perform sex- and accent-label verification above chance. Finally, releasing only short probe texts (50 words) degrades the strongest adversaries the most, offering a partial reduction in observed linkage.
1
1
1
Our code and data are available at
https://huggingface.co/datasets/timtsapras23/SPARC
and
https://github.com/bowenyi-pierre/SPARC
.
1
Introduction
Conversational language is one of the most abundant forms of personal data. People speak to voice assistants, dictate messages, attend recorded meetings, and publish podcasts; even much social-media text approaches the register of speech. Regulatory frameworks have responded to the acoustic side of this reality: under the GDPR
Regulation (2016)
, voice recordings constitute biometric personal data, and voiceprint-based speaker recognition is treated as a well-understood re-identification risk
(
Nautsch et al., 2019
;
Tigunova et al., 2020
)
. Far less attention has been paid to what lies beyond acoustic signals, to the words and phrases themselves, and how language is being used.
Transcription is often understood as separating
what
was said from
how
it sounded, and this distinction carries privacy weight: once pitch, timbre, and other acoustic characteristics are removed, conventional speaker-recognition systems no longer apply. Yet a transcript preserves word choice, syntax, discourse markers, and conversational habits, and these linguistic traces may suffice to link an anonymous transcript to a known speaker or to infer sensitive characteristics of that speaker
(
Aggazzotti et al., 2024
)
. Prior work shows that speakers can be distinguished in human-transcribed conversations and that attribution survives ASR errors
(
Aggazzotti et al., 2024
;
Aggazzotti et al., 2025
)
, but reports that performance declines under conversational topic controls. Whether this pattern holds against modern LLM adversaries, and whether
demographic attribute labels
can be verified alongside identity, remain open questions.
To answer them, we introduce
SPARC
(Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus), a transcript-privacy benchmark built from two large-scale podcast corpora comprising over 12,500 speakers, 1.5M quality-filtered utterances, and speaker-level inferred or source-provided labels for sex, age, and accent. SPARC pairs speaker- and attribute-verification trials under a unified protocol, using episode- and metadata-based topic proxies to assess speaker-linked information in transcripts.
Our comprehensive benchmark results show that transcribed speech
retains speaker-linked information.
Overall, embedding-based attackers degrade in the within-episode condition (0.350 to 0.460 EER, approaching the 0.5 chance rate), but LLM adversaries retain speaker-verification signal in the same setting (0.322–0.345 EER) and reach 0.253–0.285 EER in the cross-episode condition on both corpora. Moreover, LLMs detect agreement on inferred sex and accent labels more reliably than the embedding models, while age-label agreement stays near chance. We further trace how leakage scales with the adversary’s resources. Shortening the exposed probe text degrades the strongest attackers the most. Even an adversary with extensive reference material is bottlenecked by the probe. Limiting the amount of released text is thus a partial mitigation, although it attenuates rather than eliminates leakage. Finally, we show that average-case metrics could misstate the threat. Specifically, at a 1% false-positive rate, two LLMs with nearly identical AUC and EER differ by more than
2
×
2\times
in the fraction of positive trials they accept, so the models that matter most for privacy are not captured by AUC or EER alone.
Our contributions are: (i) SPARC, a large-scale benchmark dataset for pairwise speaker and attribute-label verification in transcribed natural speech, with standardized trials across probe-length and enrollment budgets; (ii) a systematic evaluation of embedding-based and LLM adversaries showing that LLMs retain speaker-verification signal under episode-context controls; (iii) evidence that attribute-label agreement remains difficult to verify, though LLMs detect a coarse sex- and accent-label signal; (iv) ablations showing that limiting exposed text degrades LLM attackers even under extensive enrollment, offering a practical but partial mitigation; and (v) a low-FPR analysis demonstrating that average-case metrics mischaracterize trial-level linkage risk, with implications for how transcript privacy should be evaluated.
2
Related Work
2.1
Text-Based Authorship Attribution and Verification
Recent authorship attribution and verification systems learn author representations that transfer across documents and domains. LUAR, for instance, learns general-purpose author embeddings for open-set verification
(
Rivera-Soto et al., 2021
)
. A persistent concern is that such representations may encode what an author discusses rather than how they use language, motivating content-independent style representations, topic-regularized training, and probing studies that separate stylistic from topical information
(
Wegmann et al., 2022
;
Sawatphol et al., 2022
;
Wang et al., 2023
)
. Most recently, LLMs have been applied to zero-shot, end-to-end verification and, beyond pairwise verification, to identity linking, extracting identity-relevant cues from unstructured profiles to retrieve candidate users across platforms
(
Huang et al., 2024
;
Lermen et al., 2026
)
.
A parallel line of work provides datasets and benchmarks for authorship analysis. VALLA standardizes datasets, splits, and metrics to compare attribution and verification methods
(
Tyo et al., 2023
)
, and RAVEN tests whether verification models exploit topic-dependent shortcuts
(
Sawatphol et al., 2024
)
. Closer to our setting, HANSEN aggregates 17 human speech-transcript datasets, along with AI-generated spoken text, for attribution, verification, and human–AI detection
(
Tripto et al., 2023
)
. Most directly,
Aggazzotti et al. (2024)
construct speaker-verification trials from human-transcribed conversations and find that performance declines once conversational topic is controlled; follow-up work examines how ASR errors affect transcript-based attribution
(
Aggazzotti et al., 2025
)
. Text-only verification on VoicePrivacy data also reveals speaker-linked cues, partly through semantic keyword overlap
(
Gaznepoglu et al., 2025
)
. SPARC complements these resources with large-scale, naturally occurring podcast transcripts, episode- and metadata-based controls, and a single protocol to evaluate speaker verification and attribute-label agreement.
2.2
Personal Attribute Inference from Text
Early efforts in author profiling focused on developing feature-based and neural classifiers for age and gender prediction, such as in the PAN author-profiling shared tasks
(
Rangel et al., 2013
)
.
Recent work reframes this capability as a privacy risk:
Staab et al. (2024)
show on PersonalReddit, a manually annotated dataset of 520 real Reddit profiles with eight attributes, that pretrained LLMs can infer personal information from text without relying on verbatim training-data memorization. Because the underlying profiles are sensitive, the dataset is not publicly released, making dataset construction a central challenge in this area. RedDust labels more than 300,000 Reddit users with profession, hobby, family status, age, and gender using high-precision self-disclosure patterns
(
Tigunova et al., 2020
)
, while SynthPAI uses LLM agents seeded with synthetic profiles to generate over 7,800 Reddit-like comments annotated with personal attributes, yielding a public, privacy-preserving benchmark whose conclusions are validated against real data
(
Yukhymenko et al., 2024
)
. These resources offer either broad scale or wide attribute inventories, but all concern authored social-media text, leaving attribute leakage in transcribed speech unexplored.
2.3
Speech and Text Anonymization
VoicePrivacy studies acoustic anonymization while preserving linguistic content
(
Tomashenko et al., 2024
)
. Text-anonymization work evaluates authorship obfuscation and privacy–utility trade-offs
(
Loiseau et al., 2025a
;
Loiseau et al., 2025b
;
Loiseau et al., 2026
;
Aggazzotti et al., 2026
)
. SPARC evaluates existing transcripts rather than transforming them.
3
Dataset
3.1
Source Corpora
The SPARC dataset is drawn from two publicly available large-scale English podcast datasets.
NaturalVoices
(
Du et al., 2025
)
is a dataset of 5,049 hours of spontaneous podcast speech sourced from MSP-Podcast recordings, including meta-information at the utterance level with speaker identity, sex, speech quality, and transcripts. In total, the dataset has over 2,670 speakers across 6,790 episodes. We use only single-speaker speech segments from episodes released with a CC-BY 4.0 license, and we adopt the age and sex labels provided in the original metadata.
SPoRC
(
Litterer et al., 2025
)
consists of over 1.1 million English podcast episodes collected from public RSS feeds between May and June 2020. Furthermore, it has a machine-diarized subset of over 220,000 hours that identifies 386,000 hosts and 535,000 guests. Because SPoRC does not provide utterance-level speaker metadata, we use its provided single-speaker episode subset. To control speech volume variation, we retain only the middle 50% of episodes by transcript word count. We derive all demographic labels through automatic inference using speech data (Section
3.3
). Together, NaturalVoices offers richer utterance-level annotations, and the retained SPoRC subset broadens speaker and episode coverage.
3.2
Spoken Language Data Filtering
We apply a unified multi-stage data cleaning pipeline to both corpora. First, utterances with an SNR
≥
\geq
15 dB are kept for the remaining processing to ensure the quality of transcription. Specifically, we estimated SNR via WADA-SNR
Kim and Stern (2008)
for NaturalVoices and Brouhaha
Lavechin et al. (2023)
;
Bredin et al. (2020)
for SPoRC. Second, podcast recordings often contain background music, which could confound our subsequent analyses. Therefore, segments with background music are removed using an Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST) classifier
(
Gong et al., 2021
)
, retaining only utterances whose summed probability over 97 music-related categories from the AudioSet ontology
(
Gemmeke et al., 2017
)
is
≤
\leq
0.1. Third, we use agreement between two state-of-the-art ASR models, Whisper-large-v3
Radford et al. (2022)
and nvidia/canary-qwen-2.5b
Puvvada et al. (2024)
, as a reference-free proxy for transcription reliability. Notably, these two models achieved top-ranked positions on the Open ASR Leaderboard
Srivastav et al. (2026)
. Let
w
⁡
(
a
,
b
)
w(a,b)
denote the word error rate of hypothesis
a

against reference
b

; we retain a segment only if
max

, using the symmetric maximum to penalize disagreement in either direction.
Transcripts from the Canary model are used as the final transcript for SPARC.
3.3
Speaker Attribute Inference
For NaturalVoices, we take the age and sex labels from the dataset, which are inferred by a pretrained model
Burkhardt et al. (2023)
. For SPoRC, we infer age and sex using Vox-Profile
Feng et al. (2025b)
, a speech foundation-model benchmark that provides state-of-the-art classifiers for speaker traits. Accent labels in NaturalVoices and SPoRC are inferred with Voxlect
Feng et al. (2025a)
, a benchmark for dialect classification including English. Utterance-level accent is predicted by a Whisper-large-v3 model over 16 English dialect classes. On the other hand, age and sex are predicted jointly by a WavLM-large model.
We aggregate to the speaker level by averaging the predicted probability vectors across all retained utterances from the same speaker and selecting the highest-scoring class for accent and sex; age is averaged directly. Dataset statistics of SPARC are reported in Table
1
. We find that there are slightly more male speakers in both sub-datasets. Moreover, most speakers are inferred to age between 30 to 60, whereas SPoRC contains a notably larger proportion of younger speakers (<30: 36.3% vs. 15.7%). On the other hand, North American accent accounts for roughly 77–78% of speakers in both datasets, but the remaining speakers span 15 other English dialect categories with none exceeding 6%. As a result, we binarize accent classes to North American vs. Other.
Three independent annotators judged 50 recordings per attribute, sampled to balance the attribute categories. Model–majority agreement was 98% for sex, 88% for accent, and 64% for age (Appendix
A.5
).

4
Evaluation
4.1
Problem Setup
We aim to investigate whether spoken language can provide information to characterize an individual’s identity or personal attributes. To this end, we formulate our problem similarly to established approaches in the Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV), adapting two evaluation tasks from VoxGuard
Tsaprazlis et al. (2026)
(measuring
User Privacy
and
Attribute Privacy
). Concretely, we consider an adversarial setting in which the goal is to determine whether two sets of utterances originate from the same speaker, or whether they are produced by speakers sharing a specific inferred attribute label (e.g. sex). The adversary is provided with an
enrollment
set, used to construct reference representations and a
probe
utterance whose underlying identity or attribute membership is unknown. These are pairwise verification tasks, not identification from a population.

Trial Generation
We construct verification trials from NaturalVoices and SPoRC for four verification tasks:
speaker identity
,
sex
,
age group
, and
accent
. Throughout, a
podcast series
contains multiple
episodes
; we use
podcast
to refer to a single episode. For each (speaker/attribute, podcast) pair, we form a probe by traversing the transcript from the beginning and accumulating complete utterances until its length falls within

Easy Positives
pair the same speaker within the same podcast,
Hard Positives
pair the same speaker across podcasts,
Easy Negatives
pair different speakers across podcasts, and
Hard Negatives
pair different speakers within the same podcast. In NaturalVoices, the single-speaker constraint applies to segments rather than episodes: episodes may contain multiple speakers, enabling all four trial conditions. The retained SPoRC episodes contain only one speaker and therefore support only
Hard Positives
and
Easy Negatives
. For attribute tasks, positive and negative labels analogously indicate whether the two speakers share the evaluated attribute label. For reporting, we call within-episode trials
same-topic
and cross-episode trials
different-topic
. These are episode-based proxies because NaturalVoices lacks topic annotations or descriptions, and within-episode texts are expected to share more context. Comparing the conditions tests whether performance persists after controlling for episode co-membership.
This design serves two purposes. First, it allows us to measure model performance separately under easy and hard conditions and identify where models struggle. More importantly, it provides a diagnostic for spurious topical correlations: when probe and enrollment texts come from the same podcast, a model may perform well by exploiting shared content rather than speaker-specific linguistic style.
Across all SPoRC verification tasks, we control for topic by limiting episode-title/description similarity and matching positive and negative trials by this similarity and podcast category overlap. Speaker-verification negatives are additionally matched on sex, age group, and accent group. Full details and trial counts are provided in Appendix
A.1
.
4.3
Model Scoring
We evaluate eight models grouped by scoring approach. Five are representation-based baselines: four pretrained neural encoders—SentenceBERT
(
Reimers and Gurevych, 2019
)
, PCM
(
Kim et al., 2025
)
, CISR
(
Wegmann et al., 2022
)
, and LUAR
(
Rivera-Soto et al., 2021
)
—and a lexical TF–IDF
(
Sparck Jones, 1972
)
baseline. These methods construct representations of the probe and enrollment texts and score each trial using cosine similarity. The remaining three models are prompted LLMs: GPT-5-mini, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, and Qwen3.5-9B. For each trial, we provide the probe and enrollment utterances and ask the model to return a score from 0 to 100 indicating the likelihood that the speakers share the same identity or evaluated attribute. Exact prompt templates and scoring details are provided in Appendix
A.2
.
4.4
Evaluation Metrics
We report three complementary metrics that probe different regions of the ROC curve. Our primary metric is the
Equal Error Rate (EER)
: the error rate at the operating point where the false acceptance and false rejection rates coincide (lower is better; chance corresponds to 0.5). EER characterizes a concrete operating point rather than an average over thresholds, and it is not inflated by skewed positive-to-negative trial ratios, a property we rely on for the imbalanced accent trials. We additionally report
AUC
, the probability that a randomly chosen positive pair receives a higher score than a randomly chosen negative pair, as a complementary rank-based summary of overall separability. Because neither metric reflects the stringent operating points at which re-identification becomes consequential, we follow
Tsaprazlis et al. (2026)
and report
TPR@FPR
at 1% and 0.1% false-positive rates, the fraction of positive trials accepted at thresholds with the stated false-positive rates.

5.2
Attribute Verification
We next ask whether transcripts support inferred demographic-label verification, evaluating sex, age, and accent under the same three conditions. As before, we focus on SentenceBERT as the representative embedding-based model and on GPT-5-mini and Llama-3.3-70B. We report results on NaturalVoices here; on the SPoRC attribute trials models show similar behavior, and that analysis, together with full results for all systems, is provided in Appendix
A.3
.
5.2.1
Sex-Label Verification
Verification on sex reveals a sharp divide between model families. Embedding-based models operate near chance across all conditions, with SentenceBERT EERs of 0.468–0.508, indicating little separation on this label-verification task.
Instead, GPT-5-mini and Llama-3.3-70B reach 0.377 and 0.420 EER in the realistic different-topic setting. Moreover, they retain this advantage under the same-topic control (0.437 and 0.422 EER). Their performance in the within-episode comparison suggests a modest label-agreement signal, although the responsible linguistic cues remain unclear.
5.2.2
Age Group
The benchmark results show that age-group agreement is the most difficult attribute task, where performance remains near chance in all three main conditions. The best EERs are only 0.447 in the different-topic and 0.440 in the same-topic condition, both from PCM (Table
11
); among the main-text models, GPT-5-mini reaches 0.459 in the different-topic setting. Embedding-model AUCs in the different-topic setting range from 0.517 to 0.556, and Llama-3.3-70B falls below chance in the combined condition (0.546 EER, 0.433 AUC), suggesting a systematic bias in its age judgments rather than useful sensitivity. Given these small and inconsistent effects, we find no reliable evidence that the tested systems can verify age-group agreement from transcripts.
5.2.3
Accent/Dialect
Accent yields the clearest two-tier separation of all attributes. Embedding-based models sit at chance in the different-topic setting (0.494 EER for SentenceBERT; 0.494–0.534 AUC across the embedding baselines) and gain little in the within-episode condition. LLMs, by contrast, extract a markedly stronger signal. For example, GPT-5-mini achieves a 0.268 EER (0.771 AUC) in the different-topic setting and 0.350 under the same-topic control; Llama-3.3-70B reaches 0.320 and 0.332 EER, the best same-topic result. These results show agreement on accent labels, but do not identify which linguistic cues the LLMs use. Because the task uses an imbalanced North American vs. non–North-American distinction, these results do not establish performance on individual dialects but only on this binary coarse distinction.

6
Conclusion
We introduced SPARC, a large-scale benchmark for pairwise speaker and attribute verification from speech transcripts and evaluated five attribution models and three LLMs across four verification tasks. Our results show that speaker-linked information persists under the evaluated episode and metadata controls. Removing the acoustic signal therefore does not completely remove the speaker information and speech privacy evaluations should consider linguistic content as well as voice. Moreover, attribute agreement remains challenging to verify, with a modest signal for biological sex and accent labels, while age-group agreement is near chance for every system. Shorter transcripts reduce speaker-verification performance, especially for the strongest models, but do not eliminate it. Moreover, similar EER and AUC scores can conceal large differences in trial-level TPR at low false-positive rates.
We hope SPARC supports the development and evaluation of transcript-level privacy defenses.
Limitations
Data Scope
SPARC contains only English podcast speech and retains relatively clean, single-speaker segments through SNR, music, and dual-ASR-agreement filters. The findings may therefore not generalize to noisier or overlapping speech, other conversational domains, or multilingual and code-switched settings.
Attribute Labels and Accent Evaluation
SPARC’s sex, age, and accent labels are model-derived rather than independently verified demographics. The category-balanced, 50-recording audit measures perceptual consistency on a small selected sample, not corpus-wide accuracy; agreement is weakest for age. Attribute results therefore measure agreement with proxy labels. Approximately 77–78% of speakers are assigned a North American accent, and no other individual dialect exceeds 6%, motivating the North American/Other grouping. This imbalanced binary task cannot support conclusions about fine-grained accent verification, especially for lower-resourced dialects
(
Pan et al., 2025
)
. Negative pairs also constitute only 19% of the combined NaturalVoices accent trials, reducing statistical precision. A more balanced corpus is needed for individual-dialect evaluation.
Model and Score Scope
We evaluate three LLMs using a single zero-shot scoring prompt. Because of inference cost, we obtain one response per LLM-trial pair and therefore do not quantify variability across repeated generations. In addition, we notice that LLMs’ uncalibrated 0–100 scores often cluster at a few rounded values, limiting ROC resolution at low FPR. The findings are therefore specific to the evaluated model–prompt configurations; calibrated or likelihood-based scoring could produce different rankings.
Linguistic Cue Attribution
We do not attribute individual decisions to lexical, syntactic, discourse, stylistic, or ASR-derived cues. Such analysis is needed to separate speaker habits from residual context, particularly for the coarse accent-label result.
Scope of Topic Control
For NaturalVoices, episode membership is only a proxy for topical overlap: one episode may span multiple topics, while different episodes may discuss similar subjects. The within- and cross-episode conditions therefore control episode context rather than semantic topic identity. For SPoRC, title/description filtering and category matching provide additional metadata-based proxies but cannot eliminate residual topical overlap. In the original SPoRC speaker protocol, 81.4% of positive trials are within-series whereas all negatives cross series; the additional cross-series control reduces this imbalance and yields higher EERs. Neither analysis isolates speaker style from correlated textual cues, including personal facts and speaker-relevant ASR errors
(
Aggazzotti et al., 2024
)
.
Ethical Considerations
SPARC is intended to audit privacy leakage from speech transcripts, but the capabilities it evaluates are inherently dual use. The recordings were collected from publicly available podcast feeds; for NaturalVoices, we retain only episodes released under CC-BY 4.0. Nevertheless, public availability does not imply that speakers anticipated automated linkage or demographic profiling. We therefore position SPARC as a resource for privacy research and discourage its use in forensic, law-enforcement, employment, eligibility, or other high-stakes decisions.
Because SPoRC does not provide verified age, sex, or accent labels, we use Vox-Profile and Voxlect as reproducible proxies
(
Feng et al., 2025b
;
Feng et al., 2025a
)
. Vox-Profile’s strongest models report 98.0% accuracy for binary speaker-sex classification and 69.5% for three-way age-group classification, while the Voxlect Whisper-Large model used in our study reports 83.0% accuracy for English dialect classification. We reduce utterance-level noise by averaging predictions across each speaker’s retained utterances and report a small perceptual audit in Appendix
A.5
. These labels nevertheless remain model-inferred, and source-benchmark performance or agreement on a selected audit sample may not transfer fully to SPARC. The binary sex and coarse age and accent categories should therefore not be interpreted as verified demographic identities. We use them only for trial construction and aggregate analysis, not for downstream profiling or individual-level decisions. Any reuse should preserve their inferred provenance and comply with the source licenses, Voxlect’s Responsible AI License, and applicable privacy requirements.
